shard.title: The South Atlantic, the Antarctic, the outposts, and the empire without a flag
shard.author: South Atlantic, Antarctic and outposts historian
shard.note: Three things the pink map leaves out. First, the South Atlantic and Antarctic possessions Britain still holds. Second, informal empire: the places Britain controlled through debt, tariffs, railways and consular courts without ever colouring them pink. Third, the short-lived holdings, taken and lost, that prove the imperial map was never fixed. The shard region is 'empire-wide' because these territories sit on five continents; each territory carries its own region for the legend. Havana 1762-63 and Willoughbyland are covered as territories in the Caribbean shard; the events here attach to those records rather than duplicating them.

territories.name: Saint Helena
territories.formalName: Colony of Saint Helena and its Dependencies

namesOverTime.name: Santa Helena

from.note: Portuguese sailors named the island after St Helena of Constantinople; the sighting is traditionally dated 21 May 1502 and credited to Joao da Nova, but the log does not survive and some accounts give 1501 or 1503.

namesOverTime.note: The Portuguese watered and grazed there for 150 years and deliberately kept its position secret. They never settled it.

geoCoverage.label: The island itself
geoCoverage.change: A volcanic cone of 122 square kilometres, 1,950 kilometres from Africa and 2,900 from Brazil. Its extent has never changed; what changed was what Britain used it for.

acquisitions.how: The East India Company, wanting a watering station on the homeward run from Asia, sent Captain John Dutton with about 30 settlers and a few enslaved people to fortify the only landing place and grow food for passing ships.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: St Helena is one of a handful of places in this atlas where 'empty' is literally true. It is 1,950 kilometres from the nearest continent, was never reached by any pre-modern seafaring people, and had no human inhabitants until the Portuguese began leaving goats and the occasional marooned sailor after 1502.

counterparties.name: The Dutch East India Company
counterparties.lost: The Dutch had formally claimed the island in 1633 and used it as a refreshment stop; the English settlement pre-empted their plan to fortify it, and they took it back by force for four months in 1673.
counterparties.note: The Dutch preference for the Cape after 1652 is why they never garrisoned St Helena, and why an English company could simply move in.

instrument.name: Charter of the East India Company under the Protectorate, and letters patent of Charles II, 1661
instrument.note: Cromwell's Council of State approved the plantation in 1658 and Dutton sailed in 1659; Charles II confirmed the Company's title after the Restoration, and granted it again in December 1673 after the island was retaken from the Dutch.

people.name: John Dutton
people.role: first governor; landed the settlers and built the fort above the bay that became Jamestown

people.name: Richard Munden
people.role: captain who retook the island from the Dutch in May 1673 by landing men at Prosperous Bay behind the defences

acquisitions.resistance: There was nobody on the island to resist. The only fighting was between Europeans: the Dutch took the fort in the winter of 1672-73 and Munden took it back in May 1673.

evidence.author: Stephen A. Royle
evidence.work: The Company's Island: St Helena, Company Colonies and the Colonial Endeavour
evidence.supports: The East India Company's purpose in settling the island and how it governed it.

to.note: Accounts date the Dutch capture to either late December 1672 or the first days of January 1673.

statusPeriods.label: East India Company plantation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London shareholder company owned the island, appointed the governor, fixed the price of everything and forbade settlers to trade with passing ships except through its own stores.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jamestown, under the Court of Directors in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The governor and a council of Company servants ruled; planters petitioned and mutinied instead, twice, in 1684 and 1693.

from.note: Accounts date the Dutch capture to either late December 1672 or the first days of January 1673.

statusPeriods.label: Dutch occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Dutch squadron drove the Company's people off the island and held it for about five months, until an English fleet landed men at night behind the defences and took it back.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Occupied by another power: British authority on St Helena was nil for these months. The status is 'occupied' with degree 0, as the model prescribes for enemy occupation.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Dutch East India Company at the Cape

statusPeriods.label: East India Company colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Company ran a fortified market garden: it owned the land, licensed the ships, held people in slavery on its own plantations, and charged the Royal Navy for water.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jamestown, under the Court of Directors in London
statusPeriods.franchise: No elections of any kind. Enslaved people were about a third of the population through the eighteenth century and had no legal standing at all.
statusPeriods.note: Slavery on St Helena was ended in stages by the Company itself: Governor Alexander Beatson's order of 1818 freed all children born after Christmas Day 1818, and the last people held in slavery were freed in the 1830s.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown took the island off the Company under the India Act of 1833, cut the garrison, sacked most of the establishment and ran it through a governor with a nominated council answering to the Colonial Office.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jamestown, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: An elected Legislative Council came only in 1967, after a century and a half of Crown rule. Universal adult suffrage arrived with it.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1840 and 1874 the island housed the Royal Navy's depot for Africans freed from captured slave ships, and between 1900 and 1902 a prisoner-of-war camp for Boer combatants.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: St Helena governs its own internal affairs through an elected Legislative Council; Britain appoints the governor, pays most of the budget and keeps defence and foreign affairs.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jamestown, with a UK-appointed governor
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage. St Helenians lost the right to live in Britain under the British Nationality Act 1981 and got it back under the British Overseas Territories Act 2002.
statusPeriods.note: Ascension and Tristan da Cunha are governed as dependencies of St Helena, and since 2009 the three have been legally equal parts of one territory.

departures.how: St Helena has never left. It has been continuously under British authority since 1659 apart from five months of Dutch occupation in 1673, which makes it one of the oldest British possessions anywhere.

stillBritish.note: St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha form one British Overseas Territory of about 4,700 people, with its capital at Jamestown and an airport, opened in 2016, that cost the British taxpayer roughly 285 million pounds.

slavery.note: The East India Company held people in slavery on St Helena from the 1650s, mostly Malagasy and Indian, and then from 1840 the same island became the Royal Navy's depot for Africans taken off intercepted slave ships. Both facts are true and they sit sixty years apart.

emancipationDate.note: Governor Beatson's order freed all children born from Christmas Day 1818; people already enslaved were freed gradually over the following two decades, ahead of the imperial Act of 1833.

toll.note: This range counts Africans landed at Rupert's Valley between 1840 and 1872 from ships condemned by the Vice-Admiralty court, not people enslaved by the Company. Andrew Pearson's study of the depot gives about 25,000 to 27,000 landed and roughly 5,000 dead within weeks of arrival.

warrant.author: Andrew Pearson
warrant.work: Distant Freedom: St Helena and the Abolition of the Slave Trade, 1840-1872
warrant.supports: This range counts Africans landed at Rupert's Valley between 1840 and 1872 from ships condemned by the Vice-Admiralty court, not people enslaved by the Company.
warrant.check: Liverpool University Press, 2016. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Three separate forced movements passed through one small island: enslaved Malagasy and Indian people brought in by the Company, about 26,000 Africans landed from captured slavers after 1840, and some 5,000 Boer prisoners of war between 1900 and 1902.

violence.note: St Helena was a prison as much as a colony: Napoleon from 1815 to 1821, the Zulu king Dinuzulu kaCetshwayo from 1890 to 1897, Boer prisoners from 1900, and three Bahraini nationalists from 1957 to 1961.

consequences.economicLegacy: The island's economy died twice: when steamships and the Suez Canal removed the reason to stop there after 1869, and again in 1966 when the British Post Office stopped buying St Helena flax for mailbags and the last mill closed.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English law, an Anglican cathedral built in 1774, and a population descended from English settlers, enslaved Malagasy and Indian people, Chinese labourers hired by the Company and Africans freed from slave ships.

peak.populationNote: The 1901 figure includes roughly 5,000 Boer prisoners of war and the garrison guarding them; the resident population was around 3,300. The 2021 census counted 4,439 residents.

evidence.supports: Company rule, the island's economy and its transfer to the Crown in 1834.

evidence.author: Andrew Pearson
evidence.work: Distant Freedom: St Helena and the Abolition of the Slave Trade, 1840-1872
evidence.supports: The Liberated African Depot at Rupert's Valley, the numbers landed and the mortality there.

evidence.author: Philip Gosse
evidence.work: St Helena 1502-1938
evidence.supports: The long narrative of the island from Portuguese sighting to the twentieth century.

contested.note: The number of Africans landed at Rupert's Valley is an estimate built from Vice-Admiralty court records that are incomplete, and the death toll there rests partly on the 325 burials excavated in 2007-08 during construction of the airport access road. Both figures are ranges, not counts.

pedagogy.hook: More Africans are buried in one valley on St Helena than there are people living on the whole island today.

misconception.belief: St Helena matters because Napoleon died there.
misconception.correction: Napoleon was on the island for five and a half years. The Royal Navy's Liberated African Depot at Rupert's Valley ran for thirty-two, landed something like 26,000 people taken off intercepted slave ships, and buried around 5,000 of them in the valley floor. Excavations for the airport road in 2007-08 found 325 of those graves.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: St Helena shows both faces of the same empire on one small island: a company that held people in slavery for 160 years, and then a naval depot that freed 26,000 people from other people's slave ships and let a fifth of them die of dysentery on arrival. Neither fact cancels the other.

Napoleon arrives under guard

territories.name: Ascension Island
territories.formalName: Ascension Island, a dependency of St Helena

namesOverTime.name: Ilha da Ascensao
namesOverTime.note: Named by Afonso de Albuquerque, who sighted it on Ascension Day 1503. An earlier sighting by Joao da Nova in 1501 is often claimed but poorly evidenced.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Eighty-eight square kilometres of clinker and cinder cones, 1,300 kilometres north-west of St Helena and 1,600 from Africa. Nobody had ever lived there.

acquisitions.how: One week after Napoleon landed on St Helena, the Royal Navy put a detachment of marines ashore on Ascension so that no rescue expedition could use it as a base, and then kept it for the next two centuries.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Ascension is a mid-ocean volcano roughly one million years old, 1,600 kilometres from the African coast. There is no archaeological evidence of any human presence before the Portuguese, and no fresh water at sea level. Taking it deprived nobody of anything.

counterparties.name: The United States and France as naval rivals
counterparties.lost: Both had used the island as an unclaimed watering and turtling stop; the garrison closed it to them and made the mid-Atlantic a British lake for the rest of the century.
counterparties.note: American whalers had been the heaviest users of Ascension's green turtles before 1815.

people.name: Edward Nicolls
people.role: Royal Marines officer who commanded the first garrison and began the works at Georgetown

people.name: Joseph Dalton Hooker
people.role: botanist who visited in 1843 and designed the deliberate afforestation of Green Mountain, planting a cloud forest on a bare volcano

acquisitions.resistance: None was possible; there was nobody there.

evidence.author: Duff Hart-Davis
evidence.work: Ascension: The Story of a South Atlantic Island
evidence.supports: The 1815 garrisoning, the naval administration and the greening of Green Mountain.

statusPeriods.label: Run by the Admiralty as a ship: HMS Ascension
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Admiralty rated the island as a sloop-of-war and commissioned it as HMS Ascension. Everyone on it was on a ship's books, ranks and watches applied ashore, and the captain was the government.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Admiralty, London
statusPeriods.franchise: None. A ship's company does not vote.
statusPeriods.note: From the 1820s Ascension was the victualling and hospital station for the West Africa Squadron hunting slave ships; sick sailors were landed there rather than at fever-ridden Freetown.

statusPeriods.label: Dependency of St Helena
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Navy handed the island to the Colonial Office, which made it a dependency of St Helena; for forty years the resident manager of the Eastern Telegraph cable station doubled as the magistrate.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown, under the Governor of St Helena
statusPeriods.franchise: None, and still none: nobody has ever voted in an Ascension election for a government of Ascension.
statusPeriods.note: The United States built Wideawake airfield in 1942 under a wartime agreement; from 1966 it also carried a NASA tracking station, and from 1982 it was the springboard for the Falklands campaign.

statusPeriods.label: Part of a British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An Administrator appointed by the Governor of St Helena runs the island for the organisations that employ everyone on it: the RAF, the US Air Force, the BBC and the cable and satellite companies.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown, under the Governor of St Helena
statusPeriods.franchise: An elected Island Council existed from 2002, was suspended in 2005 and has been restored and reshaped since; there is still no right of abode, so nobody can vote as a permanent resident.
statusPeriods.note: The 2009 constitution made St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha three equal parts of one territory.

departures.how: Ascension has been British without interruption since 1815 and remains so, as the only place in the atlas with a population, an airfield and a cathedral but no citizens who belong to it.

stillBritish.note: Ascension is part of the British Overseas Territory of St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha; about 800 people live there, all of them on work permits, because nobody has the right of abode.

slavery.note: Ascension had no plantation and no enslaved population; it was the hospital and store for the Royal Navy squadron that intercepted slave ships off West Africa between the 1820s and the 1860s.

retainedTerritory.note: Ascension is still British, and its airfield is why: Wideawake carried the Vulcan bombers, tankers and Hercules of the Falklands campaign in 1982 and remains a joint British and American base.

consequences.economicLegacy: The island has never had an economy of its own. Every job on Ascension has always been paid for by an outside institution: the Admiralty, then the cable companies, then the American and British air forces and the BBC's Atlantic Relay Station.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English law administered by a magistrate, and a population drawn mostly from St Helena, whose people supply most of the workforce and none of the citizenship.

peak.populationNote: Ascension's population peaked during the Falklands campaign in 1982, when the island handled more air traffic than most European airports. The 2021 count was 806.

evidence.work: Green Imperialism: Colonial Expansion, Tropical Island Edens and the Origins of Environmentalism, 1600-1860

pedagogy.hook: Nobody is born with the right to live on Ascension: you may stay only while someone employs you, and when the job ends you leave.

misconception.belief: Every British colony was a place where Britain ruled other people.
misconception.correction: Ascension had no people to rule. Britain took an empty volcano in 1815 to stop anyone rescuing Napoleon, ran it as a warship for 107 years, planted a forest on it on purpose, and then rented it out as an airfield. Some of the empire was not about population at all, but about position on a map.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Ascension is the empire reduced to its logistics: a dot chosen for where it sits, not for what is on it. The same logic put Britain in Gibraltar, Aden, Singapore and Diego Garcia, and it is why the last British territories are mostly rocks with runways.

territories.name: Tristan da Cunha
territories.formalName: Tristan da Cunha and its dependencies, Gough, Inaccessible and Nightingale Islands

namesOverTime.name: Ilha de Tristao da Cunha
namesOverTime.note: Named for the Portuguese admiral who sighted the island in 1506 and could not land on it.

namesOverTime.name: Islands of Refreshment
namesOverTime.note: The name given by Jonathan Lambert of Salem, Massachusetts, who declared himself sole proprietor and sovereign of the group in 1811 and drowned in 1812.

geoCoverage.label: Tristan and its outer islands
geoCoverage.change: One active volcano 2,400 metres high with a single shelf of flat land, plus Inaccessible, Nightingale and, 400 kilometres to the south, Gough Island. The nearest inhabited land is St Helena, 2,430 kilometres away.

acquisitions.how: A British garrison landed and annexed the island for the same reason as Ascension: to make sure no French expedition could use it to reach Napoleon on St Helena, 2,400 kilometres to the north.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: The islands had never been permanently inhabited. The only prior claimant was Jonathan Lambert, an American who proclaimed himself sovereign in 1811 and drowned in 1812, leaving one survivor, Thomas Currie, who was still there in 1816.

counterparties.name: The United States as a maritime rival
counterparties.lost: American whalers and sealers had worked the group freely and one American had claimed it outright; annexation closed both options.
counterparties.note: The annexation came ten months after the USS Essex had used Tristan waters against British whalers in the war of 1812-15, which sharpened British interest.

people.name: Josias Cloete
people.role: officer who formally took possession of the island for the Crown in August 1816

people.name: William Glass
people.role: Scottish corporal of the Royal Artillery who asked to stay when the garrison left in 1817 and founded the settlement with his wife Maria Magdalena Leenders and their two children

people.name: Maria Magdalena Leenders
people.role: Cape-born woman, of Khoikhoi and mixed descent, who settled with Glass and is the ancestor of much of the present population

acquisitions.resistance: None. The garrison found one American sealer living there and left him alone.

evidence.author: Peter A. Munch
evidence.work: Crisis in Utopia: The Ordeal of Tristan da Cunha
evidence.supports: The founding of the settlement, its constitution of equal shares, and the 1961 evacuation.

statusPeriods.label: Military garrison
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An artillery detachment held the island under orders from the Cape, purely to deny it to anyone else. The garrison was withdrawn after fifteen months as an unnecessary expense.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Cape of Good Hope

statusPeriods.label: British in law, self-governing in practice
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain claimed the island and then ignored it for a century. Fifteen households ran their own affairs under a written agreement that no one should take precedence over anyone else and that land and boats were held in common.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Formally a British possession, but for 121 years there was no British official, no garrison, no tax and no court on the island. The islanders governed themselves entirely; degree 1 records the gap between the legal claim and the actual administration.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere. The nearest British official was at Cape Town or St Helena.
statusPeriods.franchise: The community decided matters in meetings of household heads; from the 1930s an Island Council was elected, and women have voted in it since 1938.
statusPeriods.note: The population grew from six adults in 1817 through shipwrecked sailors, five women recruited from St Helena in 1827, and two Italian castaways from the Italia in 1892: Gaetano Lavarello and Andrea Repetto, whose surnames are still on the island.

statusPeriods.label: Dependency of St Helena
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Letters patent made Tristan a formal dependency of St Helena; from 1942 the Royal Navy manned a wartime station there, and an Administrator and a money economy arrived with it.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the crown-colony default of 5 because the Administrator governed by agreement with an Island Council that could and did overrule him on island matters; the community's collective landholding was never abolished.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, under the Governor of St Helena
statusPeriods.franchise: All adult islanders. Women sat on the Island Council from its creation.
statusPeriods.note: The naval station of 1942-46 was commissioned as HMS Atlantic Isle. It brought the island its first shop, its first wages and its first radio.

statusPeriods.label: Part of a British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An Administrator sent from Britain works with an elected Island Council; the land is still held in common, outsiders still cannot buy it, and the community still decides who may settle.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, under the Governor of St Helena
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage among the islanders, who number a little over 200.
statusPeriods.note: In 2020 Tristan declared a marine protection zone of 687,000 square kilometres, closing almost 90 per cent of its waters to fishing.

departures.how: Tristan da Cunha has been British since 1816 and its people, offered the chance to stay in England after the 1961 eruption, voted overwhelmingly to go back to the volcano.

stillBritish.note: Tristan da Cunha is the most remote permanently inhabited place on Earth: about 235 people, eight surnames, one settlement, no airstrip, and a six-day voyage from Cape Town.

populationTransfer.note: The entire population, 264 people, was evacuated to England after the volcano erupted beside the settlement on 10 October 1961; when the islanders were polled in 1962, 148 of 163 adults voted to return, and most were home by November 1963.

consequences.economicLegacy: Tristan has one export, rock lobster, sold under licence, and a stamp and coin trade. It has never taken a development grant it did not ask for and pays for its own government.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English, spoken with a dialect that preserves nineteenth-century Scots and St Helenian forms, and a land system in which nobody may own more than anyone else.

peak.populationNote: The 1961 figure is the population evacuated to England after the eruption. The area includes Gough, Inaccessible and Nightingale as well as Tristan itself.

evidence.author: Peter A. Munch
evidence.work: Crisis in Utopia: The Ordeal of Tristan da Cunha
evidence.supports: The settlement's egalitarian constitution, the 1961 evacuation and the decision to return.

evidence.author: Allan B. Crawford
evidence.work: Tristan da Cunha and the Roaring Forties
evidence.supports: The 1937-38 Norwegian expedition, the wartime station and island life before the eruption.

pedagogy.hook: In 1961 a volcano forced all 264 Tristan islanders to England; offered permanent homes in Hampshire, they voted 148 to 5 to sail back to the volcano.

misconception.belief: British colonies were places Britain governed and profited from.
misconception.correction: For 121 years after the garrison left in 1817, Tristan had no British official, no tax, no police and no court. Britain owned it on paper and forgot about it, while fifteen households ran a community with common land, common boats and a written rule that nobody should take precedence over anyone else.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Tristan is the clearest test of what a colony actually was. Strip out the governor, the garrison, the revenue and the trade, and what remains is a line on a map that mattered only when someone else wanted it. That is also how most Antarctic and South Atlantic claims work.

keyDates.what: Britain annexes the island to protect the guard on Napoleon
The garrison leaves; William Glass and his family stay and found the settlement
Tristan becomes a formal dependency of St Helena
The volcano erupts and the whole population is evacuated
The islanders return home

territories.name: Falkland Islands
territories.formalName: Colony of the Falkland Islands and its Dependencies

namesOverTime.name: Iles Malouines
namesOverTime.note: Bougainville named them for the sailors of Saint-Malo who fished there. The Spanish turned this into Malvinas, which is the name Argentina uses today.

namesOverTime.name: Falkland's Sound, then the Falkland Islands
namesOverTime.note: Captain John Strong named the strait between the two main islands after Anthony Cary, Viscount Falkland, then Treasurer of the Navy. The name spread from the water to the land.

namesOverTime.name: Islas Malvinas
namesOverTime.note: Used by Spain from its purchase of the French settlement in 1767 and by Argentina ever since. The United Nations uses both names.

namesOverTime.name: Falkland Islands
namesOverTime.note: Britain re-took the settlement on 3 January 1833 and has used the English name in every official document since. Argentina has used Islas Malvinas throughout. Both names are current; which one a map prints is itself the dispute.

geoCoverage.label: Port Egmont only
geoCoverage.change: Britain held one blockhouse and a garden on Saunders Island, a few square kilometres at the north-west corner of the group. Spain held Puerto Soledad at the other end. Neither controlled the islands.

geoCoverage.label: The whole archipelago
geoCoverage.change: Britain returned after a 59-year absence, expelled the Buenos Aires garrison and this time claimed and settled the entire group: 778 islands and about 12,000 square kilometres.

acquisitions.how: Commodore John Byron landed at a harbour on Saunders Island, named it Port Egmont, claimed the whole group for George III, and sailed away; a garrison under Captain John MacBride arrived a year later and found the French already living at the other end.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: There is no evidence of any indigenous population on the Falklands. The islands lie 480 kilometres from Patagonia across open ocean, and no pre-European crossing has been demonstrated. The only land mammal, the warrah or Falklands wolf, may have arrived with people on the ice or on a raft, but the argument is unresolved.

counterparties.name: France, and then Spain
counterparties.lost: Bougainville had founded Port Louis on East Falkland ten months earlier, in April 1764; France sold its settlement to Spain in 1767, and Spain claimed the whole group under the Treaty of Tordesillas and the papal division of 1493.
counterparties.note: Britain and France each planted a settlement without knowing the other was there. That accident is the root of a dispute that is still live.

people.name: John Byron
people.role: commodore who took formal possession at Port Egmont in January 1765

people.name: Louis Antoine de Bougainville
people.role: founded the first settlement in the islands, Port Louis, in April 1764 with Acadian refugees

people.name: Juan Ignacio de Madariaga
people.role: Spanish commander who expelled the British garrison from Port Egmont with five frigates in June 1770

acquisitions.resistance: The only opposition was Spanish. In June 1770 a Spanish force of about 1,400 men expelled the 100-strong British garrison; Britain and Spain came within weeks of war, and Spain restored Port Egmont in September 1771 rather than fight without French support.

contested.note: Spain has always maintained that when it restored Port Egmont in 1771 the British government privately promised to withdraw later, and that the 1774 evacuation honoured that promise. No such written undertaking has been found in the British archives, but the timing is suggestive and historians have never settled it.

evidence.author: Julius Goebel
evidence.work: The Struggle for the Falkland Islands: A Study in Legal and Diplomatic History
evidence.supports: The eighteenth-century settlements, the 1770 expulsion and the 1771 restoration; Goebel argues the Argentine case.

acquisitions.how: Captain James Onslow of HMS Clio told the commander of the Buenos Aires garrison at Puerto Soledad to strike his flag and leave; the schooner Sarandi sailed on 5 January 1833 under protest, and the British flag went up in its place.

counterparties.name: The United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata, later Argentina
counterparties.lost: A garrison of about 25 soldiers and the claim to the islands that Buenos Aires had asserted since David Jewett raised its flag at Puerto Soledad in November 1820. Argentina has protested continuously ever since.
counterparties.note: Argentina's case is that it inherited Spain's title at independence, that its possession was peaceful and public between 1820 and 1833, and that a British warship ended it by force. Britain's case is that its own claim ran from 1765, was never renounced, and that Buenos Aires' possession was short and contested.

counterparties.name: The civilian settlers at Puerto Soledad
counterparties.lost: Nothing immediately: unlike the garrison, most of the roughly 25 gauchos and settlers were told they could stay, and most did. Eight months later some of them, led by the gaucho Antonio Rivero, killed five of the settlement's leaders in a dispute over pay and worthless paper money.
counterparties.note: Whether the 1833 events amount to expelling a population is one of the sharpest points in the dispute. The garrison was expelled; the civilian settlement was not. Argentine accounts and British accounts weight this differently, and the primary sources support the narrower reading.

people.name: James Onslow
people.role: captain of HMS Clio; delivered the ultimatum that ended Buenos Aires' garrison

people.name: Jose Maria Pinedo
people.role: commander of the Argentine schooner Sarandi, who protested and withdrew rather than fight a stronger ship with a partly British crew

people.name: Luis Vernet
people.role: Hamburg-born merchant given rights over the islands by Buenos Aires in 1828; his settlement at Puerto Luis was wrecked by the American warship Lexington in December 1831, a year before the British arrived

people.name: Antonio Rivero
people.role: gaucho who led the killing of five settlement leaders in August 1833; an outlaw in British accounts and a resistance hero in Argentine ones

acquisitions.resistance: Pinedo protested and left without firing. The nearest thing to armed resistance came from Rivero's gauchos in August 1833, and it was aimed at the settlement's managers rather than at British rule.

contested.note: The 1833 action is the centre of the dispute. Argentina calls it a forcible dispossession of an established Argentine settlement; Britain calls it the reassertion of a claim never abandoned, against a garrison placed there only months earlier. Both descriptions rest on the same events and disagree about the years before them.

positions.claim: Argentina inherited Spanish sovereignty over the islands in 1816 and was in lawful possession when a British warship expelled its garrison in 1833.
positions.heldBy: The Argentine government's consistent position since 1833, argued at length by Julius Goebel (1927).

positions.claim: Britain claimed and settled the islands in 1765, never renounced that claim when it withdrew for economy in 1774, and returned in 1833 to a group with no settled population of any state.
positions.heldBy: The British government's position, set out in successive Foreign Office statements and defended by Lowell Gustafson (1988).

evidence.author: Lowell S. Gustafson
evidence.work: The Sovereignty Dispute over the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands
evidence.supports: The competing legal claims and the events of 1820-1833, examined from the British and the Argentine case alike.

statusPeriods.label: Port Egmont: a naval outpost
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: About a hundred marines and sailors under a naval officer held a blockhouse, a garden and a jetty on Saunders Island, answering to the Admiralty and controlling nothing beyond musket range.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the crown-colony default of 5 because Britain governed nobody: there was no population, no court and no revenue, and Spain held the other end of the archipelago throughout.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Admiralty, London
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The settlement had no civilians.

statusPeriods.label: Expelled by Spain
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Spanish forces from Buenos Aires held Port Egmont for fifteen months. Britain had no presence in the islands at all and prepared for war instead.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority was zero: the garrison had been shipped out. The status is 'occupied' by another power, as the model prescribes.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Spanish governor at Buenos Aires

statusPeriods.label: Port Egmont restored
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Spain handed the blockhouse back under a declaration that expressly reserved its own claim to sovereignty; Britain reoccupied it with a token party for less than three years.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Same reasoning as the first Port Egmont period: a garrison with no population, no courts and a rival power in occupation of the other island.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Admiralty, London

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Lieutenant-Governor from 1842, then a Governor with a nominated council, ran the islands from Stanley; from 1851 the Falkland Islands Company owned nearly half the land and most of the sheep, and the colony's revenue came from wool.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain held nothing in the Falklands between the evacuation of Port Egmont on 20 May 1774 and the arrival of HMS Clio on 2 January 1833. In those 59 years Spain held Puerto Soledad until 1811, the islands were empty of any government until 1820, and Buenos Aires asserted a claim from 1820 and placed a garrison there in 1832. Leaving the gap visible is the point: British sovereignty here is not continuous.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stanley, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: A nominated council until 1949, when two elected members were added; a majority-elected Legislative Council came in 1964 and full universal suffrage with it.
statusPeriods.note: In December 1914 the Royal Navy destroyed Admiral von Spee's squadron off Stanley, the only major naval battle ever fought in the South Atlantic. From 1908 the islands also administered South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and the British Antarctic claim as the Falkland Islands Dependencies.

statusPeriods.label: Argentine occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Argentine forces landed before dawn on 2 April, overwhelmed 68 Royal Marines, deported the Governor and installed a military governor who imposed Argentine law, Spanish street signs and driving on the right for ten weeks.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Occupied by another power: British authority in the islands was zero for 74 days. Degree 0 with the 'occupied' status, exactly as the model prescribes for Hong Kong under Japan.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buenos Aires, through a military governor in Stanley
statusPeriods.note: About 114 islanders from Goose Green were locked in the village hall for 29 days. Three civilians were killed by British naval gunfire on 11-12 June: Doreen Bonner, Mary Goodwin and Susan Whitley.

statusPeriods.label: Recaptured
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British forces retook Stanley on 14 June 1982 and colonial government resumed, now backed by a permanent garrison and, from 1985, a new airfield at Mount Pleasant.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stanley, under the Foreign Office in London

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Islanders elect a Legislative Assembly that controls the budget, the fisheries licences that pay for it and immigration; Britain appoints the Governor and keeps defence and foreign affairs, with about 1,200 service personnel at Mount Pleasant.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stanley, with a UK-appointed governor
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage. The British Nationality (Falkland Islands) Act 1983 gave every islander full British citizenship, which the 1981 Act had taken away.
statusPeriods.note: Squid and finfish licensing, begun in 1987, turned a wool colony that needed British grants into a territory with one of the highest incomes per head in the world.

departures.how: Lord North's government, cutting naval costs, ordered Port Egmont abandoned; Lieutenant Clayton hauled down the flag, nailed a lead plaque to the blockhouse door asserting that the islands remained the property of George III, and sailed away, leaving Spain in sole occupation for 37 years.

becomes.name: Spanish Puerto Soledad, administered from Buenos Aires until 1811

led.name: Frederick North, Lord North
led.role: Prime Minister whose government ordered the withdrawal to save money

led.name: Samuel Wallis Clayton
led.role: the officer who struck the flag and left the plaque

cost.note: Nobody was killed. The cost was diplomatic: Britain kept a claim it could not enforce, and left evidence for Spain and later Argentina that it had walked away.

departures.borders: No border moved. Britain left the archipelago physically and stayed on it legally, which is precisely the ambiguity every later argument has been fought over.

contested.note: This entry uses 'transfer to another power' for something better described as abandonment with a reservation of rights. The atlas has no word for leaving a place while claiming it, which is itself worth noticing: it is the manoeuvre on which the whole Falklands dispute turns.

departures.how: The Falklands are still British, defended by a garrison since 1982 and claimed by Argentina under the First Transitory Provision of its 1994 constitution, which declares the recovery of the Malvinas a permanent and unrenounceable objective of the Argentine people.

stillBritish.note: The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory of about 3,660 people, claimed by Argentina as the Islas Malvinas; the United Nations keeps them on its list of non-self-governing territories and calls for negotiation, which Britain refuses while the islanders object.

violence.note: The war of 1982 killed 649 Argentines, 255 British service personnel and three Falkland Islanders in 74 days, over islands with a population then of about 1,800.

toll.note: The standard totals are 649 Argentine dead, 255 British and three islanders. Argentine figures include 323 lost when the cruiser General Belgrano was sunk on 2 May 1982. Some counts add later suicides among British and Argentine veterans, which no official total covers.

warrant.author: The British and Argentine ministries of defence
warrant.work: The official casualty rolls of the 1982 Falklands/Malvinas war
warrant.supports: The standard totals are 649 Argentine dead, 255 British and three islanders. Argentine figures include 323 lost when the cruiser General Belgrano was sunk on 2 May 1982. Some counts add later suicides among British and Argentine veterans, which no official total covers.
warrant.check: The British roll of honour is published by the Ministry of Defence and the Commonwealth War Graves Commission; the Argentine roll by the Ministerio de Defensa.
warrant.note: Two governments counted their own dead, and for once the two counts agree.

populationTransfer.note: There was no population to displace and none was displaced. The islanders are descended mainly from Scottish, Welsh and English shepherds recruited from the 1840s onwards, and about a third of today's residents were born elsewhere.

consequences.borderLegacy: Argentina's claim is written into its constitution and taught in every Argentine school; British and Argentine relations were broken from 1982 to 1990 and remain strained. The dispute is unresolved and is the main reason a British garrison sits 12,700 kilometres from London.
consequences.economicLegacy: Wool paid for the colony from 1850 to 1980 and never made it self-supporting. A 200-mile fisheries zone declared in 1986 changed that in a decade: squid licences now fund almost the entire government.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an elected Assembly, and place names that record every claimant: Port Louis from the French, Puerto Soledad and San Carlos from the Spanish, Stanley and Port Egmont from the British.

peak.populationNote: The Falklands population has never exceeded about 3,700 civilians. It was around 1,800 at the time of the 1982 war, plus a British garrison that has usually outnumbered the islanders since.

evidence.author: Lowell S. Gustafson
evidence.work: The Sovereignty Dispute over the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands
evidence.supports: The competing sovereignty claims from 1764 to the 1980s, argued from the British and the Argentine case alike.

evidence.author: Lawrence Freedman
evidence.work: The Official History of the Falklands Campaign
evidence.supports: The diplomacy of 1965-1982, the invasion and the war, from the British government's own papers.

evidence.author: Julius Goebel
evidence.work: The Struggle for the Falkland Islands: A Study in Legal and Diplomatic History
evidence.supports: The eighteenth- and nineteenth-century record, presented as a case against the British title.

contested.note: Sovereignty over these islands is genuinely disputed, not merely asserted. Argentina relies on inheritance from Spain, geographical proximity and the expulsion of 1833; Britain relies on its claim of 1765, continuous administration since 1833 and the islanders' right of self-determination. The United Nations has called for negotiations since Resolution 2065 of 1965 and neither side has moved.

pedagogy.hook: Britain has been on the Falklands for 193 of the last 261 years: it walked away in 1774 and did not come back for 59 years.

misconception.belief: Britain has held the Falklands continuously since it discovered them, so Argentina's claim is simply invented.
misconception.correction: Britain settled Port Egmont in 1765, was expelled by Spain in 1770, was restored in 1771 and abandoned the islands for economy in 1774, leaving only a lead plaque. Spain held Puerto Soledad until 1811. Buenos Aires claimed the islands from 1820 and put a garrison there in 1832. Britain removed it in January 1833. Both claims have real history in them; that is why the dispute has lasted.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Falklands is where the empire's oldest argument and its newest war meet. It shows that colonial title is often a chain of claims with gaps in it, that self-determination and territorial integrity are both real principles that can collide, and that in 1982 a British government fought a war to keep 1,800 people British.

territories.name: South Georgia
territories.formalName: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands

namesOverTime.name: Isle of Georgia
namesOverTime.note: Named by James Cook for George III on the day he landed at Possession Bay.

namesOverTime.name: Islas Georgias del Sur
namesOverTime.note: Argentina formally claimed the island in 1927 and includes it in its Malvinas claim.

namesOverTime.name: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands
namesOverTime.note: Split from the Falkland Islands Dependencies as a territory in its own right on 3 October 1985, three years after the Argentine landing at Leith Harbour.

geoCoverage.label: A claim with nobody on it
geoCoverage.change: Cook's claim of 1775 was a flag on a beach. For 129 years Britain administered nothing there; sealers of every nation worked the coast unlicensed and unsupervised.

geoCoverage.label: The Falkland Islands Dependencies
geoCoverage.change: Letters patent of 21 July 1908 put South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands, the South Orkneys, the South Shetlands and Graham Land under the Governor at Stanley, so that Britain could licence and tax the whaling companies.

acquisitions.how: James Cook landed at Possession Bay, took the island for George III, sailed along its coast in fog and sleet, decided it was worthless, and reported that its seas were full of seals and whales, which is what brought everyone else.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: South Georgia has never had an indigenous population and is 1,400 kilometres from the nearest inhabited land. Cook wrote that the island was 'doomed by nature' to lie under ice; a merchant read the same journal and sent sealers.

counterparties.name: The fur seals and southern right whales of the Scotia Sea
counterparties.lost: Sealers took an estimated 1.2 million fur seal skins from South Georgia between 1786 and 1825 and left the species commercially extinct; from 1904 to 1965 the shore stations processed roughly 175,000 whales.
counterparties.note: This atlas records who lost what. On South Georgia the answer is not a people but an ecosystem, and it is the clearest case in the empire of a territory taken purely to be harvested.

people.name: James Cook
people.role: claimed the island on 17 January 1775 and named the South Sandwich Islands eleven days later

people.name: Anthony de la Roche
people.role: English merchant blown south in 1675 who probably saw the island a century before Cook

acquisitions.resistance: None was possible. The nearest thing to a contest was commercial: American, British and Argentine sealers raced each other to strip the beaches.

evidence.author: Robert K. Headland
evidence.work: The Island of South Georgia
evidence.supports: Discovery, sealing and whaling statistics, and the administrative history of the island.

acquisitions.how: Letters patent issued in London declared South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands, the South Orkneys, the South Shetlands and Graham Land to be dependencies of the Falkland Islands, so that a magistrate at Grytviken could sell whaling licences and collect a tax on every barrel of oil.

counterparties.name: Argentina and Chile
counterparties.lost: Both were pushed out of ground they were already using: Argentina had run the meteorological station on Laurie Island in the South Orkneys since 1904, and both states later claimed the same sectors. Argentina formally claimed South Georgia in 1927 and the South Sandwich Islands in 1948.
counterparties.note: The 1908 letters were drafted so loosely that they also claimed a slice of southern Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, which are Argentine and Chilean. New letters patent in 1917 quietly fixed the mistake.

counterparties.name: The Norwegian and Argentine whaling companies
counterparties.lost: They had begun operating at Grytviken from 1904 without asking anyone; from 1908 they paid Britain for the right, which was the entire purpose of the annexation.
counterparties.note: Carl Anton Larsen, the Norwegian who founded Grytviken, took out a British lease from Stanley in 1906 and became a naturalised British subject.

instrument.name: Letters Patent constituting the Falkland Islands Dependencies
instrument.note: Replaced by new letters patent on 28 March 1917 which redrew the boundary to exclude South American territory and defined the sector between 20 and 80 degrees west, south of 50 degrees south.

people.name: Carl Anton Larsen
people.role: Norwegian whaling captain who founded Grytviken in November 1904 and took a British lease for it

people.name: William Allardyce
people.role: Governor of the Falkland Islands who pressed London to claim the whole sector so that whaling could be licensed and taxed

acquisitions.resistance: Argentina protested in writing and kept its Laurie Island station running; nobody fought.

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The 1908 and 1917 letters patent and the whaling-revenue motive behind the Antarctic claim.

statusPeriods.label: A claim on paper
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed anything. Sealers of several nations worked the beaches for 130 years without a licence, a magistrate or a law, and the British claim existed only in Cook's journal and on Admiralty charts.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: There was no administration of any kind: no official, no revenue, no court. Degree 1 records a bare claim, far below the crown-colony default of 5.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere

statusPeriods.label: Falkland Islands Dependency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A resident magistrate at King Edward Point, appointed from Stanley, issued whaling licences, collected the oil tax, held the court and registered the deaths of the men killed in the flensing yards.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: King Edward Point, under the Governor of the Falkland Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The population was a few hundred Norwegian and British whalers on annual contracts, and after 1965 a handful of scientists.
statusPeriods.note: The whaling stations closed between 1961 and 1965 when there were too few whales left to catch. Ernest Shackleton is buried at Grytviken, where he died on 5 January 1922.

statusPeriods.label: Argentine occupation of South Georgia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Argentine marines took Grytviken on 3 April 1982 after a two-hour fight in which 22 Royal Marines under Lieutenant Keith Mills damaged a corvette and shot down a helicopter before surrendering.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Occupied by another power for 22 days; British authority was nil. Southern Thule in the South Sandwich Islands had already been occupied by Argentina since 1976 and was not recovered until 20 June 1982.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buenos Aires

statusPeriods.label: Recaptured, still a Falklands dependency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British forces retook Grytviken on 25 April 1982 without a single death on either side, and a garrison replaced the magistrate for the next twenty years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: King Edward Point, under the Governor of the Falkland Islands

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory in its own right
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands were separated from the Falklands in 1985 and are run by a Commissioner, who is also the Governor at Stanley, with no resident population and an income from fishing licences and tourism.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stanley, through a Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: There is nobody to enfranchise: the population is about 20 people at a time, all of them government officers, scientists or museum staff on contracts.
statusPeriods.note: In 2018 the territory was declared free of rats and mice after the largest rodent eradication ever attempted, restoring seabird colonies destroyed by animals brought ashore in sealers' ships.

departures.how: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands remain British, claimed by Argentina, and are the only British territory whose entire population is on a fixed-term contract.

stillBritish.note: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands have been a separate British Overseas Territory since 1985, with about twenty residents at any time and a claim from Argentina that dates from 1927 and 1948.

violence.note: The recapture of South Georgia on 25 April 1982 killed nobody, but the war it opened killed more than 900 people; the scrap-metal party that landed at Leith on 19 March 1982 is where it started.

consequences.economicLegacy: Whaling built everything on South Georgia and then destroyed its own basis: seven shore stations, 175,000 whales, and by 1965 not enough animals left to make a season pay. The territory now lives on fishing licences and about 10,000 cruise passengers a year.
consequences.borderLegacy: Argentina claims the islands as part of the Malvinas, Georgias del Sur y Sandwich del Sur province. The claim is written into the Argentine constitution and has never been withdrawn.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English law administered from Stanley, and a landscape of Norwegian place names, rusting oil tanks and a cemetery at Grytviken where Shackleton is buried.

peak.populationNote: The summer population of the whaling stations peaked at roughly 2,000 men before the First World War. There has never been a permanent civilian population.

evidence.work: The Island of South Georgia
evidence.supports: Discovery, sealing and whaling figures, and the administration of the dependency.

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The politics of the Falkland Islands Dependencies and the Argentine and Chilean counter-claims.

evidence.author: Roland Huntford
evidence.work: Shackleton
evidence.supports: The James Caird voyage, the crossing of South Georgia in May 1916 and Shackleton's death at Grytviken.

contested.note: Argentina claims both island groups and has occupied parts of them twice: Southern Thule from 1976 to 1982, and South Georgia for 22 days in 1982. The number of whales taken is well documented from station returns; the fur seal figures for 1786-1825 are estimates from incomplete cargo records.

pedagogy.hook: Britain claimed a slice of Antarctica in 1908 for one reason: so it could charge Norwegian whalers a tax on every barrel of oil.

misconception.belief: Polar territories were claimed for science and exploration.
misconception.correction: The Falkland Islands Dependencies were created in 1908 by a governor who wanted licence fees. Whale-oil duties paid for the magistrate, the post office and eventually the Discovery Investigations that studied the whales being killed. Science came second and was funded by the killing.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: South Georgia shows the empire operating with no population to rule at all: no subjects, no taxes on people, no independence movement. What was being governed was a resource, and when the resource ran out in 1965 the territory emptied. It is empire reduced to a licence book.

namesOverTime.name: Graham Land
namesOverTime.note: Named by John Biscoe for Sir James Graham, First Lord of the Admiralty. Americans called the same peninsula Palmer Land; the two names were only reconciled in 1964, with Graham Land north of a line at about 69 degrees south and Palmer Land to its south.

namesOverTime.name: Tierra de San Martin / Antartida Argentina
namesOverTime.note: Argentina's name for the sector it claims, which overlaps the British claim entirely and the Chilean claim in part.

geoCoverage.label: The sector between 20 and 80 degrees west
geoCoverage.change: Britain claimed a wedge running from 60 degrees south to the Pole, 1.7 million square kilometres of ice with no inhabitants, no economy and, until 1943, no British person permanently on it. It is drawn hatched because British authority there has never been more than a handful of huts.

acquisitions.how: Letters patent signed in London declared a sector of Antarctica to be a dependency of the Falkland Islands, so that Britain could licence the whaling fleets working the Weddell Sea and tax the oil they rendered.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Antarctica is the only continent no human being reached before the modern era. It is the one place in this atlas where the phrase 'empty land' is not a euphemism for people who were killed, driven off or ignored. Every other claim of emptiness in the empire deserves suspicion; this one does not.

counterparties.name: Argentina and Chile
counterparties.lost: Both later claimed the same ice. Argentina had operated the Orcadas station on Laurie Island since 1904, taking it over from a Scottish expedition, and declared its own sector in 1943; Chile declared its sector in 1940. The three claims overlap between 53 and 74 degrees west.
counterparties.note: Britain claimed first, in 1908. That is a real argument in international law, and it is also the reason Argentina and Chile spent the 1940s and 1950s building huts to prove effective occupation.

instrument.name: Letters Patent constituting the Falkland Islands Dependencies
instrument.note: The 1908 wording accidentally claimed part of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. New letters patent of 28 March 1917 corrected it and defined the sector between 20 and 80 degrees west, south of 50 degrees south.

people.name: William Allardyce
people.role: Governor of the Falkland Islands whose despatches persuaded London to claim the sector so whaling could be licensed

people.name: William Speirs Bruce
people.role: Scottish scientist whose expedition built the Laurie Island station in 1903 and handed it to Argentina in 1904, giving Argentina its oldest Antarctic foothold

acquisitions.resistance: None from anyone living there, because nobody did. The contest was diplomatic and, in the 1950s, briefly armed: Argentine troops fired over the heads of a British landing party at Hope Bay on 1 February 1952.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The 1908 and 1917 letters patent, the overlapping claims and the road to the Antarctic Treaty.

statusPeriods.label: A claim administered from Stanley
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Governor of the Falkland Islands was on paper the governor of a wedge of Antarctica. In practice Britain issued whaling licences and left the ice alone; not one British person lived on the mainland of the claim.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain administered nothing on the continent for 35 years. The claim existed in letters patent and on charts. Degree 1 marks a legal title with no administration behind it, far below the crown-colony default of 5.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stanley, Falkland Islands

statusPeriods.label: Occupied in earnest: Operation Tabarin and the survey
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain finally put people on the ice. A wartime expedition built bases at Port Lockroy and Hope Bay in early 1944, ostensibly against German raiders and actually against Argentine and Chilean claims; it became the Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey and stayed.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority now rested on occupied bases, but over a territory with no population and with two other states building rival huts inside it. Degree 3 rather than the crown-colony default of 5.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stanley, Falkland Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: There has never been anyone to enfranchise.
statusPeriods.note: In 1953 a British party removed Argentine and Chilean huts from Deception Island and deported two Argentines. In 1955 Britain took both states to the International Court of Justice; both refused the court's jurisdiction and the case was struck out in 1956.

statusPeriods.label: British Antarctic Territory, under the Antarctic Treaty
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Commissioner in London, not a resident governor, administers a territory of scientists. British law applies to British nationals there, the British Antarctic Survey runs Rothera and Halley, and Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty holds every sovereignty argument in suspension.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Foreign Office in London, through a Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Between about 40 and 200 people are present at any time, all of them employees, and none of them resident in law.
statusPeriods.note: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 does not extinguish the claim. Article IV says no act while the treaty is in force may support or weaken any claim, and no new or enlarged claims may be made. The claim is frozen, not withdrawn, and Britain still calls the territory British.

departures.how: The British Antarctic Territory is still claimed by Britain, still claimed in whole or part by Argentina and Chile, and recognised by almost nobody else, because the Antarctic Treaty asks its 58 parties to recognise no claims at all.

stillBritish.note: The British Antarctic Territory covers about 1.7 million square kilometres, has no permanent population, and exists as a claim suspended by Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty rather than as a possession anyone else acknowledges.
stillBritish.disputedWith: Argentina and Chile, whose sectors overlap it; and, in a different sense, the other 55 parties to the Antarctic Treaty, which recognise no Antarctic claim at all.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain still holds the oldest of the seven Antarctic claims and shows no sign of dropping it: in December 2012 it named the southern part Queen Elizabeth Land, which Argentina protested within a day.

violence.note: The nearest thing to fighting was on 1 February 1952, when Argentine troops fired machine-gun bursts over a British landing party at Hope Bay, and in February 1953, when British marines removed Argentine and Chilean huts from Deception Island.

consequences.economicLegacy: The claim was made to tax whale oil and outlived the industry that paid for it by sixty years. It survives now on science budgets and on the argument that whoever holds a claim will be at the table if Antarctic minerals or fisheries are ever opened.
consequences.borderLegacy: Seven states claim Antarctic sectors, three of them overlapping here; the United States and Russia recognise none and reserve the right to claim. The Antarctic Treaty works by refusing to answer the question, which is why it has lasted since 1961.

peak.populationNote: There is no permanent population and never has been. British Antarctic Survey stations hold roughly 200 people in summer and around 40 in winter. The area is the official figure for the sector; the map draws only the exposed land and rock, because Natural Earth's coastline excludes the great ice shelves.
