evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The making of the claim, Operation Tabarin, and the Anglo-Argentine and Anglo-Chilean disputes.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The legal basis of the claims, the ICJ case of 1955-56 and the negotiation of the Antarctic Treaty.

evidence.author: Stephen Haddelsey
evidence.work: Operation Tabarin: Britain's Secret Wartime Expedition to Antarctica 1944-46
evidence.supports: The wartime occupation of the claim and its political purpose.

contested.note: Everything about this territory is disputed. Argentina and Chile claim overlapping sectors; the United States, Russia and most treaty parties recognise no claim at all; and the Antarctic Treaty deliberately leaves the question open. The area figure of 1.71 million square kilometres is Britain's own; the map here draws only about 1.13 million because the ice shelves are not in the coastline dataset.

pedagogy.hook: Britain claims a piece of Antarctica seven times the size of the United Kingdom, and almost no other country in the world admits that the claim exists.

misconception.belief: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 abolished national claims to Antarctica.
misconception.correction: It did no such thing. Article IV freezes the argument: no act done while the treaty is in force can strengthen or weaken a claim, and no new claims may be made. Britain, Argentina, Chile, Norway, France, Australia and New Zealand all still claim their sectors. The treaty works because it changes the subject, not because anyone gave anything up.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the last piece of the empire that is still growing in importance rather than shrinking. It shows that a territorial claim can survive with no people, no economy and no recognition, kept alive by two huts, a postage-stamp office and the possibility that the ice will one day be worth something.

keyDates.what: Britain claims the sector as a Falklands dependency
Operation Tabarin builds Base A at Port Lockroy
The Antarctic Treaty is signed in Washington
The British Antarctic Territory is created south of 60 degrees
The southern half is named Queen Elizabeth Land; Argentina protests

namesOverTime.name: Victoria Land
namesOverTime.note: Named by James Clark Ross for the young Queen Victoria, four days before he found the ice shelf that carries his own name.

modernSuccessors.name: New Zealand
modernSuccessors.note: New Zealand has administered the sector from the day it was claimed and now treats it as a New Zealand claim; the United Kingdom does not claim it and the rest of the world mostly does not recognise it.

geoCoverage.label: The sector between 160 degrees east and 150 degrees west
geoCoverage.change: An Order in Council in London claimed 450,000 square kilometres of ice and the Ross Ice Shelf, and handed the whole of it to New Zealand to govern on the day it was claimed.

acquisitions.how: An Order in Council claimed the Ross Sea sector for the Crown and placed it under the Governor-General of New Zealand, drafted in a hurry because a Norwegian factory ship was about to start whaling there and Britain wanted to be the one selling the licence.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: Nobody had ever lived in the Ross sector. It had been visited by Ross in 1841, by Scott in 1902 and 1911, by Shackleton in 1908 and by Amundsen in 1911, and had been permanently occupied by no one.

counterparties.name: Norwegian whaling companies
counterparties.lost: Carl Anton Larsen's factory ship Sir James Clark Ross entered the Ross Sea in the summer of 1923-24 expecting open water and no landlord, and found itself required to take a British licence.
counterparties.note: The same man, the same argument and the same solution as South Georgia twenty years earlier. Antarctic sovereignty in the 1920s was a whaling revenue question with a flag on top.

instrument.name: Order in Council of 30 July 1923 constituting the Ross Dependency
instrument.note: It defined the sector from 160 degrees east to 150 degrees west, south of 60 degrees south, and appointed the Governor-General of New Zealand as its governor.

people.name: James Clark Ross
people.role: naval officer who found the sea, the shelf and Victoria Land in 1841 and claimed them for the Crown

people.name: Leo Amery
people.role: First Lord of the Admiralty and imperial enthusiast who pressed for British claims across the whole Antarctic before other states got there

acquisitions.resistance: None. The nearest thing to opposition was American: the United States has never recognised the claim and built McMurdo Station inside it in 1956.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The 1923 Order in Council, its whaling-licence motive and the British scheme for claiming the whole continent.

statusPeriods.label: A British claim governed by New Zealand
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The claim was British and the administration was never British for a day: the Order in Council made the Governor-General in Wellington the governor of the sector, and New Zealand made every regulation that followed.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: London made the claim and then did nothing with it. There was no British official, no British base and no British revenue in the sector; New Zealand issued the whaling licences. Degree 1, not the crown-colony default of 5.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Wellington, New Zealand
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody has ever lived there to vote.

departures.how: No single act handed the Ross Dependency over: New Zealand governed it from the first day, and when New Zealand adopted the Statute of Westminster on 25 November 1947 the claim it had been administering for 24 years became unambiguously its own rather than Britain's.

becomes.name: The Ross Dependency of New Zealand

led.name: Peter Fraser
led.role: Prime Minister of New Zealand whose government adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947 and took full responsibility for the dependency

led.name: Edmund Hillary
led.role: led the New Zealand party that built Scott Base in 1957 and drove tractors to the South Pole in January 1958, giving the claim its first real occupation

cost.note: Nothing was fought over and nobody was displaced, because nobody was there. The only cost was to the whales: about 25,000 were taken from the Ross Sea between 1923 and 1939.

departures.borders: The border did not move a metre. The sector runs from 160 degrees east to 150 degrees west and converges on the South Pole, and it is drawn on exactly the lines an Order in Council fixed in London in 1923.

instrument.name: Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1947 (New Zealand)
instrument.note: The Act did not mention Antarctica. It is used here as the point at which the claim stopped being administered on Britain's behalf, because no clearer moment exists.

contested.note: There is no agreed date for when the Ross Dependency stopped being British and became New Zealand's, because no instrument ever said so. Some accounts date it to 1923, when New Zealand took over the administration; others to 1947 and the Statute of Westminster; others treat the question as never having been asked. This record uses 1947 and says so.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept nothing here. The Ross Dependency is the one Antarctic claim Britain made and then let go entirely, and it is now the largest territory New Zealand claims anywhere.

commonwealth.note: New Zealand is a Commonwealth realm; the King is head of state, and the Ross Dependency's formal head is still the Governor-General acting in his name.

consequences.economicLegacy: The claim was made to sell whaling licences and now sells nothing. Scott Base and the American McMurdo Station, four kilometres apart, are the only settlements, and the United States, which recognises no claim, has by far the larger one.
consequences.borderLegacy: The Ross Dependency shows how Antarctic borders were made: straight lines of longitude drawn in a European capital, meeting at a pole nobody had stood on when the first of them was drawn.

peak.populationNote: No permanent population. Scott Base holds about 85 people in summer and 10 to 14 in winter; American McMurdo, inside the same sector, holds over 1,000 in summer.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The 1923 Order in Council, the British sector scheme and New Zealand's administration.

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Geopolitics in Antarctica: Views from the Southern Oceanic Rim
evidence.supports: How the southern Commonwealth states inherited and used their Antarctic claims.

contested.note: The date at which the Ross Dependency ceased to be a British possession is genuinely unsettled, because Britain claimed it and New Zealand administered it from the same day. The status of the claim itself is unsettled too: the Antarctic Treaty suspends it and most states do not recognise it.

pedagogy.hook: Britain claimed 450,000 square kilometres of Antarctica in 1923 and gave it to New Zealand the same afternoon, because a Norwegian whaling ship was already on its way.

misconception.belief: The dominions built their own empires separately from Britain's.
misconception.correction: New Zealand's only overseas claim of any size was handed to it by an Order in Council written in London, as part of a British plan to claim the whole Antarctic continent sector by sector and let the dominions administer the pieces. Australia got its slice the same way in 1933.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Ross Dependency shows the empire doing something students rarely see: expanding by delegation. London made the claim, Wellington did the work, and the map went imperial pink at no cost to the British taxpayer. It is also the clearest case of a claim that quietly stopped being British without any ceremony at all.

keyDates.what: James Clark Ross finds Victoria Land and claims it
The Ross Dependency is created and given to New Zealand
Scott Base opens for the International Geophysical Year
The Antarctic Treaty suspends the claim

namesOverTime.name: Enderby Land, Kemp Land, Wilkes Land and the rest

from.note: The coast was named piecemeal by sealing captains and expeditions across a century; no single date applies.

modernSuccessors.name: Australia
modernSuccessors.note: Australia claims 5.9 million square kilometres, about 42 per cent of Antarctica, more than any other state. Four countries recognise the claim: Britain, France, New Zealand and Norway, which all recognise each other's.

geoCoverage.label: The sectors from 45 to 160 degrees east, minus Adelie Land
geoCoverage.change: A British Order in Council claimed everything between 45 and 160 degrees east except the French wedge of Adelie Land, and declared it to be under Australian authority as soon as Australia passed a law to accept it.

acquisitions.how: An Order in Council in London claimed nearly half of Antarctica on the strength of Douglas Mawson's flag-raisings from the ship Discovery in 1929-31, and assigned the lot to Australia before Norway or Japan could claim the same coast.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: East Antarctica has never had inhabitants. Mawson's proclamations were read aloud to nobody, at points of bare rock along 3,000 kilometres of ice cliff.

counterparties.name: Norway
counterparties.lost: Norwegian whalers and the Lars Christensen expeditions had charted much of the same coast and had a strong practical claim to it; Britain and Norway settled the argument by agreement, with Norway taking Queen Maud Land to the west in 1939.
counterparties.note: The claim was a race. Mawson was under written instructions to raise the flag at as many landing points as possible, precisely to build a record of effective occupation.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: France kept Adelie Land, a narrow wedge between 136 and 142 degrees east that Dumont d'Urville had claimed in 1840; the Australian claim is cut in two by it to this day.
counterparties.note: The boundary was fixed by an Anglo-French exchange of notes in 1938.

instrument.name: Australian Antarctic Territory Acceptance Act 1933 and the Order in Council of 7 February 1933
instrument.note: The Order in Council was made in London on 7 February 1933; the Australian Acceptance Act followed in June 1933 and the transfer took effect by proclamation on 24 August 1936.

people.name: Douglas Mawson
people.role: geologist who led the 1929-31 expedition and raised the flag at five landing points to manufacture the record of occupation the claim needed

people.name: Lars Christensen
people.role: Norwegian shipowner whose expeditions charted the same coast and whose claims Britain was racing

acquisitions.resistance: None from anyone on the ground. The competition was between whaling nations and was settled by diplomacy, not force.

evidence.author: Tom Griffiths
evidence.work: Slicing the Silence: Voyaging to Antarctica
evidence.publisher: University of New South Wales Press
evidence.supports: Mawson's expeditions, the making of the Australian claim and its meaning in Australian politics.

statusPeriods.label: A British claim awaiting Australian acceptance
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: For three and a half years the largest claim in Antarctica belonged to Britain on paper and to nobody in practice, while the Australian parliament passed the Act that would take it over.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: No administration existed: no station, no official, no revenue. Australia's first permanent base, Mawson, did not open until 1954. Degree 1 rather than the crown-colony default of 5.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: London, in name only
statusPeriods.franchise: There has never been anyone there to vote.

departures.how: A proclamation under the Australian Antarctic Territory Acceptance Act brought the sector under Australian law on 24 August 1936, transferring 5.9 million square kilometres from Britain to Australia without a shot, a settler or a single inhabitant.

led.name: Douglas Mawson
led.role: the expedition leader whose proclamations gave the claim its legal basis and who lobbied Canberra to accept it

led.name: Joseph Lyons
led.role: Prime Minister of Australia whose government legislated to accept the territory in 1933

cost.note: Nobody was killed, displaced or governed. The transfer cost nothing because the territory contained nothing but ice, and Australia did not build a station on it for another eighteen years.

departures.borders: The borders are lines of longitude drawn in London: 45 to 136 degrees east and 142 to 160 degrees east, with a French wedge cut out of the middle by an exchange of notes in 1938.

instrument.name: Australian Antarctic Territory Acceptance Act 1933
instrument.note: Assented to in June 1933; brought into force by proclamation on 24 August 1936.

commonwealth.note: Australia is a Commonwealth realm. Its Antarctic territory is administered from Hobart by the Australian Antarctic Division.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept nothing in East Antarctica. Australia holds the largest Antarctic claim in the world because a British Order in Council gave it away in 1933.

consequences.economicLegacy: The claim's original purpose was whaling licences. Its modern value is a claimed exclusive economic zone in the Southern Ocean and a seat at the table if Antarctic minerals are ever opened, which the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans indefinitely.
consequences.borderLegacy: Only four states recognise the Australian claim, and they are the four that recognise each other's: Britain, France, New Zealand and Norway. That mutual-recognition club is the whole legal support for half of Antarctica.

peak.populationNote: No permanent population. Mawson, Davis and Casey stations hold a few hundred people in summer and about 60 through the winter.

evidence.author: Tom Griffiths
evidence.work: Slicing the Silence: Voyaging to Antarctica
evidence.publisher: University of New South Wales Press
evidence.supports: Mawson, the making of the claim and Australia's relationship with its Antarctic territory.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The British sector scheme, the 1933 Order in Council and the pattern of mutual recognition among claimants.

contested.note: The claim is recognised by only four states and is suspended by Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty. Australia's maritime claims off the territory have been protested by several countries, and Japanese whaling inside them was the subject of an International Court of Justice case decided in 2014.

pedagogy.hook: Forty-two per cent of Antarctica belongs to Australia, and it belongs to Australia because a committee in London gave it away in 1933.

misconception.belief: Australia claimed its Antarctic territory itself, as an independent country.
misconception.correction: The claim was made by a British Order in Council on 7 February 1933, on the strength of flag-raisings by an expedition Britain had helped fund, and handed to Australia by proclamation in 1936. Australia did not put a permanent station on the ice until 1954, twenty-one years after the claim was made in its name.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Half of Antarctica is claimed by two countries, Australia and Britain's other heirs, on the basis of British paperwork from the 1920s and 1930s. It is the last surviving example of the empire drawing lines on a map and expecting the world to accept them, and the world has mostly declined.

keyDates.what: Mawson raises the flag along the East Antarctic coast for BANZARE
A British Order in Council claims the sector
The territory passes to Australia
Mawson Station opens, the first permanent base on the Antarctic mainland
The Antarctic Treaty suspends the claim

territories.name: The River Plate
territories.formalName: British occupations of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, 1806-1807

namesOverTime.name: Virreinato del Rio de la Plata
namesOverTime.note: The Spanish viceroyalty Britain attacked. Its collapse four years later produced Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia.

modernSuccessors.name: Argentina
modernSuccessors.note: The militias that beat the British in 1806 and 1807 became the political and military force behind the May Revolution of 1810 and independence in 1816.

modernSuccessors.name: Uruguay
modernSuccessors.note: Montevideo, held by Britain for seven months in 1807, became the capital of a state Britain helped invent twenty-one years later.

geoCoverage.label: Buenos Aires city and its immediate hinterland
geoCoverage.change: Sixteen hundred British soldiers held the largest city on the Atlantic coast of South America and nothing beyond a day's ride from it.

geoCoverage.label: Montevideo and the Banda Oriental coast
geoCoverage.change: After losing Buenos Aires, Britain stormed Montevideo across the river in February 1807 and held it as a base for a second attempt, which failed in July.

acquisitions.how: Commodore Home Popham, without orders from London, took 1,600 soldiers from the newly captured Cape of Good Hope across the Atlantic; Colonel William Beresford landed at Quilmes and walked into Buenos Aires two days later against almost no resistance.

counterparties.name: The Spanish Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata
counterparties.lost: Its capital, its treasury of about a million silver dollars which was shipped to London and paraded through the City, and any remaining belief among its own subjects that Spain could defend them.
counterparties.note: Viceroy Rafael de Sobremonte fled inland with the treasury and was later deposed by the people of Buenos Aires, not by Spain.

counterparties.name: The people of Buenos Aires
counterparties.lost: Nothing they kept: within seven weeks they had organised their own militias, retaken the city and discovered they no longer needed a viceroy.
counterparties.note: The invasion is taught in Argentina as the moment the criollos learned they could fight without Spain. The reconquista and defensa are national holidays.

people.name: Home Riggs Popham
people.role: commodore who launched the invasion on his own initiative and was court-martialled and reprimanded for it in 1807

people.name: William Carr Beresford
people.role: commanded the landing force, governed Buenos Aires for 46 days and surrendered it

people.name: Santiago de Liniers
people.role: French-born officer in Spanish service who crossed from Montevideo, gathered a force and retook the city on 12 August 1806

people.name: Martin de Alzaga
people.role: merchant and mayor who organised and armed the city's militia companies for the second defence in 1807

acquisitions.resistance: Overwhelming, and it came from the city rather than from Spain: within weeks Liniers had 4,000 men, and on 12 August 1806 they took the city back street by street, with civilians throwing tiles and boiling water from the roofs.

evidence.author: Ian Fletcher
evidence.work: The Waters of Oblivion: The British Invasion of the Rio de la Plata, 1806-1807
evidence.supports: The course of both invasions, the forces involved and the casualties.

acquisitions.how: Reinforcements from Britain under Sir Samuel Auchmuty stormed the walls of Montevideo before dawn on 3 February 1807 after a breaching battery brought them down, and held the city for seven months as a base for a second attack on Buenos Aires.

counterparties.name: The Spanish Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata
counterparties.lost: Its second city and only fortified port on the estuary, together with control of the river trade for seven months, during which British merchants sold so much cheap cotton that they broke the local market.
counterparties.note: A British newspaper, The Southern Star, was printed in Montevideo in English and Spanish during the occupation. It is the first newspaper published in what is now Uruguay.

people.name: Samuel Auchmuty
people.role: commanded the storming of Montevideo

people.name: John Whitelocke
people.role: arrived in May 1807 to command the whole expedition and destroyed it in the streets of Buenos Aires in July

cost.note: Roughly 600 to 900 British and Spanish soldiers were killed or wounded in the assault of 3 February 1807; contemporary British returns give about 120 British dead and Spanish losses of several hundred, and no complete count of civilians was made.

warrant.author: The British expedition, in its own returns
warrant.work: British returns of the River Plate expeditions
warrant.supports: Roughly 600 to 900 British and Spanish soldiers were killed or wounded in the assault of 3 February 1807; contemporary British returns give about 120 British dead and Spanish losses of several hundred, and no complete count of civilians was made.
warrant.check: Campaign returns, casualty states and despatches are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew; the despatches were printed in the London Gazette and the totals in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

acquisitions.resistance: The garrison and militia fought the assault at the breach and lost the city in a few hours; resistance afterwards took the form of a blockade of the countryside by irregular horsemen who cut the British off from supplies.

evidence.author: John Lynch
evidence.work: The Spanish American Revolutions 1808-1826
evidence.supports: The political effect of the invasions on the River Plate and the road to the May Revolution.

statusPeriods.label: Beresford governs Buenos Aires for 46 days
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Beresford kept the Spanish officials in place, guaranteed the Catholic religion and private property, cut the customs duty to 12.5 per cent and told the merchants they could trade freely with Britain. Then the city rose and took itself back.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buenos Aires, by a British general with no instructions from London
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The cabildo, the city council, continued to sit and was the body that organised the recapture.

statusPeriods.label: Montevideo under British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British general ruled the walled city, opened the port to British goods, printed a bilingual newspaper, and could not move ten miles inland without being shot at.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain held nothing at all in the River Plate between Beresford's surrender at Buenos Aires on 12 August 1806 and the storming of Montevideo on 3 February 1807. The gap is real and is the point: this was an invasion in instalments, not a colony.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Montevideo
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: A force raised in the city and across the river, under Santiago de Liniers, fought its way into Buenos Aires on 12 August 1806 and forced Beresford to surrender his whole command in the main square.

becomes.name: Buenos Aires, under a viceroy the city itself had chosen

led.name: Santiago de Liniers
led.role: led the recapture and was made viceroy by acclamation of the city, not by appointment from Madrid

led.name: Juan Martin de Pueyrredon
led.role: raised the first militia cavalry from the countryside and later became Supreme Director of the United Provinces

led.name: Manuela Pedraza
led.role: known in Argentine accounts as la Tucumana; fought in the recapture beside her husband and was granted a soldier's pay for it

cost.note: British returns give about 165 killed and wounded and 1,300 taken prisoner; local losses are usually given as around 300 killed and wounded. No count includes civilians killed in the street fighting.

warrant.author: The British expedition, in its own returns
warrant.work: British returns of the River Plate expeditions
warrant.supports: British returns give about 165 killed and wounded and 1,300 taken prisoner; local losses are usually given as around 300 killed and wounded. No count includes civilians killed in the street fighting.
warrant.check: Campaign returns, casualty states and despatches are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew; the despatches were printed in the London Gazette and the totals in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

departures.borders: No border changed. What changed was who held the guns: the city discovered it had defended itself without Spain, and four years later it deposed the viceroy it had itself installed.

departures.how: After Whitelocke lost about 2,500 men in the streets of Buenos Aires on 5 July 1807, he signed a capitulation agreeing to evacuate the entire River Plate within two months; the last British troops left Montevideo on 9 September 1807.

becomes.name: The Spanish Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata, for three more years

led.name: Santiago de Liniers
led.role: organised the defence of Buenos Aires in July 1807

led.name: Martin de Alzaga
led.role: mayor who fortified the city block by block and armed its militia companies

led.name: John Whitelocke
led.role: British commander; court-martialled at Chelsea in 1808 and declared unfit and unworthy to serve the King in any military capacity

cost.note: British casualties on 5 July 1807 are usually given as about 400 killed, 650 wounded and 1,900 captured, out of roughly 8,000 engaged. Local losses are less well recorded and were certainly in the hundreds, including civilians firing from rooftops.

departures.borders: Britain gave up every foot of ground it held in South America and never took any again. The territory it left became Argentina and Uruguay within twenty-two years, and Britain shaped both without ever governing either.

instrument.name: Capitulation signed by Whitelocke and Liniers at Buenos Aires
instrument.note: It required the British to evacuate the whole of the River Plate, including Montevideo, within two months, and exchanged all prisoners.

evidence.author: Ian Fletcher
evidence.work: The Waters of Oblivion: The British Invasion of the Rio de la Plata, 1806-1807
evidence.supports: Whitelocke's attack, the capitulation and the court-martial.

violence.note: Two invasions in fourteen months killed something like 1,500 people and put nearly 3,000 British soldiers into captivity; several hundred of them deserted and stayed, and their descendants are still in Argentina.

consequences.economicLegacy: The occupations dumped so much cheap British cotton on the River Plate that they created a permanent constituency for free trade. British merchant houses stayed after the soldiers left, and by 1825 Britain was the dominant trading partner of a country it had failed to conquer.
consequences.borderLegacy: Failure here shaped two countries. Argentine national identity dates its birth to the militias of 1806-07, and Britain, having learned it could not take the region by force, spent the next century controlling its trade instead.

peak.populationNote: Buenos Aires had roughly 45,000 inhabitants in 1806 and Montevideo about 9,000 in 1807. Britain never controlled more than the two cities and their immediate surroundings.

evidence.author: Ian Fletcher
evidence.work: The Waters of Oblivion: The British Invasion of the Rio de la Plata, 1806-1807
evidence.supports: The military narrative of both invasions and the casualty figures.

evidence.author: John Lynch
evidence.work: The Spanish American Revolutions 1808-1826
evidence.supports: The political consequences for the River Plate and the road to independence.

evidence.author: Klaus Gallo
evidence.work: Great Britain and Argentina: From Invasion to Recognition, 1806-26
evidence.supports: British aims in the River Plate and the shift from conquest to commerce.

contested.note: Casualty figures for both invasions come from British regimental returns and from Spanish and criollo accounts written to celebrate the victory, and they do not agree. Historians also disagree about whether Popham's expedition had any tacit approval in London or was entirely freelance; the court-martial found it unauthorised, but ministers took the silver.

pedagogy.hook: A British commodore invaded Argentina in 1806 without asking London, and by losing, helped invent the country he had tried to take.

misconception.belief: The British Empire expanded because British armies won.
misconception.correction: Britain took Buenos Aires twice and lost it twice, to militias raised by shopkeepers and cattle traders rather than by Spain. The commander of the second attempt was cashiered for it. Empire is also a record of defeats, and this one was decisive: Britain never again tried to conquer South America, and controlled it by trade instead.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the hinge between the two kinds of empire. Britain tried formal conquest in the River Plate, failed badly, and then got most of what it wanted anyway through loans, railways and shipping. The story of informal empire begins with a British defeat.

keyDates.what: Beresford takes Buenos Aires with 1,600 men
The city's own militia forces him to surrender
Britain storms Montevideo
Whitelocke loses 2,500 men in the streets of Buenos Aires
The last British troops leave the River Plate

territories.name: Argentina
territories.formalName: Argentina within the British informal empire, 1825-1948

namesOverTime.name: United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata

modernSuccessors.name: Argentina
modernSuccessors.note: Argentina was never a British colony. The map marks it because leaving it off makes the empire look smaller than it was: by 1913 British investors owned more of Argentina than of any colony except India.

geoCoverage.label: Buenos Aires and the pampas
geoCoverage.change: Britain never governed one acre of Argentina. The map marks the province where British capital, British railways and British meat packers concentrated, and draws it hatched because this is influence, not rule.

acquisitions.how: Britain recognised the United Provinces as independent and signed a treaty of amity and commerce that gave British merchants the same rights as Argentines, exemption from military service and forced loans, and freedom of worship, and gave Britain no territory at all.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Any prospect of reconquering the River Plate. British recognition of the new republics, pushed by George Canning, closed the question and Canning said so: he had called the New World into existence to redress the balance of the Old.
counterparties.note: Recognition was not charity. It secured the market and the debts, both of which were British.

counterparties.name: Argentine manufacturers and provincial economies
counterparties.lost: The interior provinces, whose textile and wine trades could not survive competition from British imports landed duty-free at Buenos Aires; the resulting fight between the port and the provinces shaped fifty years of Argentine civil war.
counterparties.note: Free trade was not neutral. It enriched the estancieros and the port and impoverished Tucuman, Cordoba and Mendoza, which is why the federalist wars happened.

instrument.name: Treaty of Amity, Commerce and Navigation between Great Britain and the United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata
instrument.note: Signed at Buenos Aires. Britain recognised the state; the state opened its rivers and its courts to British subjects on privileged terms.

people.name: George Canning
people.role: Foreign Secretary who recognised the Spanish American republics in 1824-25 to secure their trade for Britain and keep France out

people.name: Bernardino Rivadavia
people.role: Argentine minister and later president who negotiated the treaty and the 1824 Baring loan

acquisitions.resistance: There was nothing to resist by force, which is the point. Opposition came later and was economic and political: Rosas expelled British and French warships from the Parana in 1845, and Argentine nationalists from the 1930s attacked the meat and railway contracts as a disguised protectorate.

evidence.author: H. S. Ferns
evidence.work: Britain and Argentina in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The 1825 treaty, the Baring loan and the whole structure of the Anglo-Argentine relationship.

statusPeriods.label: Sovereign, and inside the British economy
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody in London gave orders in Buenos Aires. British power worked through debt owed to Baring Brothers, two thirds of the railway network owned in London, the ships that carried the beef, the banks that discounted the bills, and the knowledge that the Royal Navy could close the river.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buenos Aires, by Argentine governments
statusPeriods.franchise: Argentina's own: a narrow and heavily manipulated franchise until the Saenz Pena law of 1912 introduced the secret ballot and compulsory male voting; women voted from 1947.
statusPeriods.note: Informal empire had limits, and Argentina found them. In 1845 Britain and France blockaded Buenos Aires and forced a convoy up the Parana; Rosas's forces fought them at the Vuelta de Obligado on 20 November 1845, and Britain eventually signed a treaty in 1849 that apologised, returned captured ships and saluted the Argentine flag. Argentina still marks the day as its Day of National Sovereignty.

departures.how: Juan Peron bought the British-owned railways for 150 million pounds, paid out of the sterling Britain owed Argentina for wartime beef and grain, and on 1 March 1948 the largest single block of British property outside the empire changed hands at Retiro station in Buenos Aires.

becomes.name: Argentina, with a nationalised railway system

led.name: Juan Domingo Peron
led.role: President who made buying the railways the centrepiece of his campaign for economic independence

led.name: Miguel Miranda
led.role: head of Argentina's economic council, who negotiated the sterling-balances deal with Britain in 1946-48

led.name: Lisandro de la Torre
led.role: senator whose 1935 inquiry into the British meat companies exposed the Roca-Runciman arrangements; his colleague Enzo Bordabehere was shot dead on the Senate floor during the hearings

cost.money: 150 million pounds, paid in blocked sterling balances that Britain could not otherwise have repaid. Argentina bought a worn-out network at close to the price of a new one and later found the rolling stock life-expired.
cost.note: Nobody died in the transfer. The dispute is about value: Argentine critics said Peron overpaid for scrap, British critics said Britain sold at a discount to clear a debt it could not honour, and both are partly right.

departures.borders: No border moved, because Britain never held any territory here. What ended was ownership: 24,000 kilometres of railway, the tramways of Buenos Aires and the port works passed from London shareholders to the Argentine state.

instrument.name: Anglo-Argentine Agreement on trade and payments, known in Argentina as the Andes Agreement
instrument.note: It settled Argentina's wartime sterling balances by transferring the British-owned railways; the formal handover ceremony was on 1 March 1948.

contested.note: This entry uses the vocabulary of departure for something that was not one, because Argentina was never British and never left. What ended was economic dependence, and the model has no word for that. It is worth noticing that the atlas can describe the end of a colony more easily than the end of informal empire.

evidence.author: Colin M. Lewis
evidence.work: British Railways in Argentina 1857-1914: A Case Study of Foreign Investment
evidence.supports: The scale, ownership and finances of the British-owned Argentine railway network.

consequences.economicLegacy: By 1913 British investors held roughly 350 million pounds in Argentina, about a tenth of all British overseas investment and more than in any colony except India; they owned about two thirds of a 33,000-kilometre railway network built to carry grain and beef to the ports and to Britain.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain drew no borders in Argentina and fought no war there after 1807 until 1982, when a dispute over islands 500 kilometres off the Argentine coast turned 160 years of economic entanglement into a war.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Argentine football, rugby, polo and the railway timetable are all British imports; so are the words used for them. British-founded schools, banks and clubs are still trading in Buenos Aires.

peak.populationNote: Britain governed no territory and no people in Argentina. The zeroes are deliberate: this is what informal empire looks like in a table designed for colonies. In 1913 Argentina's population was about 7.5 million and Britain owned roughly a third of its fixed capital.

evidence.author: H. S. Ferns
evidence.work: Britain and Argentina in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The whole relationship, argued as a partnership between two economies rather than a dependency.

evidence.author: John Gallagher and Ronald Robinson
evidence.work: The Imperialism of Free Trade
evidence.supports: The concept of informal empire, of which Argentina is the founding example in this article.

evidence.author: D. C. M. Platt
evidence.work: Latin America and British Trade, 1806-1914
evidence.supports: The sceptical case: that British influence in Latin America was commercial rather than political and that 'informal empire' overstates it.

contested.note: Whether Argentina belongs in an atlas of the British Empire at all is one of the liveliest arguments in imperial history. Gallagher and Robinson made it the type case of informal empire in 1953; Ferns argued in 1960 that Argentina was a partner that used British capital for its own purposes; Platt argued in 1972 that the Foreign Office rarely intervened and that trade is not rule. This record includes Argentina and marks the disagreement rather than settling it.

positions.claim: Britain ruled Argentina in everything but name, through debt, railways, shipping and the threat of the fleet, and the 1933 Roca-Runciman treaty proves it.
positions.heldBy: Gallagher and Robinson (1953), and the Argentine revisionist historians of the 1930s and after.

positions.claim: Argentina used British capital to build itself, kept its own foreign policy, defeated a British blockade in the 1840s, and was a partner rather than a dependency.
positions.heldBy: H. S. Ferns (1960) and D. C. M. Platt (1972).

pedagogy.hook: In 1933 Argentina's vice-president said his country was, economically, an integral part of the British Empire, and he said it to defend the deal he had just signed.

misconception.belief: The British Empire is what was coloured pink on the map.
misconception.correction: By 1913 Britain owned about two thirds of Argentina's railways, most of its trams, its meat-packing plants and its banks, and held roughly a tenth of all its overseas investment there. Argentina was never pink on any map. If you count only the colonies, you undercount the empire by an entire continent's worth of economic control.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Argentina is the test case for the idea of informal empire, and the argument about it is still running. It teaches students to ask not only who ruled a place but who owned it, who lent to it, who shipped its exports and who set the price, which are questions the pink map cannot answer.

keyDates.what: The Baring loan: Buenos Aires borrows a million pounds and defaults in 1828
Vuelta de Obligado: Argentina fights the Anglo-French blockade and now marks the day as national sovereignty day
The Baring crisis: Argentina's default nearly brings down a London bank
The Roca-Runciman treaty ties Argentine beef to British terms
Peron buys the British railways for 150 million pounds

territories.name: Uruguay
territories.formalName: The Oriental Republic of Uruguay within the British informal empire

from.note: A regional name in use through the late colonial period rather than a formal title with a start date.

modernSuccessors.name: Uruguay
modernSuccessors.note: Uruguay exists as a separate country because British mediation in 1828 required it, and because Britain wanted neither Buenos Aires nor Rio de Janeiro to control both banks of the estuary.

to.note: The British-owned railways, waterworks and trams were made over to the Uruguayan state under the sterling-balances settlement negotiated from 1948; the state railway company AFE was constituted in 1952, and accounts date the handover to either end of that process.

geoCoverage.label: A buffer state made to British specifications
geoCoverage.change: Britain never ruled Uruguay for a day after 1807. It invented it: British mediation created the state in 1828, and British capital owned its railways, its trams, its waterworks and its meat plants for the next century.

acquisitions.how: Lord Ponsonby, sent by Canning to end the war between Buenos Aires and Brazil, told Buenos Aires and Rio de Janeiro they would get peace only if they agreed on an independent state between them, and the Preliminary Peace Convention signed at Rio de Janeiro on 27 August 1828 created Uruguay to a British design.

counterparties.name: The Empire of Brazil
counterparties.lost: Its Cisplatine Province, annexed in 1821 and fought over since 1825. Brazil gave up the whole territory rather than continue a war that was closing the river to trade.
counterparties.note: Ponsonby's instructions were explicit that Britain's interest was free navigation of the River Plate and its tributaries for British shipping.

counterparties.name: The United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata
counterparties.lost: The Banda Oriental, which Buenos Aires regarded as its own and had gone to war to recover; it got neither the territory nor the war it wanted.
counterparties.note: Both belligerents had asked Britain to mediate because both were bankrupt and both owed money in London.

counterparties.name: The Charrua and Minuane peoples
counterparties.lost: Everything, and not to Britain. The new republic's army massacred the surviving Charrua at Salsipuedes on 11 April 1831, three years after independence, and four survivors were shipped to Paris and exhibited.
counterparties.note: The state Britain helped invent completed the destruction of the region's indigenous population within three years of its founding. Naming it here is the point: informal empire does not mean nobody lost anything.

instrument.name: Preliminary Peace Convention between Brazil and the United Provinces, signed at Rio de Janeiro
instrument.note: Britain mediated, drafted and guaranteed it. The convention created an independent state without naming its borders precisely, which left disputes that lasted decades.

people.name: John Ponsonby, Viscount Ponsonby
people.role: British minister at Buenos Aires and Rio who forced the buffer-state solution on both belligerents

people.name: Juan Antonio Lavalleja
people.role: led the Thirty-Three Orientals who began the rising against Brazil in 1825

people.name: Fructuoso Rivera
people.role: first president of Uruguay, and the commander responsible for the massacre of the Charrua at Salsipuedes in 1831

acquisitions.resistance: Nobody resisted the creation of the state; both belligerents accepted it because they were exhausted and in debt. Resistance to the British position in the region came later, in the long Anglo-French intervention in the Uruguayan civil war between 1843 and 1851.

evidence.author: John Lynch
evidence.work: The Spanish American Revolutions 1808-1826
evidence.supports: The Cisplatine war, British mediation and the creation of Uruguay.

to.note: The British-owned railways, waterworks and trams were made over to the Uruguayan state under the sterling-balances settlement negotiated from 1948; the state railway company AFE was constituted in 1952, and accounts date the handover to either end of that process.

statusPeriods.label: A sovereign buffer state inside the British trading system
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Uruguayan governments governed. British power came from owning the Central Uruguay Railway, the Montevideo waterworks, the gasworks, the trams and the frigorificos that froze the beef, and from being the market that bought almost everything the country sold.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Montevideo, by Uruguayan governments
statusPeriods.franchise: Uruguay's own, and it ran ahead of Britain's colonies: universal male suffrage and the secret ballot from 1918, votes for women from 1932, and a welfare state built under Jose Batlle y Ordonez from 1903.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1843 and 1851 Britain and France intervened directly in Uruguay's civil war, keeping Montevideo supplied through a nine-year siege in which Giuseppe Garibaldi commanded the Italian Legion. It is the sharpest example of informal empire using force without taking territory.

date.note: The British-owned railways, waterworks and trams were made over to the Uruguayan state under the sterling-balances settlement negotiated from 1948; the state railway company AFE was constituted in 1952, and accounts date the handover to either end of that process.

departures.how: Uruguay, like Argentina, used the sterling Britain owed it for wartime meat to buy out British-owned railways, trams and waterworks, converting a debt Britain could not pay into ownership of the infrastructure that had defined the relationship.

becomes.name: Uruguay, with nationalised railways and utilities

led.name: Luis Batlle Berres
led.role: President who pushed the buy-out of British assets as part of a programme of state ownership

led.name: Jose Batlle y Ordonez
led.role: earlier president whose nationalisations from 1903 onwards had already taken banking, insurance and power out of foreign hands and set the pattern

cost.note: No one was killed. The cost to Britain was the loss of its last major asset base in South America; the cost to Uruguay was buying a worn-out railway network at a price fixed by a debt settlement rather than by its value.

departures.borders: No border moved. Britain had never held territory in Uruguay after 1807, and what changed hands was rolling stock, track and water pipes.

contested.note: As with Argentina, this record uses the language of departure for the end of an economic relationship rather than of rule. There is also no agreed date: the sterling settlement, the transfer of the railways and the creation of the state railway company are spread across four years.

violence.note: Britain and France blockaded the River Plate and held Montevideo through the nine-year siege of the Guerra Grande between 1843 and 1851, without ever claiming an inch of Uruguayan soil.

consequences.economicLegacy: British capital built the railway network, the port of Montevideo, the trams and the first refrigerated meat plants; by 1913 British investment in Uruguay was around 45 million pounds in a country of a million people.
consequences.borderLegacy: Uruguay's existence is itself the border legacy: a state created in 1828 so that neither of its neighbours would control both banks of a river that British ships needed open.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Football arrived with British railway workers in the 1880s. The country that Britain invented as a buffer won the first World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina in Montevideo.

peak.populationNote: Britain governed no territory and no people in Uruguay. The zeroes are deliberate. Uruguay's own population in 1913 was about 1.2 million.

evidence.author: Peter Winn
evidence.work: British Informal Empire in Uruguay in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The argument that Uruguay was the clearest case of British informal empire in South America.

evidence.author: John Lynch
evidence.work: The Spanish American Revolutions 1808-1826
evidence.supports: The Cisplatine war and the British-brokered settlement of 1828.

contested.note: Peter Winn argued in 1976 that Uruguay was British informal empire in its purest form; others reply that Uruguay had a strong state, an early welfare system and a foreign policy of its own, and used British capital rather than being used by it. The same argument as over Argentina, on a smaller and clearer case.

pedagogy.hook: Uruguay exists because Britain did not want either Argentina or Brazil to own both banks of the river its ships used.

misconception.belief: Britain drew borders only inside its own empire.
misconception.correction: The border between Brazil and Argentina runs where it does because a British diplomat in 1828 refused to end a war on any other terms than an independent state in between. Britain never governed Uruguay, never garrisoned it and never coloured it pink, and it made the country anyway.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Uruguay shows informal empire doing the thing usually thought to need a flag: making a country. It also shows the limits of the idea, because the state Britain created went on to build a welfare system, nationalise foreign assets and beat Britain's other client at football.

keyDates.what: British mediation creates Uruguay as a buffer state
The nine-year siege of Montevideo begins; Britain and France hold the port
The British-owned Central Uruguay Railway opens
Batlle y Ordonez begins nationalising foreign-owned utilities
Uruguay buys out the British railways with wartime sterling balances

territories.name: The Ottoman Empire
territories.formalName: The Ottoman Empire under the capitulations and the Public Debt Administration

namesOverTime.name: Devlet-i Aliyye-i Osmaniyye

from.note: The traditional founding date of the Ottoman state; the dynasty's origins are not documented precisely.

namesOverTime.note: The Sublime Ottoman State. British despatches called it the Porte, after the gate of the grand vizier's offices.

modernSuccessors.name: Turkey
modernSuccessors.note: The republic that emerged from the Ottoman collapse abolished the last of the foreign privileges at Lausanne in 1923 and paid off the last of the Ottoman debt in 1954.

geoCoverage.label: The Ottoman core, drawn as modern Turkey
geoCoverage.change: Britain never governed Ottoman territory here. The unit stands for the empire that signed the 1838 commercial convention; the geometry has no Ottoman shape, so the map shows the Anatolian core and draws it hatched.

acquisitions.how: At Balta Liman on the Bosphorus, Britain got the Ottoman government to abolish its own trading monopolies and cap import duty at 5 per cent, in exchange for diplomatic support against Muhammad Ali of Egypt, who was threatening to take the empire apart.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman government
counterparties.lost: The power to protect its own industries or to tax trade for revenue. Ottoman merchants paid a higher internal duty than foreigners paid to import, so foreign goods were cheaper inside the empire than domestic ones.
counterparties.note: The Ottomans signed because they needed Britain against Muhammad Ali. That is the mechanism of informal empire in one sentence: a state trades its economic sovereignty for protection it cannot otherwise buy.

counterparties.name: Ottoman manufacturers and guilds
counterparties.lost: The textile trades of Aleppo, Bursa and Salonica, which could not compete with Lancashire cotton landed at 5 per cent duty; the region became an exporter of raw silk, cotton and tobacco instead of cloth.
counterparties.note: Whether the treaty caused the deindustrialisation or merely accelerated a process already under way is argued about; Sevket Pamuk's figures show the timing but not, on their own, the cause.

counterparties.name: Muhammad Ali of Egypt
counterparties.lost: His monopolies, which the convention abolished throughout the empire including Egypt, and with them the revenue base of his army; the settlement of 1840-41 cut that army from over 100,000 men to 18,000.
counterparties.note: Britain destroyed the strongest state in the eastern Mediterranean with a commercial treaty and a naval squadron, not with an invasion.

instrument.name: Convention of Balta Liman, the Anglo-Ottoman Commercial Convention
instrument.note: Other powers signed equivalent conventions within two years, so the terms Britain extracted became the terms of all Ottoman trade.

people.name: Henry Temple, Viscount Palmerston
people.role: Foreign Secretary who used the convention and then a fleet to break Muhammad Ali and prop up the Ottoman state as a barrier to Russia

people.name: Mustafa Resid Pasha
people.role: Ottoman foreign minister who negotiated the convention and, a year later, launched the Tanzimat reforms it helped pay for

people.name: John Ponsonby, Viscount Ponsonby
people.role: British ambassador at Constantinople who pressed the convention through; the same diplomat who had invented Uruguay ten years earlier

acquisitions.resistance: Not by force. Ottoman resistance took the form of reform: the Tanzimat decrees from 1839, the attempt to build a modern tax state, and repeated efforts to renegotiate the tariff, which Britain blocked until 1861 and again until 1907.

evidence.author: Sevket Pamuk
evidence.work: The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism, 1820-1913
evidence.supports: The 1838 convention, tariff levels, trade figures and the structure of Ottoman economic dependence.

statusPeriods.label: Free trade, capitulations and consular courts
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Sultan ruled. British power ran through a 5 per cent tariff ceiling he could not raise, capitulations that put British subjects and their local protected clients outside Ottoman courts and taxes, and a British fleet that could enter the Straits.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Constantinople, by the Ottoman government
statusPeriods.franchise: An absolute monarchy. A parliament opened in March 1877 and was suspended by Abdulhamid II in February 1878; it did not sit again until the Young Turk revolution of 1908.
statusPeriods.note: The capitulations began in 1580 as a privilege the Sultan granted from strength. By the 1850s they had become a right foreigners enforced from strength, and consulates were selling protection certificates to Ottoman subjects who wanted to escape Ottoman taxation.

statusPeriods.label: European bondholders collect the taxes
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After the Ottoman default of 1875 the Decree of Muharrem handed six major revenues, on salt, stamps, spirits, fish, silk and tobacco, to a Public Debt Administration run by European bondholders' representatives, which collected them directly with its own staff across the empire.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Constantinople: the Sultan's ministries for everything except the pledged revenues, which the bondholders' council ran
statusPeriods.franchise: Restored in 1908 after the Young Turk revolution, then narrowed again under the Committee of Union and Progress from 1913.
statusPeriods.note: By 1911 the Public Debt Administration employed around 8,900 people, more than the Ottoman finance ministry itself. It was not a British institution alone, but British bondholders held a large share and the British seat on its council was one of the most powerful jobs in the empire.

departures.how: On 9 September 1914 the Ottoman government told the powers that the capitulations would end on 1 October; Britain, France and Russia all protested and none could stop it, and five weeks later the empire entered the war against them.

becomes.name: The Ottoman Empire at war with Britain, then the Republic of Turkey

led.name: Mehmed Talat Pasha
led.role: interior minister in the government that abolished the capitulations unilaterally in 1914

led.name: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk
led.role: led the national struggle of 1919-22 that expelled the occupying and Greek forces and made the abolition permanent at Lausanne

led.name: Ismet Inonu
led.role: negotiated the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, which ended the capitulations and the foreign debt administration in law

cost.note: The end of the treaty system cost nothing by itself; what followed cost enormously. The Ottoman entry into the war led to the collapse and partition of the empire, to the Armenian genocide of 1915-16, and to a war of independence that ran to 1922. Death tolls for that whole sequence run into millions and are counted differently by every party to them.

departures.borders: The Ottoman Empire that escaped informal empire did not survive it. Between 1918 and 1923 its Arab provinces became British and French mandates, its capital was occupied, and the state that emerged at Lausanne was Anatolia and eastern Thrace alone.

instrument.name: Ottoman note abolishing the Capitulations, and the Treaty of Lausanne
instrument.note: The unilateral abolition of 1914 was rejected by the powers and reimposed on the defeated empire in 1920; the Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923 ended the capitulations for good and settled the Ottoman debt on the successor states.

contested.note: Dating the end of Ottoman informal empire is genuinely awkward. The capitulations were abolished unilaterally in 1914, reimposed by the victors at Sevres in 1920, and finally ended at Lausanne in 1923. This record uses 1914 because that is when the Ottoman state acted, and says plainly that the act did not stick for nine more years.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Ottoman Public Debt Administration ran until 1923 and the successor states went on paying: the Turkish Republic made its last payment on Ottoman debt in 1954, 79 years after the default that created the institution.
consequences.borderLegacy: Every border in the modern Middle East was drawn out of the Ottoman collapse, and the sequence began with a state weakened by debt and treaty privileges long before any British soldier arrived.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Ottoman commercial law was rewritten around European codes to satisfy foreign creditors and merchants, and mixed courts staffed partly by foreigners tried cases involving them.

peak.populationNote: Britain governed no Ottoman territory and no Ottoman subjects. The zeroes are deliberate: informal empire has no area and no population, which is precisely why it is invisible on the pink map. The Ottoman Empire itself had roughly 25 million people in 1881.

evidence.author: Sevket Pamuk
evidence.work: The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism, 1820-1913
evidence.supports: Trade, tariffs, foreign debt and the workings of the Public Debt Administration.

evidence.author: Donald Quataert
evidence.work: The Ottoman Empire, 1700-1922
evidence.supports: The general narrative of Ottoman decline, reform and European penetration.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how far European economic penetration caused Ottoman weakness rather than following from it. Pamuk emphasises the structural effects of free trade and debt; Quataert and others stress Ottoman agency, reform and the strength of local production well into the twentieth century. The employment figure for the Debt Administration, around 8,900 in 1911, is from its own reports.

pedagogy.hook: By 1911 a European bondholders' agency in Istanbul employed more people than the Ottoman finance ministry, and it collected the taxes on salt, fish, silk and tobacco itself.

misconception.belief: Britain's power in the Middle East began when it occupied Egypt in 1882 or took the mandates in 1920.
misconception.correction: It began in 1838 with a trade treaty. The Convention of Balta Liman capped Ottoman import duties at 5 per cent and abolished the state's monopolies; the 1881 debt decree handed six of its taxes to foreign bondholders. Britain shaped the Ottoman Empire for eighty years before a British soldier occupied any of it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Ottoman case shows informal empire's most powerful tool, which is not the gunboat but the loan. A state that cannot set its own tariff or collect its own taxes has already lost most of what sovereignty means, and it will look independent on every map ever printed.

keyDates.what: The Convention of Balta Liman caps Ottoman tariffs at 5 per cent
The Ottoman Empire defaults on its foreign debt
The Decree of Muharrem creates the Public Debt Administration
The Ottoman government abolishes the capitulations unilaterally
The Treaty of Lausanne ends the foreign privileges for good

territories.name: Egypt before 1882
territories.formalName: The Khedivate of Egypt under European financial control, 1840-1882

namesOverTime.name: Eyalet, then Khedivate, of Egypt
namesOverTime.note: Egypt was legally an Ottoman province throughout, ruled by Muhammad Ali's family as hereditary viceroys, and it stayed legally Ottoman for 32 years after the British occupation began.

namesOverTime.name: Jumhuriyat Misr al-Arabiyah (the Arab Republic of Egypt)

modernSuccessors.name: Arab Republic of Egypt
modernSuccessors.note: The British occupation that began in 1882 ran, in one form or another, until the last troops left the Canal Zone in June 1956.

geoCoverage.label: The Nile valley and delta
geoCoverage.change: Britain governed nothing in Egypt. The hatching marks a state whose monopolies had been abolished by a treaty it did not want and whose army had been cut to 18,000 men by a settlement it did not sign.

geoCoverage.label: With the Suez Canal
geoCoverage.change: The canal opened on 17 November 1869, dug largely by conscripted Egyptian labour and paid for by Egyptian borrowing. Within six years Britain owned 44 per cent of the company that ran it and Egypt owned none.

acquisitions.how: Britain led a coalition that bombarded Muhammad Ali's forces out of Syria, forced him back to Egypt, cut his army to 18,000 men and abolished the state monopolies that had funded it, leaving Egypt hereditary to his family and dependent on European money.

counterparties.name: Muhammad Ali and the Egyptian state he had built
counterparties.lost: Syria, Crete and the Hijaz, an army of over 100,000 men, and the monopoly system that had financed Egypt's cotton mills, arsenals and schools. Egypt became a supplier of raw cotton instead of a state trying to industrialise.
counterparties.note: Egypt under Muhammad Ali was the most serious non-European attempt at industrialisation before Japan's. Britain broke it in 1840 with a fleet and a commercial convention, and Egyptian nationalists have argued about it ever since.

counterparties.name: Egyptian peasants
counterparties.lost: Their labour, twice over: to the corvee that dug the Suez Canal in the 1860s, and to the taxes that serviced a foreign debt which rose from about 3 million pounds in 1863 to roughly 100 million by 1876.
counterparties.note: Contemporary estimates of the number conscripted to dig the canal run to over a million men working in rotation. Death tolls are quoted confidently in many books and are not reliably documented; this record gives the labour figure and refuses the casualty figure.

instrument.name: Convention of London for the Pacification of the Levant
instrument.note: Signed by Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia. The firman of 1 June 1841 then fixed Muhammad Ali's family in Egypt as hereditary viceroys under Ottoman suzerainty, with a capped army.

people.name: Muhammad Ali Pasha
people.role: Ottoman commander who made Egypt an autonomous state, built its army, industry and canals, and was cut down to size by a European coalition in 1840

people.name: Henry Temple, Viscount Palmerston
people.role: Foreign Secretary who organised the coalition against him

people.name: Ferdinand de Lesseps
people.role: French promoter of the Suez Canal, opened 1869, which Britain opposed until it owned a share of it

cost.money: Egypt's foreign debt rose from about 3 million pounds in 1863 to roughly 100 million by 1876, at interest rates that reached 26 per cent on some issues after discounts and commissions.
cost.note: The debt figures come from the reports of the European controllers and from the 1878 Cave and Goschen-Joubert inquiries; they are broadly agreed, though the effective interest rates are calculated differently by different historians.

warrant.author: Stephen Cave, and the Goschen–Joubert mission
warrant.work: Report on the Financial Condition of Egypt (the Cave report), and the Goschen–Joubert settlement
warrant.supports: The debt figures come from the reports of the European controllers and from the 1878 Cave and Goschen-Joubert inquiries; they are broadly agreed, though the effective interest rates are calculated differently by different historians.
warrant.check: Reports of colonial commissions and boards of inquiry are Command Papers: British Parliamentary Papers, and the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The debt figures are the bondholders’ own inquiries. They are broadly agreed; the effective interest rates are not.

acquisitions.resistance: Egyptian resistance to European control was constitutional before it was military: the Chamber of Delegates demanded control of the budget from 1879, and Colonel Ahmad Urabi's movement, with the slogan Egypt for the Egyptians, forced the Khedive to accept a nationalist ministry in February 1882.

evidence.author: Juan R. I. Cole
evidence.work: Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East: Social and Cultural Origins of Egypt's Urabi Movement
evidence.supports: The social basis of the Urabi movement and the effects of debt and European control on Egyptian society.

acquisitions.how: Disraeli bought the bankrupt Khedive Ismail's 176,602 Suez Canal shares for 3,976,582 pounds, borrowing the money overnight from Rothschild because Parliament was not sitting, and made the British government the largest single shareholder in a French-run company on Egyptian soil.

counterparties.name: The Khedive Ismail and the Egyptian state
counterparties.lost: Egypt's 44 per cent stake in the canal its own people had dug, sold at a distress price to meet debt payments. Egypt got no dividend from the canal for the next eighty years and Britain's stake paid for itself many times over.
counterparties.note: Ismail was deposed four years later, at British and French request, by the Ottoman Sultan. His son Tewfik replaced him and depended entirely on the powers who had installed him.

instrument.name: Contract for the purchase of the Khedive's shares in the Suez Canal Company
instrument.note: Disraeli told Queen Victoria: 'You have it, Madam.' The Commons voted the money retrospectively in 1876.

people.name: Benjamin Disraeli
people.role: Prime Minister who bought the shares without parliamentary authority

people.name: Ismail Pasha
people.role: Khedive who borrowed to modernise Egypt, sold the canal shares to service the debt and was deposed in 1879

people.name: Lionel de Rothschild
people.role: lent the British government four million pounds overnight at 2.5 per cent commission

acquisitions.resistance: None at the point of sale; Ismail needed the money in days. The consequences drove the resistance: European control of the budget from 1876, a European cabinet in 1878, the deposition of 1879 and the Urabi movement that followed.

evidence.author: P. J. Cain and A. G. Hopkins
evidence.work: British Imperialism: Innovation and Expansion 1688-1914
evidence.supports: The financial motives behind British policy in Egypt and the role of the City in it.

statusPeriods.label: An Ottoman province in the European money market
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Khedive governed and borrowed. British power came from the fleet that had beaten his father, the tariff treaty that had abolished the monopolies, and the London and Paris houses that lent him money at rates no European state would have paid.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cairo, by the Khedive under Ottoman suzerainty
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1866, when Ismail created a Chamber of Delegates elected indirectly by village headmen. It had no power until it demanded some in 1879.
statusPeriods.note: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and Britain had opposed it for fifteen years as a French project; within six years of its opening the British government owned the largest single block of its shares.

statusPeriods.label: The Caisse de la Dette and the Dual Control
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After Egypt suspended payments, a commission of European bondholders' agents took charge of the pledged revenues; in 1878 a British controller took the finance ministry and a French one public works, and in 1879 the powers had the Khedive deposed for resisting them.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Kept at 0 because Egypt remained legally an Ottoman province with its own government: no British official held Egyptian sovereign authority. The number is a poor description of what was happening, and the atlas records that tension rather than hiding it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cairo, by a Khedive the powers had installed, with British and French controllers inside his cabinet
statusPeriods.franchise: The Chamber of Delegates, indirectly elected, demanded control of the budget in 1879 and got a nationalist ministry in February 1882. Britain and France ended both by invading.
statusPeriods.note: About two thirds of Egyptian state revenue was going to foreign creditors by 1880.

departures.how: The Royal Navy bombarded Alexandria on 11 July 1882, Wolseley destroyed Urabi's army at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September and British troops entered Cairo the next day, turning eighty years of financial pressure into a military occupation that lasted until 1956.

becomes.name: British-occupied Egypt, legally still an Ottoman province

led.name: Ahmad Urabi
led.role: Egyptian-born colonel who led the army and the nationalist movement, became war minister in 1882, was defeated at Tel el-Kebir and exiled to Ceylon

led.name: Garnet Wolseley
led.role: commanded the invasion and won Tel el-Kebir in a dawn attack lasting under an hour

led.name: William Ewart Gladstone
led.role: Prime Minister who had denounced imperial adventures and ordered this one, and whose government promised to withdraw as soon as order allowed

led.name: Evelyn Baring, Lord Cromer
led.role: Consul-General from 1883 to 1907, who ran Egypt for 24 years from an office with no constitutional standing at all

cost.note: British losses at Tel el-Kebir were 57 killed. Egyptian dead there are usually estimated at about 2,000, from British reports; no Egyptian count was made. Roughly 250 Egyptians and 50 Europeans died in the Alexandria riots of 11 June 1882, and an unknown number in the bombardment and the fire that followed.

warrant.author: The British expeditionary force, in its own returns
warrant.work: British returns of the Egyptian campaign of 1882
warrant.supports: British losses at Tel el-Kebir were 57 killed. Egyptian dead there are usually estimated at about 2,000, from British reports; no Egyptian count was made. Roughly 250 Egyptians and 50 Europeans died in the Alexandria riots of 11 June 1882, and an unknown number in the bombardment and the fire tha…
warrant.check: Campaign returns, casualty states and despatches are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew; the despatches were printed in the London Gazette and the totals in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

departures.borders: No border changed. Egypt stayed an Ottoman province in law, with an Egyptian government, an Egyptian flag and a British army, which is why Britain could occupy it for 32 years without ever annexing it.

instrument.name: None. There was no treaty, no annexation and no declaration of protectorate until 1914.
instrument.note: The absence of an instrument is the fact worth teaching. Britain governed Egypt for three decades through a consul-general advising a nominally independent ruler, a system Cromer called the Veiled Protectorate.

contested.note: This is the only entry in the atlas where a departure makes a place more British, not less: what ends here is informal empire, and what replaces it is occupation. The model has no word for that, so the record uses 'transfer to another power' and says exactly what happened.

positions.claim: Britain invaded Egypt to protect the route to India after a local nationalist crisis threatened order, not to protect investors.
positions.heldBy: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher, Africa and the Victorians (1961).

positions.claim: Britain invaded to protect bondholders and the Suez Canal Company shares, and the strategic argument was assembled afterwards.
positions.heldBy: A. G. Hopkins (1986) and Cain and Hopkins, British Imperialism (1993).

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The strategic explanation of the 1882 occupation and its place in the partition of Africa.

populationTransfer.note: The Suez Canal was dug largely by Egyptian peasants conscripted under the corvee, working in rotation in their tens of thousands until the practice was curtailed in 1864 after international protest.

violence.note: The bombardment of Alexandria on 11 July 1882 burned much of the European quarter, and Tel el-Kebir two months later broke the Egyptian army in under an hour.

consequences.economicLegacy: Egypt's cotton became a single-crop export economy geared to Lancashire; its canal paid dividends to Paris and London for eighty-seven years; and its debts were serviced ahead of its own budget until the 1940s.
consequences.borderLegacy: The occupation of 1882 set off the scramble for Africa: France's resentment at being excluded from Egypt pushed it into West and Central Africa, and Britain followed up the Nile into Sudan to protect the water supply of the country it had occupied.

peak.populationNote: Britain governed no Egyptian territory and no Egyptians before September 1882. The zeroes are deliberate: this record covers the years of influence without rule. Egypt's own population in 1882 was about 6.8 million.

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The classic strategic account of why Britain occupied Egypt in 1882.

evidence.author: P. J. Cain and A. G. Hopkins
evidence.work: British Imperialism: Innovation and Expansion 1688-1914
evidence.supports: The financial account: debt, bondholders and the City as drivers of the occupation.

evidence.author: Juan R. I. Cole
evidence.work: Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East: Social and Cultural Origins of Egypt's Urabi Movement
evidence.supports: The Egyptian side: who Urabi's supporters were and what they wanted.

contested.note: Why Britain occupied Egypt is one of the most argued questions in imperial history, and the answer decides how you read the whole scramble for Africa. Robinson and Gallagher say strategy and a crisis on the periphery; Cain and Hopkins and A. G. Hopkins say finance and the City. Both camps use the same cabinet papers. The date Britain took Egypt is disputed too: 1882 by occupation, 1914 by protectorate, and never by annexation.

pedagogy.hook: Egypt dug the Suez Canal with conscripted labour, borrowed to pay for it, went bankrupt, and sold its share of the canal to Britain for less than four million pounds.

misconception.belief: Britain took Egypt in 1882 and that is when Egypt became part of the British Empire.
misconception.correction: Egypt was never annexed. In 1882 Britain invaded and occupied a province that remained legally Ottoman, ruled by an Egyptian khedive, with an Egyptian government and its own flag. Britain declared a protectorate only in December 1914, ended it in 1922, and kept troops there until 1956. Ask when Egypt became British and there is no single answer, which is the answer.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Egypt is where informal empire turns into formal empire in front of you, and you can watch the mechanism: a loan, a default, a foreign commission, a nationalist movement, an invasion to protect the creditors, and a promise to leave that lasted 74 years.

keyDates.what: European powers break Muhammad Ali and cap Egypt's army at 18,000
The Suez Canal opens
Disraeli buys the Khedive's canal shares for under 4 million pounds
The Caisse de la Dette puts European bondholders in charge of Egypt's revenues
The Royal Navy bombards Alexandria

namesOverTime.name: Nihon-koku (Japan)
namesOverTime.note: The 1947 constitution renounced the empire, the army and the emperor's sovereignty in the same document.

modernSuccessors.name: Japan
modernSuccessors.note: Japan is the only state in this atlas that entered the European treaty system and got out of it on its own terms, then built an empire of its own and imposed unequal treaties on its neighbours.

geoCoverage.label: The treaty ports and the foreign settlements
geoCoverage.change: Britain governed no Japanese territory. It held consular courts, a fixed tariff and, from 1863 to 1875, a garrison at Yokohama; the unit is drawn hatched because the reach was into the ports, not over the country.

acquisitions.how: Lord Elgin arrived at Edo four weeks after burning his way through the Second Opium War in China, and the Tokugawa government, which had watched what happened there, signed a treaty giving Britain consular courts, a fixed 5 per cent tariff and residence at five ports.

counterparties.name: The Tokugawa shogunate
