counterparties.lost: Control of its own tariffs and jurisdiction over foreigners on its soil, and with them its authority: the treaties split the Japanese elite and the shogunate fell ten years later, partly because it had signed them.
counterparties.note: The shogunate signed under the shadow of China's defeat rather than under direct attack. Its critics used the word for expelling barbarians as their slogan, and then, in power, kept the treaties and modernised instead.

counterparties.name: Japanese merchants and the domain economies
counterparties.lost: A protected market. The gold-silver exchange ratio written into the treaties let foreign traders drain Japanese gold in 1859-60, and the tariff ceiling kept Japan from protecting new industries for forty years.
counterparties.note: Recovering tariff autonomy took Japan until 1911, twelve years after it recovered its courts.

instrument.name: Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Amity and Commerce
instrument.note: One of the Ansei treaties, signed with the United States, Netherlands, Russia, Britain and France in 1858. Britain had already signed a limited convention at Nagasaki in October 1854.

people.name: James Bruce, Earl of Elgin
people.role: negotiated the 1858 treaty weeks after commanding the campaign that forced the Treaty of Tianjin on China

people.name: Harry Parkes
people.role: British minister from 1865 to 1883, who backed the Satsuma and Choshu domains against the shogunate and shaped the settlement that followed

people.name: Mutsu Munemitsu
people.role: foreign minister who negotiated the 1894 treaty that ended British extraterritoriality

acquisitions.resistance: Violent and effective. Attacks on foreigners culminated in the killing of the merchant Charles Richardson in 1862; Britain bombarded Kagoshima in August 1863 and, with three allies, destroyed the Choshu forts at Shimonoseki in September 1864. Both domains then bought British ships and became Britain's partners.

evidence.author: W. G. Beasley
evidence.work: Great Britain and the Opening of Japan 1834-1858
evidence.supports: The negotiation of the 1854 and 1858 treaties and British aims in Japan.

statusPeriods.label: Sovereign, with foreign courts inside it
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese governments governed Japan. British power meant a consular court that tried British subjects under British law, a tariff Japan could not raise, a foreign settlement at Yokohama and, for twelve years, British and French troops guarding it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Edo and then Tokyo, by Japanese governments
statusPeriods.franchise: None until the Meiji constitution of 1889 created a Diet elected in 1890 by about 1 per cent of the population, on a tax qualification.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1863 and 1875 a British garrison of up to 1,500 men was stationed on the Bluff at Yokohama to protect the foreign settlement. It is the only time British troops were quartered on Japanese soil before 1945, and it is usually left out of the story of Japan's opening.

departures.how: Japan spent thirty years rewriting its legal codes on European models specifically so that the powers would have no excuse, and Britain signed away its consular courts in 1894; they closed on 17 July 1899, with Japan regaining full control of its tariffs only in 1911.

led.name: Mutsu Munemitsu
led.role: foreign minister who negotiated the 1894 Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation

led.name: Aoki Shuzo
led.role: minister in London who conducted the negotiations and signed the treaty on 16 July 1894

led.name: John Wodehouse, Earl of Kimberley
led.role: British Foreign Secretary who agreed to give up extraterritoriality, making Britain the first power to do so

cost.note: Nobody died in the revision. The price was paid earlier and elsewhere: at Kagoshima in 1863, at Shimonoseki in 1864, and in the indemnity of three million dollars that the shogunate was made to pay for the second.

departures.borders: No border moved, because Britain never held Japanese territory. What ended was jurisdiction: from 17 July 1899 a British subject who committed a crime in Japan was tried in a Japanese court under Japanese law.

instrument.name: Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation
instrument.note: Signed in London and brought into effect on 17 July 1899, five years later, as the treaty required. Britain moved first and the other powers followed.

violence.note: Britain shelled Kagoshima for two days in August 1863 over the killing of one merchant, burning much of the town, and led a four-nation squadron that destroyed the Choshu batteries at Shimonoseki in September 1864.

consequences.economicLegacy: Britain built the Japanese navy that destroyed the Russian fleet at Tsushima in 1905: the battleship Mikasa was launched at Barrow-in-Furness in 1900, and most of the fleet's capital ships were British-built.
consequences.borderLegacy: Japan escaped the treaty system and then applied it: it imposed extraterritoriality and tariff control on Korea in 1876, took Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910, and by 1941 was fighting Britain for the rest of Asia.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Japan's civil, criminal and commercial codes were written between 1880 and 1898 largely to convince the powers that its courts were fit to try Europeans. Legal reform as a foreign policy is Japan's distinctive contribution to escaping informal empire.

peak.populationNote: Britain governed no Japanese territory and no Japanese people. The zeroes are deliberate. Japan's own population in 1890 was about 40 million; the British community at Yokohama numbered a few thousand.

evidence.author: Marius B. Jansen
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Japan
evidence.supports: The opening of Japan, the fall of the shogunate and the campaign for treaty revision.

evidence.author: Michael R. Auslin
evidence.work: Negotiating with Imperialism: The Unequal Treaties and the Culture of Japanese Diplomacy
evidence.supports: How Japanese diplomats used the treaty system itself to escape it.

evidence.author: W. G. Beasley
evidence.work: Great Britain and the Opening of Japan 1834-1858
evidence.supports: British policy and the negotiation of the 1854 and 1858 treaties.

pedagogy.hook: The Japanese flagship that sank the Russian fleet in 1905 was built in Barrow-in-Furness, by the country that had shelled a Japanese city forty years earlier.

misconception.belief: Countries that fell under European influence in the nineteenth century could not get out of it.
misconception.correction: Japan did. It signed unequal treaties in 1858, was bombarded twice in the 1860s, rewrote its entire legal system to remove the powers' excuse, and got British extraterritoriality abolished in 1899 and tariff autonomy in 1911. Then it imposed the same treaties on Korea. Escaping informal empire and joining the club that ran it were the same manoeuvre.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Japan is the control experiment. It had the same treaty ports, the same consular courts and the same tariff ceiling as China and the Ottoman Empire, and it ended up on the other side of the table. Comparing why is the best way to see what informal empire actually did and did not determine.

keyDates.what: Elgin's treaty gives Britain consular courts and a 5 per cent tariff
The Royal Navy bombards Kagoshima over the killing of one merchant
A four-nation squadron destroys the Choshu forts at Shimonoseki
Britain agrees to give up its consular courts in Japan
Extraterritoriality ends; British subjects come under Japanese law
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance, Britain's first with an Asian power

territories.name: Nootka Sound
territories.formalName: The British trading post at Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound

namesOverTime.name: Yuquot

from.note: Archaeology at Yuquot shows continuous occupation for over four millennia. The date is a marker for that depth, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: The summer village of the Mowachaht, whose name means 'where the wind blows from all directions'. It is still Mowachaht/Muchalaht territory.

namesOverTime.name: Friendly Cove, Nootka Sound
namesOverTime.note: Cook misheard a Nuu-chah-nulth phrase, possibly an instruction to sail round the point, and wrote it down as the name of the people and the place.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Yuquot is in British Columbia and remains the territory of the Mowachaht/Muchalaht First Nation, which has never signed a treaty ceding it.

geoCoverage.label: One cove on the outer coast
geoCoverage.change: The British holding was a house, a shipyard and a stretch of beach at Friendly Cove, bought or borrowed from Chief Maquinna depending on whose account you read. The map draws Vancouver Island because there is no unit smaller.

acquisitions.how: John Meares held no charter: he was a fur trader sailing under Portuguese colours precisely to dodge the East India Company's monopoly. He landed at Friendly Cove, put up a house on ground he said Maquinna had sold him for eight or ten sheets of copper, and built the first European-made ship on the coast.

counterparties.name: The Mowachaht, of the Nuu-chah-nulth peoples
counterparties.lost: Nothing they recognised as a sale. Maquinna later said he had allowed the traders the use of ground, not given it away, and Meares's own claim was written up after the event to support a compensation case against Spain.
counterparties.note: Two European empires nearly went to war over title to land that neither had bought and whose owners were not consulted at any point in the negotiations. Yuquot has been Mowachaht for over 4,000 years and is Mowachaht today.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Its claim to exclusive sovereignty over the whole Pacific coast of the Americas, which the Nootka Conventions of 1790-94 forced it to abandon in favour of shared access.
counterparties.note: This was the real prize. The conventions killed the Spanish doctrine that discovery and papal grant were enough, and established that only actual occupation creates title, which every later British Pacific claim relied on.

people.name: Maquinna
people.role: chief of the Mowachaht at Yuquot, who controlled access to the sound, traded sea-otter pelts with British, Spanish and American ships and played them against each other

people.name: John Meares
people.role: trader who built the post, lost it to Spain and then persuaded Parliament that Britain should go to war over it

people.name: Esteban Jose Martinez
people.role: Spanish commander who seized British ships and the post in the summer of 1789 and built a fort at the cove

people.name: James Cook
people.role: anchored at the sound for a month in 1778; his crew's sale of sea-otter pelts in Canton for enormous prices started the entire trade

acquisitions.resistance: The Mowachaht did not resist by force in 1789; they traded with all comers and profited. The one violent break came later, in 1803, when Maquinna's people seized the American ship Boston and killed most of its crew after repeated insults and thefts.

contested.note: Whether Meares bought land at all is disputed. His own memorial to Parliament in 1790 claimed a purchase; his testimony was self-interested, Spanish officers denied it, and Maquinna is recorded as saying he had granted use rather than ownership. The British government based a war threat on evidence it never tested.

evidence.author: Warren L. Cook
evidence.work: Flood Tide of Empire: Spain and the Pacific Northwest, 1543-1819
evidence.supports: The Spanish seizure, the crisis and the Nootka Conventions.

statusPeriods.label: A fur trader's house at Friendly Cove
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: There was no British authority of any kind. A private trader kept a house and a shipyard on ground he occupied at Maquinna's pleasure, and left for the winter.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere; the ships were registered at Macau under Portuguese colours
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Maquinna governed Yuquot throughout.

statusPeriods.label: Seized and held by Spain
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Martinez seized four British vessels, arrested their crews and built Fort San Miguel; Spain held the cove for five years while Madrid and London argued, and Britain's presence was reduced to a diplomatic claim.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Held by another power throughout. British authority at the cove was nil from July 1789 until the handover ceremony of March 1795, at which Britain took possession and left the same day.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: San Blas, Mexico, under the Viceroy of New Spain
statusPeriods.note: In 1790 Britain mobilised the fleet and Parliament voted a million pounds to fight Spain over this cove. France, in revolution, would not back Spain, and Spain backed down.

departures.how: On 28 March 1795 the Spanish and British commissioners met at Friendly Cove, Spain hauled down its flag, Britain raised and lowered its own, both parties dismantled their buildings, and everyone sailed away, leaving the cove to the Mowachaht who had never left it.

becomes.name: Yuquot, the Mowachaht village it had always been

led.name: Thomas Pearce
led.role: British commissioner who took formal possession and immediately abandoned the site, leaving the British flag with Maquinna

led.name: Jose Manuel de Alava
led.role: Spanish commissioner who handed the cove over and demolished the Spanish fort

led.name: Maquinna
led.role: the chief on whose land both empires had built, and who was left with the cove, the flag and the fur trade

led.name: George Vancouver
led.role: negotiated for Britain in 1792 and could not agree with the Spanish commander Bodega y Quadra on what was to be handed back; his survey named the island for them both

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the crisis. Britain spent roughly three million pounds mobilising the fleet in 1790 for a war that did not happen, and paid Meares 210,000 Spanish dollars in compensation extracted from Spain.

departures.borders: The conventions drew no border and that was the point: both powers gave up exclusive claims to the coast and agreed on shared access, which kept the Northwest open for the Anglo-American argument that produced the 49th parallel in 1846.

instrument.name: The Nootka Conventions of 1790, 1793 and 1794
instrument.note: Three conventions: the first, in October 1790, settled restitution and access; the third, in January 1794, provided for the mutual abandonment of the site, carried out in March 1795.

consequences.economicLegacy: Cook's crew sold sea-otter pelts in Canton in 1779 for prices that started a rush; within twenty years the sea otter was almost gone from the coast, and the trade moved north and inland into the fur companies that became the Hudson's Bay Company's Pacific department.
consequences.borderLegacy: The Nootka Conventions established that occupation, not discovery, gives title. Britain used that principle against Spain in 1790, against Russia in 1825 and against the United States in the Oregon dispute that was settled at the 49th parallel in 1846.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Nootka, the name Cook wrote down by mistake, was attached to a people, a language family and a sound for two centuries. The people's own name is Nuu-chah-nulth, adopted formally in 1978.

peak.populationNote: The Mowachaht summer population at Yuquot was estimated at over 1,000 by visiting Europeans. The British presence was one house and a handful of men, seasonally.

evidence.author: Warren L. Cook
evidence.work: Flood Tide of Empire: Spain and the Pacific Northwest, 1543-1819
evidence.supports: The Spanish presence, the seizure of 1789 and the conventions that followed.

evidence.author: Barry M. Gough
evidence.work: The Northwest Coast: British Navigation, Trade, and Discoveries to 1812
evidence.supports: British trading interests on the coast and the strategic meaning of the Nootka crisis.

evidence.author: Daniel Clayton
evidence.work: Islands of Truth: The Imperial Fashioning of Vancouver Island
evidence.supports: How European claims were constructed on Nuu-chah-nulth land and what Maquinna's people made of them.

contested.note: Almost every fact in the crisis was contested at the time and remains so: whether Meares bought land, whether his ships were British or Portuguese, how many were seized, and what Spain actually restored in 1795. The British case for war rested on a merchant's uncorroborated memorial.

pedagogy.hook: Britain and Spain nearly went to war in 1790 over a house on a beach, on land that belonged to neither of them and that the owners had not agreed to sell.

misconception.belief: Colonial land disputes were between Europeans and the people who lived on the land.
misconception.correction: At Nootka the dispute was entirely between two European empires about which of them owned a cove in Mowachaht territory. Maquinna, whose people had lived at Yuquot for over 4,000 years, was not a party to the Nootka Conventions, was not compensated, and got the site back in 1795 only because both empires walked away from it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Nootka crisis fixed the rule that occupation, not discovery, creates title, and Britain built its Pacific and Australian claims on that rule for the next century. It also shows how thin the line between a trading post and an empire could be: one house, one seizure, and a fleet mobilised on the other side of the world.

keyDates.what: Cook anchors at Yuquot; his crew's pelts start the sea-otter trade
Meares builds a house and a shipyard at Friendly Cove
Martinez seizes British ships and the post for Spain
The first Nootka Convention: Spain gives up exclusive claims
Both empires strike their flags and abandon the cove

territories.name: Balambangan
territories.formalName: The East India Company settlement on Balambangan Island
territories.subregion: The Sulu Sea and northern Borneo

namesOverTime.name: Balambangan
namesOverTime.note: A low island of about 100 square kilometres off the northern tip of Borneo, between the Sulu Sea and the South China Sea.

modernSuccessors.name: Malaysia
modernSuccessors.note: Balambangan is part of the Malaysian state of Sabah. The Sulu grants that Britain obtained in the 1760s were used a century later to justify the North Borneo Company's charter, and the Philippines still cites them in its claim to Sabah.

geoCoverage.label: One island off the tip of Borneo
geoCoverage.change: The Company held a stockade, a warehouse and a few hundred people on a small island. The map draws Sabah because the geometry has no unit for Balambangan itself; the marker stands for the island, not the state.

geoCoverage.label: The second attempt
geoCoverage.change: Britain came back to the same island in 1803 with a larger garrison, found it as unhealthy and as indefensible as before, and left again in 1805 without being attacked.

acquisitions.how: The East India Company took possession of an island the Sultan of Sulu had signed over in 1762 as thanks for being rescued from Spanish captivity in Manila, and built a stockaded factory there to break into the China trade from the east.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Sulu
counterparties.lost: The island and, in the grants of 1762 and 1763, a claim to much of northern Borneo, signed away by a sultan the Company had freed from a Spanish prison and who needed British support against Spain.
counterparties.note: Sultan Muhammad Alimuddin I signed under obligation, not under threat. His successors argued that he had granted use and alliance, not sovereignty, and the meaning of those documents is still argued in a live dispute between Malaysia and the Philippines.

counterparties.name: Spain, in the Philippines
counterparties.lost: Its claim to exclusive influence over Sulu, which the British grants directly contradicted; Spain protested and later spent a century subduing the sultanate.
counterparties.note: The grants were the Company's reward for the capture of Manila in 1762.

instrument.name: Grants of Balambangan and northern Borneo from Sultan Muhammad Alimuddin I of Sulu
instrument.note: Confirmed by further grants in January 1763 and 1764. Alexander Dalrymple took formal possession on 23 January 1763; the settlement itself was not built until December 1773.

people.name: Alexander Dalrymple
people.role: Company servant and hydrographer who negotiated the Sulu grants and spent his career arguing for an eastern entrepot; later the Admiralty's first hydrographer

people.name: Muhammad Alimuddin I
people.role: Sultan of Sulu, freed from Spanish captivity in Manila by the British in 1763, who signed the grants

people.name: John Herbert
people.role: chief of the settlement, whose embezzlement and mismanagement made it indefensible and who fled when it was attacked

people.name: Datu Teteng
people.role: Sulu leader who stormed and burned the settlement in 1775

cost.money: The Company lost goods and specie valued at around 375,000 pounds in the sack of 1775, on top of the cost of building the settlement.
cost.note: The loss figure comes from the Company's own claim and is likely to be inflated, since Herbert had reasons to overstate what was stolen and understate what he had taken himself.

acquisitions.resistance: Decisive. On the night of 5 March 1775 a Sulu force under Datu Teteng stormed the stockade, killed several Europeans, looted the warehouses and burned the settlement; the survivors escaped by sea to Labuan and then Brunei.

contested.note: The date of the attack is given as 26 February 1775 in some accounts and 5 March 1775 in others, probably because Company clerks were still using the Old Style calendar in correspondence. The meaning of the Sulu grants is more seriously disputed and is now a matter of international law.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Sulu and Sabah: A Study of British Policy towards the Philippines and North Borneo from the late Eighteenth Century
evidence.supports: The Sulu grants, the two settlements and their use in later claims to North Borneo.

acquisitions.how: During the wars with France the Company sent a garrison back to Balambangan to watch the eastern approaches to China, occupied the ruins of the old settlement, and abandoned the island again within two years as too expensive and too unhealthy.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Sulu
counterparties.lost: Nothing lasting. The Company returned on the strength of its old grants, without a new agreement, and left again before anything came of it.
counterparties.note: The second attempt is barely remembered even in specialist accounts, which is why it belongs in an atlas about how unstable the imperial map was.

people.name: Robert Townsend Farquhar
people.role: commissioner who reoccupied Balambangan in 1803 and recommended abandoning it; later governor of Mauritius

acquisitions.resistance: None recorded. The island defeated the garrison by itself: fever, poor anchorage and no trade.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Sulu and Sabah: A Study of British Policy towards the Philippines and North Borneo from the late Eighteenth Century
evidence.supports: The 1803-05 reoccupation and its abandonment.

statusPeriods.label: A Company factory in the Sulu Sea
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The East India Company's chief ran a stockade, a warehouse and a free port, dependent on the Sultan of Sulu's goodwill for food, labour and safety, and lost all three within fifteen months.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort William, Calcutta, at four months' distance
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: The second settlement
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A small Company garrison held the ruins for two years and did no trade worth recording before being withdrawn on grounds of cost and sickness.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain held nothing on Balambangan between the destruction of the first settlement in March 1775 and the second occupation in 1803. The 28-year gap is the point: this is a place the empire visited twice and kept neither time.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort William, Calcutta

departures.how: A Sulu force under Datu Teteng stormed the stockade at night, killed several of the Europeans, looted the warehouses and burned the settlement; the survivors fled by sea and the Company did not come back for 28 years.

led.name: Datu Teteng
led.role: led the assault that destroyed the settlement

led.name: John Herbert
led.role: the Company chief whose mismanagement and private trading left the place indefensible; he escaped

cost.note: Accounts of the sack give a handful of Europeans killed and an unrecorded number of Asian employees and Sulu attackers dead. The Company documented its lost goods far more carefully than its lost people.

departures.borders: No border changed. What survived was paperwork: the Sulu grants of 1762-64, which the North Borneo Company invoked in 1878 and which the Philippines still cites in its claim to Sabah.

departures.how: The Company withdrew the second garrison in 1805 on the recommendation of its own commissioner, who reported that the island had no trade, no safe anchorage and a fever that killed his men, and Britain never returned.

becomes.name: The Sultanate of Sulu, and after 1881 the British North Borneo Company

led.name: Robert Townsend Farquhar
led.role: recommended abandonment and carried it out

cost.note: No one was killed in the withdrawal. The cost was in fever cases and in Company money spent twice on the same worthless island.

departures.borders: None. The lasting mark of Balambangan is not on any border but in a chain of documents: Sulu grant to Company, Company claim to Dent and Overbeck, charter to the North Borneo Company, and a dispute over Sabah that is live today.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Philippines bases its claim to Sabah partly on what the Sultans of Sulu did and did not sign away, and the chain of documents begins with the grants Britain took in 1762-64 for a settlement that lasted fifteen months.
consequences.economicLegacy: Balambangan was meant to be the eastern hinge of the China trade, a free port where British goods met Chinese junks outside Dutch and Spanish control. That role went instead to Penang in 1786 and to Singapore in 1819.

peak.populationNote: The settlement held a few hundred people: Company servants, sepoys, Chinese and Bugis traders and labourers. No census was ever taken.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Balambangan’s largest recorded population: 300 people, counted in 1774.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Sulu and Sabah: A Study of British Policy towards the Philippines and North Borneo from the late Eighteenth Century
evidence.supports: The Sulu grants, both settlements, and the long afterlife of the documents in the Sabah dispute.

evidence.author: Howard T. Fry
evidence.work: Alexander Dalrymple and the Expansion of British Trade
evidence.supports: Dalrymple's negotiations with Sulu and the strategic thinking behind the Balambangan scheme.

contested.note: The date of the 1775 attack, the value of the goods lost, and above all the legal meaning of the Sulu grants are all disputed. The last of these is not an academic question: Malaysia and the Philippines have argued over Sabah since 1962 on the basis of what those documents did.

pedagogy.hook: A British trading post that failed twice in the 1770s and 1800s is one reason the Philippines still claims a Malaysian state.

misconception.belief: The empire grew steadily: places became British and then stayed British until independence.
misconception.correction: Balambangan was British for fifteen months, was burned down, was reoccupied 28 years later and abandoned again in two. Java was British for five years, Manila for twenty months, Havana for eleven. The map churned constantly, and the pink map printed in 1900 shows only the survivors.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Failures leave paperwork, and paperwork outlives settlements. Nothing British remained on Balambangan after 1805 except three grants signed by a grateful sultan, and those grants were still being argued over in international law two centuries later.

keyDates.what: The Sultan of Sulu grants Balambangan and part of Borneo to the Company
The settlement is founded
Datu Teteng's force storms and burns it
A second British garrison reoccupies the island
Britain abandons Balambangan for good

territories.name: Hawaii
territories.formalName: The provisional cession of the Hawaiian Islands to Great Britain, 1843

namesOverTime.name: Ko Hawaii Pae Aina
namesOverTime.note: The Hawaiian Kingdom, unified under Kamehameha I by 1810 and recognised as an independent state by Britain and France in 1843.

namesOverTime.name: Sandwich Islands
namesOverTime.note: Cook's name for the group, after the Earl of Sandwich. It fell out of use as Hawaiians insisted on their own.

namesOverTime.name: Hawai'i
namesOverTime.note: Annexed by the United States in 1898 and a state of the union from 21 August 1959. The Hawaiian name never stopped being used.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: The Kingdom was overthrown by American settlers with US Marines present in January 1893 and annexed by the United States in 1898. Congress formally apologised for the overthrow in 1993.

geoCoverage.label: The whole kingdom
geoCoverage.change: For five months and six days the entire Hawaiian archipelago was British, on the strength of a demand made by one naval captain acting without instructions.

acquisitions.how: Lord George Paulet brought the frigate Carysfort into Honolulu, presented demands over a British consul's land claims, threatened to open fire on the town, and on 25 February 1843 Kamehameha III ceded the kingdom to Queen Victoria under written protest, appealing to London over Paulet's head.

counterparties.name: The Hawaiian Kingdom
counterparties.lost: Its sovereignty for five months, its flag, and the fiction that a recognised state with treaties and a constitution was safe from a single warship. The King's protest, sent to London by his own envoys, was the basis on which the cession was undone.
counterparties.note: Hawaii was not a stateless island group. It had a written constitution from 1840, a legislature, a legal code and diplomats in Europe, and it had asked the powers to recognise its independence. Paulet took it anyway.

counterparties.name: The United States and France
counterparties.lost: Nothing lasting, and both objected loudly. The episode pushed all three powers into the Anglo-French declaration of 28 November 1843 recognising Hawaiian independence, which the United States endorsed separately.
counterparties.note: The seizure produced the opposite of what it intended: it made Hawaii the first non-European state whose independence the European powers formally guaranteed.

instrument.name: Deed of provisional cession of the Hawaiian Islands to Great Britain
instrument.note: Signed by Kamehameha III and Kekauluohi under protest, expressly reserving the right of appeal to the British government. That reservation is what made restoration possible.

people.name: Kamehameha III, Kauikeaouli
people.role: King of Hawaii, who ceded under protest rather than see Honolulu shelled, and appealed to London

people.name: George Paulet
people.role: captain of HMS Carysfort, who demanded and took the cession without any authority from his government

people.name: Richard Charlton
people.role: British consul whose disputed land claims and complaints provoked the crisis

people.name: Richard Thomas
people.role: Rear-Admiral commanding the Pacific station, who arrived in July, found Paulet had exceeded his orders and handed the kingdom back

people.name: Timoteo Haalilio
people.role: Hawaiian envoy who travelled to Washington, London and Paris to secure recognition of the kingdom's independence, and died on the voyage home in 1844

acquisitions.resistance: The King's resistance was legal and diplomatic and it worked: he signed under protest, kept his own envoys in Europe pressing the case, and had the cession reversed in five months without a shot fired.

evidence.author: Ralph S. Kuykendall
evidence.work: The Hawaiian Kingdom, Volume 1: 1778-1854, Foundation and Transformation
evidence.supports: The Paulet episode, the cession, the restoration and the 1843 recognition of Hawaiian independence.

statusPeriods.label: Paulet's commission governs the kingdom
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A four-man commission with Paulet on it ruled in the Queen's name, raised a British regiment from Hawaiian soldiers, seized the kingdom's ships and issued its own currency, while Kamehameha III refused to sit on the commission and sent his protest to London.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Honolulu, by a naval captain acting on his own authority
statusPeriods.franchise: None under the commission. The kingdom's own constitution of 1840 had created a legislature with an elected house of representatives, the first in the Pacific.

departures.how: Rear-Admiral Richard Thomas arrived on 26 July, read Paulet's actions and disowned them, and on 31 July 1843 restored the kingdom at a ceremony on the plain outside Honolulu where Kamehameha III said that the life of the land is perpetuated in righteousness.

led.name: Kamehameha III, Kauikeaouli
led.role: King, whose protest and envoys got the kingdom back; his speech that day supplied Hawaii's state motto

led.name: Richard Thomas
led.role: the British admiral who reversed his own captain and handed the kingdom back; Thomas Square in Honolulu is named for him

led.name: George Simpson
led.role: Hudson's Bay Company governor who carried the Hawaiian case to London and helped secure the 1843 recognition of independence

cost.note: Nobody was killed. The cost was to the kingdom's confidence and to its treasury, which paid for a British occupation it had not asked for; and to Britain's standing in the Pacific, which the restoration was designed to repair.

departures.borders: No border moved. What Hawaii gained was recognition: on 28 November 1843 Britain and France jointly declared the islands an independent state, the first such recognition given to a non-European government.

instrument.name: Restoration by Rear-Admiral Thomas, and the Anglo-French Declaration recognising Hawaiian independence
instrument.note: The restoration was a ceremony rather than a document; the declaration of 28 November 1843, signed in London, is the instrument that mattered.

contested.note: Hawaiian sovereignty scholars read 1843 not as a curiosity but as a precedent: the powers recognised an independent Hawaiian state, and that recognition is part of the legal argument that the overthrow of 1893 and annexation of 1898 were unlawful. The United States Congress conceded in 1993 that the overthrow was carried out with US participation and without the consent of the Hawaiian people.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept nothing, and left one mark that has never been removed: the Union Jack in the canton of the Hawaiian flag, adopted under Kamehameha I around 1816 and still flying over the fiftieth American state.

consequences.borderLegacy: The episode made Hawaiian independence an international commitment. Britain and France recognised the kingdom in November 1843, the United States followed, and Hawaii signed treaties as a sovereign state with more than twenty countries before the Americans took it in 1898.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Kamehameha III's words at the restoration, Ua mau ke ea o ka aina i ka pono, became Hawaii's motto and are on the state seal. The 31st of July is still marked in Honolulu as Restoration Day.

peak.populationNote: Estimates of the Hawaiian population in the 1840s cluster around 100,000, down from perhaps 400,000 or more before Cook's arrival in 1778; the collapse was caused by introduced disease and the figures are heavily disputed.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Hawaii’s greatest extent, 16,635 km² in 1843: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 16,897 km², within 1.6% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Ralph S. Kuykendall
evidence.work: The Hawaiian Kingdom, Volume 1: 1778-1854, Foundation and Transformation
evidence.supports: The Paulet episode, the restoration and the diplomacy of 1843.

evidence.author: Jonathan Kay Kamakawiwoole Osorio
evidence.work: Dismembering Lahui: A History of the Hawaiian Nation to 1887
evidence.supports: The Hawaiian side of the story: what the kingdom's leaders were trying to build and what foreign pressure did to it.

pedagogy.hook: Britain ruled Hawaii for five months in 1843 because one naval captain decided to take it, and then gave it back and apologised.

misconception.belief: Empires were built by governments that decided to conquer places.
misconception.correction: Paulet had no orders. Neither did Popham when he invaded Argentina in 1806, or Rajah Brooke when he took Sarawak in 1841. A great deal of imperial expansion was carried out by men on the spot, and London then chose whether to keep it. Here London said no, and reversed the seizure inside five months.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Hawaii shows that the empire also had brakes. The same navy that took the kingdom handed it back, and the embarrassment pushed Britain and France into recognising Hawaiian independence, which is now part of the legal case Hawaiian sovereignty campaigners make against the American annexation of 1898.

keyDates.what: Kamehameha III cedes the kingdom to Britain under protest
Admiral Thomas restores Hawaiian sovereignty
Britain and France recognise Hawaii as an independent state
American settlers overthrow the kingdom with US Marines ashore
The United States annexes Hawaii

events.title: The East India Company settles St Helena
events.summary: Captain John Dutton landed about thirty settlers on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the South Atlantic and built a fort above its only landing place, to give East Indiamen somewhere to take on water on the run home from Asia.
events.significance: It gave the Company, and later Britain, the mid-Atlantic. For two centuries every homeward-bound Indiaman stopped there, which made a 122-square-kilometre rock one of the most strategically valuable places in the world until the Suez Canal opened in 1869 and emptied it.

places.name: Jamestown
places.note: The only landing place on the island, in a gorge between 300-metre cliffs.

people.name: John Dutton
people.role: first governor; led the settlement party

people.name: Oliver Cromwell
people.role: Lord Protector, whose Council of State approved the Company's plantation of the island in 1658

evidence.author: Stephen A. Royle
evidence.work: The Company's Island: St Helena, Company Colonies and the Colonial Endeavour
evidence.supports: The date, purpose and early organisation of the settlement.

events.title: The Dutch take St Helena, and lose it again

date.note: Accounts date the Dutch landing to late December 1672 or the first days of January 1673.

events.summary: A Dutch squadron drove the East India Company off St Helena during the third Anglo-Dutch war and held it for about five months, until Captain Richard Munden landed men at night at Prosperous Bay and took the fort from behind.
events.significance: The only time St Helena has changed hands in 366 years, and the reason Charles II granted the island to the Company by a fresh charter in December 1673. It is also a reminder that in the seventeenth century the Atlantic islands were contested ground, not safe British property.

places.name: Prosperous Bay
places.note: Where Munden's men landed and climbed the cliffs to take the defences from the rear.

people.name: Richard Munden
people.role: commanded the squadron that retook the island in May 1673

people.name: Jacob de Gens
people.role: Dutch commander who took the island for the Dutch East India Company

evidence.author: Philip Gosse
evidence.work: St Helena 1502-1938
evidence.supports: The Dutch capture and the English recapture.

contested.note: The dates of the Dutch landing and of the English evacuation differ between accounts, partly because English writers were using the Old Style calendar and partly because no full narrative survives from the Dutch side.

events.title: Napoleon is exiled to St Helena
events.summary: HMS Northumberland anchored off Jamestown with Napoleon Bonaparte aboard; he was landed on 17 October 1815, housed at Longwood on the island's exposed plateau, and died there on 5 May 1821 with a garrison of some 2,800 men and a naval squadron guarding him.
events.significance: One prisoner reorganised the South Atlantic. To hold him, Britain took the island back from the East India Company's control for the duration, garrisoned Ascension in October 1815 and annexed Tristan da Cunha in August 1816. Two British Overseas Territories exist today because of one man on a third.

places.name: Longwood House
places.note: Napoleon's residence from December 1815, damp, wind-scoured and 500 metres above the sea.

people.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
people.role: prisoner of the British government from 1815 until his death in 1821

people.name: Hudson Lowe
people.role: governor from 1816, whose management of the prisoner became an international scandal

people.name: Betsy Balcombe
people.role: the fourteen-year-old daughter of a St Helena merchant whose family housed Napoleon for two months and whose memoir is a main source on his exile

pedagogy.hook: Guarding one man cost Britain a garrison of 2,800 soldiers, a naval squadron and two extra colonies.

misconception.belief: St Helena was chosen for Napoleon because it was a remote British colony.
misconception.correction: It was chosen because it was remote and because the British government could take it over: it belonged to the East India Company, and the Crown assumed control of it for the duration of the exile. Being remote was not enough, as Elba had shown the year before, when Napoleon walked off a Mediterranean island and reconquered France in three weeks.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows imperial geography being made by a single security problem: three islands, thousands of kilometres apart, garrisoned because of one prisoner, and two of them still British today.

evidence.author: Philip Gosse
evidence.work: St Helena 1502-1938
evidence.supports: The arrangements for the exile and its effect on the island.

events.title: The Liberated African Depot at Rupert's Valley
events.summary: The Royal Navy set up a depot on St Helena to receive Africans taken off slave ships intercepted in the South Atlantic. Around 26,000 people were landed at Rupert's Valley over three decades, and about 5,000 of them died within weeks of arrival.
events.significance: This is what abolition looked like on the ground: a Vice-Admiralty court, a hulk in a bay, tents in a treeless valley, and people freed from one ship and then indentured onto another bound for the Caribbean. It is the strongest single corrective to the idea that Britain abolished slavery and the story ends there.

places.name: Rupert's Valley
places.note: The depot and the burial ground; 325 graves were excavated here in 2007-08 during construction of the airport access road.

people.name: George Middlemore
people.role: governor when the depot opened, who reported that the first arrivals were landed in a condition he could not describe in an official despatch

people.name: Andrew Pearson
people.role: archaeologist who directed the 2007-08 excavation of the burial ground and published the study of the depot

toll.note: Estimates of deaths at the depot run from about 5,000 to 8,000 out of roughly 26,000 people landed. The figures come from Vice-Admiralty and naval records that are incomplete, and from the 2007-08 excavation, which found 325 burials in a small part of the ground.

pedagogy.hook: St Helena's population today is 4,439. Around 5,000 Africans freed from slave ships are buried in one valley on the island.

misconception.belief: Africans rescued by the Royal Navy's anti-slavery patrols were returned home and freed.
misconception.correction: Almost none went home. Ships condemned in the South Atlantic were taken to St Helena, where survivors were held in tents and hulks and then sent, mostly as indentured labourers, to the British Caribbean and to the Cape. Freedom in the legal sense arrived long before freedom in any other sense.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The same empire built the largest slave-trading operation of the eighteenth century and then spent sixty years and a naval squadron trying to suppress everyone else's. Both facts belong in the same sentence, and Rupert's Valley is where they meet.

evidence.author: Andrew Pearson
evidence.work: Distant Freedom: St Helena and the Abolition of the Slave Trade, 1840-1872
evidence.supports: The depot, the numbers landed, the mortality and the archaeology of the burial ground.

contested.note: The total landed and the number who died are both estimates. Naval and Vice-Admiralty registers are incomplete, deaths at sea before landing were recorded separately or not at all, and the excavated sample covers only part of one burial ground.

events.title: Boer prisoners of war on St Helena
events.summary: Britain shipped about 5,000 Boer prisoners from South Africa to camps at Deadwood and Broadbottom on St Helena, starting with General Piet Cronje and the men who surrendered with him at Paardeberg. For two years the prisoners outnumbered the islanders.
events.significance: It shows the empire used as a single system: a prisoner taken in the Free State could be held on a rock in the mid-Atlantic, as Napoleon had been, as Dinuzulu of the Zulu had been in the 1890s, and as three Bahraini nationalists would be in 1957. Small islands were the empire's prisons.

places.name: Deadwood Plain
places.note: The larger of the two camps, on the exposed plateau near Longwood.

people.name: Piet Cronje
people.role: Boer general captured at Paardeberg in February 1900 and held on the island with his wife

people.name: Dinuzulu kaCetshwayo
people.role: Zulu king exiled to St Helena from 1890 to 1897, a decade before the Boer prisoners arrived

toll.note: Between 150 and 200 prisoners died on the island, mostly of typhoid and pneumonia, and are buried at Knollcombes. The camp registers are the source and are broadly consistent.

evidence.author: Stephen A. Royle
evidence.work: The Company's Island: St Helena, Company Colonies and the Colonial Endeavour
evidence.supports: The camps, their size and their effect on the island's economy and population.

events.title: Ascension is commissioned as a warship
events.summary: A week after Napoleon reached St Helena, Royal Marines landed on the uninhabited island of Ascension and claimed it. The Admiralty rated the island as a sloop-of-war and ran it as HMS Ascension for the next 107 years.
events.significance: It is the purest example of empire as logistics: a place with no people, no water at sea level and no economy, taken and held for a century because of where it sits. Ascension went on to victual the anti-slavery squadron, carry the Atlantic cable, and launch the bombing raids of the Falklands war.

places.name: Georgetown
places.note: The settlement below the pier, laid out by the Royal Marines in 1815-16.

people.name: Edward Nicolls
people.role: Royal Marines officer who commanded the first garrison

evidence.author: Duff Hart-Davis
evidence.work: Ascension: The Story of a South Atlantic Island
evidence.supports: The garrisoning, the naval administration and the island's later uses.

events.title: Britain annexes Tristan da Cunha
events.summary: A garrison from the Cape annexed the Tristan group to stop it being used as a base for rescuing Napoleon or by American privateers. The soldiers left in 1817; Corporal William Glass asked to stay, and with his wife Maria Magdalena Leenders founded the community that is still there.
events.significance: It produced the most remote inhabited settlement on Earth and the empire's least governed colony: for 121 years Tristan had no British official, no tax and no court, and ran itself on a written rule that nobody should take precedence over anyone else.

places.name: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas
places.note: The only settlement, on the one patch of flat land under a 2,000-metre volcano.

people.name: William Glass
people.role: Scottish corporal who stayed when the garrison left and founded the settlement

people.name: Maria Magdalena Leenders
people.role: Cape-born woman who settled with Glass and is an ancestor of most of the present population

people.name: Jonathan Lambert
people.role: American from Salem who proclaimed himself sovereign of the islands in 1811 and drowned in 1812

evidence.author: Peter A. Munch
evidence.work: Crisis in Utopia: The Ordeal of Tristan da Cunha
evidence.supports: The annexation, the founding of the settlement and its egalitarian constitution.

events.title: The volcano erupts and Tristan is evacuated
events.summary: A vent opened a few hundred metres from the settlement and all 264 islanders were taken off by boat to Nightingale Island, then to Cape Town and to England, where they were housed at a former RAF camp at Calshot in Hampshire.
events.significance: Offered permanent homes, jobs and the British welfare state, the islanders voted 148 to 5 in 1962 to go home to a volcano. It is the sharpest question a student can be asked about what a colony is for and what belonging means, and the answer came from the colonised, not from London.

places.name: Calshot, Hampshire
places.note: The former RAF station where the islanders lived in England for two years.

people.name: Peter Wheeler
people.role: the Administrator who organised the evacuation in a few hours

people.name: Peter A. Munch
people.role: sociologist who had lived on Tristan in 1937-38 and studied the community during and after the exile

toll.note: The entire population, 264 people, was evacuated. Nobody was killed by the eruption. Several islanders died in England, which the community counted as a cost of the exile.

pedagogy.hook: Given a free choice between the British welfare state and an active volcano 2,400 kilometres from anywhere, the Tristan islanders voted 148 to 5 for the volcano.

misconception.belief: People in small colonies wanted to move to Britain.
misconception.correction: The Tristan islanders spent two years in Hampshire with jobs, schools and the National Health Service, and almost all of them went home to an island with no airstrip, no doctor for most of its history and a volcano that had just destroyed the crawfish factory. What they valued was the community and the common land, not the standard of living.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest available test of the assumption that the metropole is what everyone wants, and the answer, delivered by ballot, was no.

evidence.author: Peter A. Munch
evidence.work: Crisis in Utopia: The Ordeal of Tristan da Cunha
evidence.supports: The evacuation, the two years in England, the 1962 vote and the return.

events.title: Byron claims the Falklands at Port Egmont
events.summary: Commodore John Byron landed on Saunders Island, named the harbour Port Egmont and claimed the whole archipelago for George III, without knowing that Bougainville had founded a French settlement at the other end of the group ten months earlier.
events.significance: This is the act on which the British claim to the Falklands still rests. Everything argued since, in 1770, 1833, 1965 and 1982, goes back to what a naval officer did on a beach in January 1765 and whether it was ever validly given up.

places.name: Port Egmont, Saunders Island
places.note: The British settlement, a blockhouse and garden on a harbour at the north-west corner of the group.

places.name: Port Louis
places.note: Bougainville's French settlement of April 1764, sold to Spain in 1767 and renamed Puerto Soledad.

people.name: John Byron
people.role: commodore who claimed the islands; grandfather of the poet

people.name: Louis Antoine de Bougainville
people.role: founded Port Louis with Acadian refugees in April 1764, before the British arrived

evidence.author: Lowell S. Gustafson
evidence.work: The Sovereignty Dispute over the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands
evidence.supports: The 1764-65 settlements and the legal weight later placed on them.

events.title: Spain expels the British from Port Egmont
events.summary: Five Spanish frigates and about 1,400 men from Buenos Aires forced the hundred-strong British garrison out of Port Egmont. Britain and Spain mobilised for war; France would not back Spain, and Spain restored the settlement in September 1771 while expressly reserving its claim.
events.significance: Europe nearly went to war over a blockhouse in the South Atlantic, and the settlement of 1771 left the sovereignty question deliberately unanswered. Spain always maintained that Britain privately promised to leave later, which is why the British withdrawal of 1774 has been argued about for 250 years.

people.name: Juan Ignacio de Madariaga
people.role: Spanish commander of the expelling force

people.name: George Farmer
people.role: British captain who surrendered Port Egmont after a token resistance

people.name: Samuel Johnson
people.role: wrote Thoughts on the Late Transactions Respecting Falkland's Islands in 1771, arguing that no war was worth a place he called a bleak and gloomy solitude

evidence.author: Julius Goebel
evidence.work: The Struggle for the Falkland Islands: A Study in Legal and Diplomatic History
evidence.supports: The expulsion, the crisis of 1770-71 and the terms of the restitution.

contested.note: Whether Britain gave Spain a secret undertaking to withdraw later, as part of the 1771 settlement, has never been resolved. No document has been found; the timing of the 1774 evacuation is the main evidence for it and is circumstantial.

events.title: Britain abandons Port Egmont and leaves a plaque
events.summary: Lord North's government withdrew the garrison to save money. The officer in charge hauled down the flag and nailed a lead plaque to the blockhouse door stating that the islands were the sole right and property of George III, and sailed away for 59 years.
events.significance: It is the hinge of the whole Falklands dispute. Britain left the archipelago physically while claiming it legally, and Argentina's case rests on the argument that a claim abandoned for two generations, while Spain and then Buenos Aires occupied the islands, cannot be revived by a warship in 1833.

people.name: Frederick North, Lord North
people.role: Prime Minister whose government ordered the withdrawal on grounds of cost

pedagogy.hook: Britain left the Falklands in 1774 with a lead plaque nailed to a door, and did not come back for 59 years.

misconception.belief: British sovereignty over the Falklands has been continuous since 1765.
misconception.correction: It has not. Britain was expelled by Spain in 1770, restored in 1771, and left voluntarily in 1774. Spain occupied Puerto Soledad until 1811 and Buenos Aires claimed the islands from 1820. The gap is 59 years, and both governments know it: the argument is about whether a claim survives an absence that long.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is a case study in how legal claims work. Physical possession and legal title are different things, and empires learned to keep the second while giving up the first, which is why so many disputes outlived the empires that started them.

evidence.author: Lowell S. Gustafson
evidence.work: The Sovereignty Dispute over the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands
evidence.supports: The withdrawal, the plaque and the legal arguments built on both.

events.title: HMS Clio expels the Buenos Aires garrison
events.summary: Captain James Onslow told the commander of the Buenos Aires garrison at Puerto Soledad that he had orders to exercise British sovereignty; the schooner Sarandi left under written protest on 5 January 1833, and the civilian settlers were told they could stay, and mostly did.
events.significance: This is the act Argentina calls a dispossession and Britain calls a reassertion. Whether a garrison of 25 soldiers placed three months earlier constituted Argentine possession, and whether Britain's dormant claim of 1765 could be revived, are the two questions the whole dispute turns on.

places.name: Puerto Soledad, later Port Louis
places.note: The settlement founded by the French in 1764, held by Spain to 1811 and by Buenos Aires from 1832.

people.name: James Onslow
people.role: captain of HMS Clio; delivered the ultimatum

people.name: Jose Maria Pinedo
people.role: commander of the Sarandi, who protested and withdrew without fighting

people.name: Antonio Rivero
people.role: gaucho who with seven others killed five settlement leaders in August 1833, an outlaw in British accounts and a resistance figure in Argentine ones

toll.note: Nobody was killed in the January 1833 expulsion itself. Five men were killed in the settlement in August 1833 by Rivero's group, in a dispute over pay and worthless promissory notes rather than over sovereignty.

evidence.author: Lowell S. Gustafson
evidence.work: The Sovereignty Dispute over the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands
evidence.supports: The events of January 1833 and the two governments' interpretations of them.

contested.note: Argentine accounts describe the expulsion of a population; British accounts describe the expulsion of a garrison. The contemporary records show a garrison shipped out and most civilians remaining, but the Argentine reading has been the official one since 1833 and is taught in Argentine schools.

events.title: The Battle of the Falkland Islands
events.summary: Admiral von Spee's German squadron arrived off Stanley to raid the coaling station and found two British battlecruisers there. In a running fight the Royal Navy sank four German ships; about 2,200 German sailors died, including von Spee and his two sons.
events.significance: It cleared German warships from the world's oceans within five months of the war starting and showed why the empire's chain of coaling stations mattered: Stanley existed as a naval station, and the ships that won were only there because Britain could refuel them in the South Atlantic.

places.name: Stanley
places.note: The coaling station von Spee came to destroy.

people.name: Maximilian von Spee
people.role: German admiral, killed with both his sons when his squadron was destroyed

people.name: Doveton Sturdee
people.role: British admiral commanding the battlecruisers Invincible and Inflexible

toll.note: German losses are usually given as about 2,200 dead out of roughly 2,400 men in the four ships sunk. British losses were ten killed. The figures come from Admiralty and German naval records and are broadly agreed.

evidence.author: Robert K. Massie
evidence.work: Castles of Steel: Britain, Germany, and the Winning of the Great War at Sea
evidence.supports: The pursuit of von Spee's squadron and the battle off Stanley.

events.title: The Falklands War
events.summary: Argentina's military government invaded the Falklands, South Georgia and the outlying dependencies; Britain sent a task force 12,700 kilometres and retook them in 74 days. The war killed 649 Argentines, 255 British service personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
events.significance: The last war Britain fought to keep a colony, and it won. It destroyed the Argentine junta within three days of the surrender, secured Margaret Thatcher's re-election in 1983, and hardened the Falklands question into a position neither government has been able to move since.

places.name: Stanley
places.note: Invaded on 2 April 1982 and retaken on 14 June.

places.name: Goose Green
places.note: Where about 114 islanders were locked in the community hall for 29 days.

places.name: Wideawake airfield, Ascension
places.note: The staging base, 6,300 kilometres from the Falklands, from which the Black Buck raids flew.

people.name: Leopoldo Galtieri
people.role: head of the Argentine junta who ordered the invasion and was removed three days after the surrender

people.name: Margaret Thatcher
people.role: British Prime Minister who sent the task force

people.name: Rex Hunt
people.role: Governor of the Falklands, deported to Uruguay after the invasion and returned in June

people.name: Doreen Bonner, Mary Goodwin and Susan Whitley
people.role: the three Falkland Islanders killed, by British naval gunfire in Stanley on the night of 11-12 June 1982

toll.note: 649 Argentine dead, including 323 lost when the cruiser General Belgrano was sunk on 2 May; 255 British service personnel; and three Falkland Islanders. Both governments published these figures and they are not seriously disputed. Neither total counts veterans who took their own lives afterwards.

pedagogy.hook: In 1982 Britain sent a hundred ships 12,700 kilometres to recover islands with 1,800 residents, and 907 people died.

misconception.belief: By the 1980s the empire was over and Britain no longer fought colonial wars.
misconception.correction: Britain fought a full naval and land war in 1982, the largest since Korea, over a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic. It lost a fifth of its escorts damaged or sunk, and it won. Fourteen British Overseas Territories still exist, and one of them is defended by a garrison and an airbase built after this war.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It forces the two hardest principles in decolonisation into direct collision: self-determination, which the islanders invoke, and territorial integrity, which Argentina invokes. The United Nations charter contains both and does not say which wins.

evidence.author: Lawrence Freedman
evidence.work: The Official History of the Falklands Campaign
evidence.supports: The diplomacy, the invasion, the campaign and the casualty figures, from the British government's own papers.

evidence.author: Martin Middlebrook
evidence.work: The Argentine Fight for the Falklands
evidence.supports: The war from the Argentine side, based on interviews with Argentine participants.

events.title: The Falklands referendum
events.summary: Falkland Islanders were asked whether they wished to keep their status as a British Overseas Territory. On a turnout of about 92 per cent, 1,513 voted yes and three voted no, with international observers present.
events.significance: It made self-determination the centre of the British case and gave Argentina its sharpest counter-argument: that a population it regards as implanted after 1833 cannot vote away another state's territorial claim. Both readings of the same ballot are still in use at the United Nations.

people.name: Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner
people.role: President of Argentina, who dismissed the referendum as a vote by a transplanted population

people.name: Dick Sawle
people.role: member of the Falklands Legislative Assembly who led the campaign for the referendum

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The politics of the sovereignty dispute and the islanders' place in it, up to the early 2000s.

contested.note: The result is not disputed; its legal weight is. Britain treats it as decisive under the right of self-determination; Argentina argues that paragraph 6 of UN Resolution 1514 protects territorial integrity and that a population installed by the disputing power cannot determine the outcome.

events.title: Cook claims South Georgia and names Sandwich Land
events.summary: James Cook landed at Possession Bay and claimed South Georgia for George III; eleven days later he sighted the South Sandwich Islands. He wrote the island off as worthless and mentioned that its shores were crowded with seals and whales.
events.significance: That one observation emptied the Southern Ocean. Sealers followed within eleven years and took an estimated 1.2 million fur seal skins from South Georgia by 1825; whalers followed them, and the British Antarctic claim was eventually made to tax the industry Cook's journal had started.

places.name: Possession Bay
places.note: Where Cook landed and read the claim.

people.name: James Cook
people.role: claimed the island and named the group

people.name: Anthony de la Roche
people.role: English merchant who probably sighted South Georgia in 1675 after being blown south of Cape Horn

evidence.author: Robert K. Headland
evidence.work: The Island of South Georgia
evidence.supports: Cook's landing, the sealing that followed and the figures for skins taken.

events.title: Grytviken opens and the whaling begins
events.summary: The Norwegian captain Carl Anton Larsen founded a shore station at Grytviken on South Georgia under a lease from the Falkland Islands government. Seven stations eventually worked the island, processing roughly 175,000 whales before the last one closed in 1965.
events.significance: Whaling is the reason the British Antarctic claim exists. Licence fees and an oil tax paid for the magistrate, the post office, the customs house and eventually the science; and when the whales ran out, the territory emptied and the claim carried on, as claims do.

places.name: Grytviken
places.note: The first and longest-lived of the seven shore stations; Shackleton is buried in its cemetery.

people.name: Carl Anton Larsen
people.role: Norwegian whaling captain who founded Grytviken and took British nationality

people.name: William Allardyce
people.role: Governor of the Falkland Islands who granted the lease and then pressed London to claim the whole Antarctic sector so more could be taxed

pedagogy.hook: Seven factories on one sub-Antarctic island cut up about 175,000 whales in sixty years, and then closed because there were not enough left to make a season pay.

misconception.belief: Empire in the polar regions was about exploration and science.
misconception.correction: It was about oil. Whale oil lit lamps, made soap and margarine, and hardened into glycerine for explosives in two world wars. Britain claimed the Antarctic sector in 1908 to license the industry and tax the oil, and the science came later, funded by a levy on the killing.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case in the atlas of a territory taken to extract a resource, with no population to govern, and it ends the way extraction usually ends: with the resource gone and the infrastructure rusting.

evidence.author: Robert K. Headland
evidence.work: The Island of South Georgia
evidence.supports: The stations, the leases and the catch statistics.

events.title: Shackleton crosses South Georgia
events.summary: After sailing a seven-metre boat 1,300 kilometres from Elephant Island, Ernest Shackleton, Frank Worsley and Tom Crean crossed the unmapped mountains of South Georgia in 36 hours to reach the whaling station at Stromness and raise help for the 22 men left behind.
events.significance: Every member of the Endurance expedition survived. The crossing has become the empire's favourite story about itself, which is exactly why it is worth teaching next to Grytviken: the men were rescued by an industrial whaling settlement that existed to render 175,000 animals into oil.

places.name: King Haakon Bay
places.note: Where the James Caird landed on 10 May 1916.

places.name: Stromness
places.note: The whaling station the three men walked into on 20 May 1916.

people.name: Ernest Shackleton
people.role: expedition leader; died at Grytviken on 5 January 1922 and is buried there

people.name: Frank Worsley
people.role: navigator of the James Caird, whose sextant work found an island 1,300 kilometres away

people.name: Tom Crean
people.role: Irish seaman who made both the boat journey and the crossing

evidence.author: Roland Huntford
evidence.work: Shackleton
evidence.supports: The boat journey, the crossing and the rescue of the Elephant Island party.

events.title: Argentina occupies Southern Thule
events.summary: Argentina landed engineers on Southern Thule in the South Sandwich Islands and built the Corbeta Uruguay base on British territory without permission. Britain discovered it in December 1976, protested privately, and left it there for five and a half years.
events.significance: It is the missing first chapter of the Falklands War. Argentina tested whether Britain would defend an uninhabited South Atlantic possession, found that it would not, and drew a conclusion about the Falklands. The base was removed on 20 June 1982, six days after the Argentine surrender at Stanley.

places.name: Southern Thule
places.note: The southernmost group of the South Sandwich Islands, where Corbeta Uruguay was built.

people.name: James Callaghan
people.role: British Prime Minister whose government chose to protest privately rather than remove the base

people.name: Emilio Massera
people.role: Argentine navy commander and junta member, whose service pressed the South Atlantic claims

pedagogy.hook: Argentina built a base on British territory in 1976, Britain found it a month later, and did nothing about it for five and a half years.

misconception.belief: The Falklands War began out of the blue on 2 April 1982.
misconception.correction: It began with a test. Argentina occupied Southern Thule in 1976 and Britain, told about it by its own scientists, protested in private and left the base standing. The scrap-metal party that landed on South Georgia in March 1982 was another test. The invasion came only after two probes had shown no cost.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Deterrence is invisible when it works and obvious when it fails. Southern Thule is the clearest small example of how a great power's unwillingness to defend a worthless possession can be read as unwillingness to defend a valuable one.

evidence.author: Lawrence Freedman
evidence.work: The Official History of the Falklands Campaign
evidence.supports: The occupation of Southern Thule, the British response and its place in the road to war.

events.title: Britain claims a wedge of Antarctica
events.summary: Letters patent declared South Georgia, the South Orkneys, the South Shetlands, the South Sandwich Islands and Graham Land to be dependencies of the Falkland Islands, so that the Governor at Stanley could licence whaling and tax the oil. The wording accidentally claimed part of Patagonia too.
events.significance: It is the oldest Antarctic claim in existence and the model for the six that followed. It also shows the machinery of imperial expansion at its plainest: a governor wanting revenue, a draftsman in London, a sector of a continent nobody had crossed, and a boundary error nobody noticed for nine years.

places.name: Stanley
places.note: The colonial capital that administered a wedge of Antarctica for 54 years.

people.name: William Allardyce
people.role: Governor of the Falkland Islands, who pressed for the claim so that whaling could be taxed

pedagogy.hook: The 1908 letters patent claiming British Antarctica were drafted so carelessly that they also claimed a slice of Argentina and Chile.

misconception.belief: Imperial borders were drawn by experts with maps.
misconception.correction: The 1908 claim used a sector defined from 50 degrees south, which swept in southern Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, both of them long-settled parts of two sovereign states. New letters patent quietly fixed it in 1917. Empire's paperwork was often produced quickly, by people who had never seen the ground.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Every Antarctic claim since has copied this template: a wedge of longitude converging on the Pole, declared from a European capital, justified by exploration and paid for by resource licences.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The letters patent of 1908 and 1917, their motives and their defects.

events.title: Operation Tabarin puts Britain on the ice
events.summary: A secret wartime expedition sailed south to build permanent bases in the British Antarctic claim, at Deception Island in February 1944 and Port Lockroy days later. The stated purpose was to deny anchorages to German raiders; the real one was to hold the claim against Argentina and Chile.
events.significance: It converted a claim on paper into occupation on the ground, 36 years after the claim was made. The expedition became the Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey and then, in 1962, the British Antarctic Survey, which is still the instrument by which Britain maintains its Antarctic position.

places.name: Port Lockroy
places.note: Base A, established 11 February 1944; now a museum and the most-visited site in Antarctica.

places.name: Hope Bay
places.note: Base D, established in February 1945; where Argentine troops fired machine-gun bursts over a British landing party in February 1952.

people.name: James Marr
people.role: led the expedition; a zoologist who had been a boy scout on Shackleton's last voyage

people.name: Andrew Taylor
people.role: Canadian engineer who took over command in 1944 and led the first surveys inland

evidence.author: Stephen Haddelsey
evidence.work: Operation Tabarin: Britain's Secret Wartime Expedition to Antarctica 1944-46
evidence.supports: The expedition, its cover story and its political purpose.

events.title: The Antarctic Treaty freezes the claims
events.summary: Twelve states signed a treaty in Washington reserving Antarctica for peaceful use and science. Article IV holds every sovereignty claim exactly where it stood: no new claims, no enlargement, and nothing done under the treaty may support or weaken any existing claim.
events.significance: It ended a decade in which Britain, Argentina and Chile had removed each other's huts, fired warning shots and gone to the International Court. It is also the only place in this atlas where an imperial claim was neither kept nor surrendered but suspended, and it has held for over sixty years.

places.name: Washington DC
places.note: Where the treaty was signed by the twelve states active in the International Geophysical Year.

people.name: Brian Roberts
people.role: British polar official who drafted much of the language of Article IV, the formula that made agreement possible by refusing to decide anything

people.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
people.role: US President who convened the conference; the United States claims nothing in Antarctica and recognises no claim

pedagogy.hook: The Antarctic Treaty did not settle who owns Antarctica. It made an agreement to stop asking, and that agreement is now 66 years old.

misconception.belief: Antarctica belongs to nobody because the Antarctic Treaty says so.
misconception.correction: Seven states still claim sectors of Antarctica: Britain, Argentina, Chile, Norway, France, Australia and New Zealand. Article IV freezes those claims rather than abolishing them, and expressly protects them. Britain still calls its sector the British Antarctic Territory, issues its stamps and named part of it Queen Elizabeth Land in 2012.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the one imperial dispute that was solved by agreeing not to solve it, and the technique is worth understanding: unresolvable claims can be managed indefinitely if every party gains more from cooperation than from winning.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The negotiation of the treaty, the drafting of Article IV and the position of the claimant states.

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The Anglo-Argentine and Anglo-Chilean confrontations of the 1940s and 1950s that made the treaty necessary.

events.title: The British Antarctic Territory is created
events.summary: An Order in Council separated everything south of 60 degrees south from the Falkland Islands Dependencies and made it a territory in its own right, administered by a Commissioner in London. South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, north of that line, stayed with the Falklands.
events.significance: The new boundary was drawn to match the Antarctic Treaty, which applies south of 60 degrees. Britain reorganised its colonial map to fit an arms-control agreement, which is a small but exact illustration of how the post-1945 international order reshaped what was left of the empire.

places.name: Rothera Research Station
places.note: The main British station in the territory, opened in 1975.

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The 1962 reorganisation and its relationship to the Antarctic Treaty.

events.title: The British invasions of the River Plate
events.summary: Two British expeditions attacked the Spanish River Plate. The first took Buenos Aires in June 1806 and was thrown out by the city's own militia in August; the second took Montevideo in February 1807 and was destroyed in the streets of Buenos Aires in July.
events.significance: Britain never tried to conquer South America again and controlled it by trade instead. For the River Plate the effect was the opposite of intended: the criollos who beat the British twice, without help from Spain, deposed the viceroy in 1810 and declared independence in 1816.

places.name: Buenos Aires
places.note: Taken in June 1806, lost in August; attacked again and lost in July 1807.

places.name: Montevideo
places.note: Stormed on 3 February 1807 and held for seven months.

people.name: Home Riggs Popham
people.role: commodore who launched the first invasion without orders and was court-martialled for it

people.name: Santiago de Liniers
people.role: retook Buenos Aires in 1806 and organised its defence in 1807; made viceroy by the city

people.name: John Whitelocke
people.role: lost 2,500 men in one morning in July 1807 and was cashiered

people.name: Martin de Alzaga
people.role: mayor of Buenos Aires who organised the militia companies that beat the second attack

toll.note: British returns give roughly 400 killed on 5 July 1807 alone, with 650 wounded and 1,900 captured, and about 165 killed and wounded in August 1806. Spanish and criollo losses across both campaigns are less well recorded and civilians were not counted at all.

pedagogy.hook: A British commodore invaded Argentina in 1806 without permission from London, and the general who tried to finish the job was thrown out of the army for failing.

misconception.belief: The empire expanded because Britain decided to expand it.
