misconception.correction: Popham took his fleet and army from the Cape to Buenos Aires on his own initiative and was court-martialled and reprimanded. So much of imperial expansion was begun by men on the spot that historians have a phrase for it, the sub-imperialism of the periphery. London's choice was usually whether to keep what someone had already taken.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the empire's clearest defeat by a colonial city's own inhabitants, and the beginning of Britain's switch from conquest to commerce in Latin America.

evidence.author: Ian Fletcher
evidence.work: The Waters of Oblivion: The British Invasion of the Rio de la Plata, 1806-1807
evidence.supports: Both campaigns, the forces involved and the casualties.

evidence.author: Klaus Gallo
evidence.work: Great Britain and Argentina: From Invasion to Recognition, 1806-26
evidence.supports: British aims and the shift from conquest to trade after 1807.

events.title: The Baring crisis
events.summary: Barings, one of London's oldest merchant banks, had underwritten so much Argentine debt that Argentina's default in 1890 nearly destroyed it. The Bank of England organised a guarantee fund of about 17 million pounds from the City to keep the bank standing.
events.significance: It showed how tightly Britain and Argentina were tied without any colonial relationship at all: a default in Buenos Aires nearly caused a banking collapse in London. That is what informal empire looks like when it goes wrong, and it explains why the Foreign Office cared so much about Argentine finance.

places.name: The Bank of England, London
places.note: Where the rescue fund was organised in five days in November 1890.

people.name: William Lidderdale
people.role: Governor of the Bank of England, who assembled the guarantee fund

people.name: Carlos Pellegrini
people.role: President of Argentina from 1890, who negotiated the debt settlement that followed

evidence.author: H. S. Ferns
evidence.work: Britain and Argentina in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The scale of British lending to Argentina and the course of the 1890 crisis.

events.title: The Roca-Runciman treaty
events.summary: Britain guaranteed Argentina a share of its meat market in exchange for Argentina spending its sterling earnings in Britain, cutting tariffs on British goods and protecting British-owned transport companies. Argentina's vice-president said his country was, economically, part of the British Empire.
events.significance: It is the single best piece of evidence that informal empire was real, and it was produced by a British attempt to protect empire markets rather than by any desire to rule Argentina. Argentine nationalists have called the 1930s the infamous decade ever since, and the treaty is why.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the treaty was negotiated after the Ottawa conference of 1932 had given empire producers preference over Argentine beef.

people.name: Julio Argentino Roca Jr
people.role: Argentine vice-president who negotiated and defended the treaty

people.name: Walter Runciman
people.role: President of the Board of Trade, who signed for Britain

people.name: Lisandro de la Torre
people.role: senator whose 1935 inquiry into the meat trade exposed how the agreement worked; his colleague Enzo Bordabehere was shot dead in the Senate chamber during the hearings on 23 July 1935

pedagogy.hook: A senator investigating the British meat contracts was shot at in the Argentine Senate in 1935, and the bullet killed the colleague standing next to him.

misconception.belief: Countries outside the empire were free of it.
misconception.correction: The 1932 Ottawa agreements gave empire producers preference in the British market, and Argentina, which sold Britain most of its beef, had to buy its way back in. The price was tariff cuts, currency controls that favoured British firms and protection for British-owned railways and trams. No British official governed anything in Argentina, and the terms were still Britain's.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire's economic border working like a wall: inside it, preference; outside it, a country the size of Argentina negotiating for access on someone else's terms.

evidence.author: H. S. Ferns
evidence.work: Britain and Argentina in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The long structure of the Anglo-Argentine trading relationship that produced the 1933 treaty.

events.title: Peron buys the British railways
events.summary: Argentina bought the British-owned railway network for 150 million pounds, paid out of the sterling Britain owed it for wartime beef and grain. Peron marked the handover at Retiro station in Buenos Aires as the end of the country's economic dependence.
events.significance: It closed the largest block of British-owned property outside the empire. Britain had spent the war buying Argentine food on credit and could not repay in cash; it paid in railways, and the informal empire that had begun with a loan from Barings in 1824 ended with a debt settlement in 1948.

places.name: Retiro station, Buenos Aires
places.note: Built by a British company in 1915 and the site of the handover ceremony in 1948.

people.name: Juan Domingo Peron
people.role: President, who made the purchase the centrepiece of his economic independence campaign

people.name: Miguel Miranda
people.role: head of Argentina's economic council and chief negotiator of the sterling-balances settlement

people.name: Clement Attlee
people.role: British Prime Minister whose government settled its wartime debts to Argentina by selling the railways

evidence.author: Colin M. Lewis
evidence.work: British Railways in Argentina 1857-1914: A Case Study of Foreign Investment
evidence.supports: The construction, ownership and finances of the network that was sold in 1948.

contested.note: Whether Argentina overpaid is argued about to this day. Argentine critics said Peron bought worn-out track at close to replacement cost; British critics said the government sold a valuable asset cheaply to clear a debt it could not honour. The Argentine and the British critics each had reasons to misrepresent the value.

events.title: The Convention of Balta Liman
events.summary: Britain persuaded the Ottoman government to abolish its own trading monopolies and cap import duties at 5 per cent, in exchange for support against Muhammad Ali of Egypt. Ottoman merchants ended up paying more in internal duties than foreigners paid to import.
events.significance: It is the founding document of informal empire in the eastern Mediterranean. Within two years every other power had the same terms; within two decades Ottoman textile production had collapsed and the state, unable to tax trade, was borrowing in London and Paris on its way to the default of 1875.

places.name: Balta Liman, on the Bosphorus
places.note: The waterside mansion of the Ottoman foreign minister, where the convention was signed.

people.name: Henry Temple, Viscount Palmerston
people.role: Foreign Secretary who used the convention and then a fleet to break Muhammad Ali and prop up the Ottoman state

people.name: Mustafa Resid Pasha
people.role: Ottoman foreign minister who signed it and launched the Tanzimat reforms a year later

pedagogy.hook: After 1838 it was cheaper to import British cloth into the Ottoman Empire than for an Ottoman merchant to move his own cloth across it.

misconception.belief: Free trade was a neutral principle that benefited everyone.
misconception.correction: Balta Liman capped Ottoman import duty at 5 per cent while leaving Ottoman traders paying 12 per cent to move goods internally. Free trade was written into treaties by the country with the most competitive industry, and the terms were not symmetrical.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single instrument of informal empire: no territory changed hands, no soldier landed, and a state lost the power to tax its own trade for eighty years.

evidence.author: Sevket Pamuk
evidence.work: The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism, 1820-1913
evidence.supports: The terms of the convention and its effects on Ottoman trade and industry.

events.title: European bondholders take over Ottoman taxes
events.summary: Six years after the Ottoman default, the Decree of Muharrem handed the revenues from salt, stamps, spirits, fish, silk and tobacco to a Public Debt Administration run by representatives of European bondholders, which collected them directly across the empire with its own staff.
events.significance: By 1911 it employed around 8,900 people, more than the Ottoman finance ministry. A sovereign empire's tax collectors worked for its foreign creditors, and it is the sharpest illustration anywhere of what debt can do that armies cannot.

places.name: Constantinople
places.note: Where the Debt Administration built its own headquarters, still standing as a school.

people.name: Vincent Caillard
people.role: British representative and president of the council of the Debt Administration in the 1880s and 1890s

people.name: Abdulhamid II
people.role: Sultan, who accepted the decree because no other terms were available and then used the restored credit to borrow again

evidence.author: Sevket Pamuk
evidence.work: The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism, 1820-1913
evidence.supports: The Decree of Muharrem, the Debt Administration's revenues and its staffing.

evidence.author: Donald Quataert
evidence.work: The Ottoman Empire, 1700-1922
evidence.supports: The place of the Debt Administration in Ottoman government and economy.

contested.note: Historians disagree about the Debt Administration's effects. Some treat it as a straightforward instrument of foreign control; others note that it stabilised Ottoman credit, improved tax collection and employed mainly Ottoman subjects. The staffing figure of about 8,900 in 1911 comes from its own annual reports.

events.title: The bombardment of Alexandria and the occupation of Egypt
events.summary: The Royal Navy shelled Alexandria for ten and a half hours; two months later Wolseley destroyed Ahmad Urabi's army at Tel el-Kebir in under an hour and British troops entered Cairo. Britain occupied Egypt while insisting it had not annexed anything.
events.significance: Informal empire turned formal in nine weeks. Britain occupied Egypt to secure the bondholders and the canal, promised repeatedly to withdraw, and stayed for 74 years. French resentment at being excluded set off the scramble for the rest of Africa.

places.name: Alexandria
places.note: Shelled on 11 July 1882; much of the European quarter burned in the fires that followed.

places.name: Tel el-Kebir
places.note: Where the Egyptian army was destroyed in a dawn attack on 13 September 1882.

people.name: Ahmad Urabi
people.role: Egyptian colonel who led the nationalist movement and the army; defeated, tried and exiled to Ceylon

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: commanded the invasion

people.name: William Ewart Gladstone
people.role: Prime Minister who ordered an occupation his own principles condemned

people.name: Beauchamp Seymour
people.role: admiral who ordered the bombardment of Alexandria

toll.note: Egyptian dead at Tel el-Kebir are usually estimated at about 2,000, from British reports; no Egyptian count was made. British losses there were 57 killed. Deaths in the Alexandria riots of 11 June and in the bombardment and fire of 11 July are separately estimated in the hundreds and are poorly documented.

pedagogy.hook: Gladstone's government occupied Egypt in 1882 promising to leave as soon as order allowed, and British troops finally left in June 1956.

misconception.belief: Britain annexed Egypt and made it a colony.
misconception.correction: Britain never annexed Egypt. From 1882 to 1914 Egypt remained legally an Ottoman province with its own ruler, government and flag, run in practice by a British consul-general with no constitutional authority whatever. A protectorate was declared only in 1914 and ended in 1922. Occupation and sovereignty are different things, and Britain used the difference deliberately.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case in the atlas of financial control hardening into military occupation, and of an empire taking a country while denying that it had done so.

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The decision to invade and its consequences for the partition of Africa.

evidence.author: Juan R. I. Cole
evidence.work: Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East: Social and Cultural Origins of Egypt's Urabi Movement
evidence.supports: The Urabi movement, its supporters and what it wanted.

contested.note: Why Britain invaded is one of the most argued questions in imperial history: strategy and a crisis on the periphery, as Robinson and Gallagher argue, or the protection of bondholders and the canal shares, as Cain and Hopkins argue. Both use the same cabinet papers.

events.title: The D'Arcy concession and Anglo-Persian oil
events.summary: A British speculator, William Knox D'Arcy, bought the right to search for oil across most of Persia for 20,000 pounds in cash, 20,000 in shares and 16 per cent of net profits. Oil was struck at Masjid-i-Suleiman in 1908, and the Anglo-Persian Oil Company followed a year later.
events.significance: In 1914 the British government bought a controlling share of the company, so the Royal Navy's fuel came from a concession over another country's ground held by a company the state part-owned. Britain's stake in Iranian oil ran until the nationalisation of 1951 and the coup that reversed it in 1953.

places.name: Masjid-i-Suleiman
places.note: Where oil was struck on 26 May 1908, the first commercial find in the Middle East.

places.name: Abadan refinery
places.note: Built from 1909; by the 1940s the largest refinery in the world.

people.name: William Knox D'Arcy
people.role: speculator who bought the concession with a fortune made in Australian gold

people.name: Mozaffar ad-Din Shah
people.role: Shah of Persia, who signed the concession to raise cash for a court in permanent deficit

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: First Lord of the Admiralty who converted the fleet from coal to oil and took the government's majority stake in the company in 1914

people.name: Mohammad Mosaddegh
people.role: Prime Minister who nationalised the company in 1951 and was removed in a British and American coup in August 1953

pedagogy.hook: Britain's navy ran on oil from a concession that covered most of Persia and paid the Persian government sixteen per cent of the profits.

misconception.belief: Britain's power in the Middle East came from ruling the region.
misconception.correction: Britain never ruled Persia. It held an oil concession, part-owned the company that worked it, kept troops in the south during two world wars and, in 1953, joined the United States in removing a prime minister who nationalised the company. Influence without sovereignty was the normal condition of British power in the Gulf, not the exception.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Oil is where informal empire outlived formal empire. The company became BP, the concession's terms were still resented in Iran fifty years later, and the coup of 1953 is still the single most cited grievance in Iranian accounts of the West.

evidence.author: Daniel Yergin
evidence.work: The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money and Power
evidence.supports: The D'Arcy concession, the founding of Anglo-Persian and the British government's stake.

evidence.author: Ervand Abrahamian
evidence.work: The Coup: 1953, the CIA, and the Roots of Modern U.S.-Iranian Relations
evidence.supports: The nationalisation of 1951 and the overthrow of Mosaddegh in 1953.

events.title: Europe partitions the Sultan of Zanzibar's mainland
events.summary: A British, German and French commission decided that the Sultan of Zanzibar's mainland dominions amounted to a coastal strip ten miles deep and a few inland towns. Britain and Germany then divided the interior behind it between themselves by agreement.
events.significance: An African state's territory was measured and reduced by a commission of European officials, and the strip that survived was leased to the British East Africa Company in 1888. Zanzibar itself became a British protectorate in 1890, traded for Heligoland in the same treaty.

places.name: Zanzibar Town
places.note: Capital of a sultanate that had claimed the coast from Mogadishu to Cape Delgado.

places.name: Mombasa
places.note: On the ten-mile coastal strip, leased from the Sultan and only ceded to Kenya at independence in 1963.

people.name: Barghash bin Said
people.role: Sultan of Zanzibar, whose mainland claims the commission cut down and who died in 1888

people.name: John Kirk
people.role: British consul at Zanzibar for two decades, whose influence over the Sultan was the model of protectorate-by-advice

pedagogy.hook: Three European governments sat down in 1886 and decided how much of East Africa the Sultan of Zanzibar was allowed to own.

misconception.belief: Before Europeans arrived, East Africa had no states, only peoples.
misconception.correction: The Sultanate of Zanzibar was a maritime state with a currency, a customs service, consulates from four continents and commercial reach from Mogadishu to the Congo. Britain spent decades governing East Africa through it, and then cut it down to a ten-mile strip when it wanted the interior directly.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is a precise example of informal empire in its African form: not conquest but advice, leases and commissions, exercised over a real state until nothing of the state was left but a coastline.

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The Anglo-German partition of East Africa and the use of the Sultan's authority to justify it.

evidence.author: Abdul Sheriff
evidence.work: Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar: Integration of an East African Commercial Empire into the World Economy, 1770-1873
evidence.supports: The extent and workings of the Zanzibari commercial state before the partition.

events.title: The Royal Navy bombards Kagoshima
events.summary: Seven British warships shelled Kagoshima to force Satsuma to pay an indemnity for the killing of the merchant Charles Richardson on the highway a year earlier. Much of the town burned. Within two years Satsuma was buying British ships and sending students to London.
events.significance: It is the sharpest short lesson in what the treaty system meant: a fleet could burn a Japanese city over the death of one Englishman. It is also the sharpest lesson in what Japan did about it, which was to buy the technology, overthrow its own government and rebuild the state.

places.name: Kagoshima
places.note: Capital of the Satsuma domain; much of it burned in the bombardment.

places.name: Namamugi
places.note: On the Tokaido road, where Charles Richardson was killed on 14 September 1862 for failing to give way to a daimyo's procession.

people.name: Augustus Leopold Kuper
people.role: British admiral who commanded the bombardment

people.name: Shimazu Hisamitsu
people.role: de facto ruler of Satsuma, whose retainers killed Richardson and who afterwards allied with Britain

people.name: Charles Lennox Richardson
people.role: Shanghai merchant whose killing on the Tokaido road provoked the bombardment

toll.note: Japanese deaths are variously reported from about five to several dozen, with most of the destruction falling on property; British losses were 13 killed, including two captains. No reliable Japanese count of civilian deaths in the fires exists.

evidence.author: Marius B. Jansen
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Japan
evidence.supports: The killing of Charles Richardson at Namamugi, the bombardment of Kagoshima and the Anglo-Satsuma alliance that followed.

events.title: Japan takes back its own courts
events.summary: The Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, signed in London on 16 July 1894, came into force five years later and abolished British consular jurisdiction in Japan. From that day a British subject who committed a crime in Japan was tried by a Japanese court.
events.significance: Japan is the only state in this atlas that entered the European treaty system and negotiated its way out. It did so by rewriting its legal codes to European specifications, which shows both how the system worked and what it cost to escape it.

places.name: Yokohama
places.note: The main foreign settlement, garrisoned by British and French troops from 1863 to 1875 and returned to Japanese jurisdiction in 1899.

people.name: Mutsu Munemitsu
people.role: foreign minister who directed the revision campaign

people.name: Aoki Shuzo
people.role: minister in London who signed the treaty

people.name: John Wodehouse, Earl of Kimberley
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who agreed to give up extraterritoriality first among the powers

pedagogy.hook: To get its own courts back, Japan rewrote its entire legal system so that Europeans would have nothing left to object to.

misconception.belief: Unequal treaties were permanent and only ended when empires collapsed.
misconception.correction: Japan ended its own in 1899 by negotiation, and completed the job with tariff autonomy in 1911. It took forty years, a constitution, new criminal, civil and commercial codes, a modern army and a war with China. The treaty system could be escaped, and the price was becoming the kind of state that had written it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the control case for every argument about informal empire. Comparing Japan with the Ottoman Empire, China, Persia and Siam is the best way to see what the treaty system determined and what it did not.

evidence.author: Michael R. Auslin
evidence.work: Negotiating with Imperialism: The Unequal Treaties and the Culture of Japanese Diplomacy
evidence.supports: The revision campaign and how Japanese diplomats used the treaty system to end it.

events.title: The capture of Havana
events.summary: A fleet of more than fifty warships and an army of over eleven thousand men besieged Havana for ten weeks, mined and stormed the Morro castle on 30 July, and took the richest port in the Spanish Americas on 13 August 1762.
events.significance: It won the largest prize money in British naval history and cost about 5,366 British lives, almost all to yellow fever. Britain gave the city back five months later in exchange for Florida, and the eleven months of open trade turned Cuba into a sugar and slavery economy.

places.name: Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro
places.note: The fortress that held for 44 days and was taken by mining the ditch.

people.name: George Keppel, Earl of Albemarle
people.role: commanded the army and governed the city; took over 122,000 pounds in prize money

people.name: Luis Vicente de Velasco e Isla
people.role: Spanish captain who held the Morro for 44 days and was killed at the breach

people.name: Pepe Antonio
people.role: Jose Antonio Gomez, militia captain from Guanabacoa who led irregular resistance and became a Cuban folk hero

toll.note: British dead during the siege and occupation are usually given as about 5,366, of whom roughly 560 were killed in action; the rest died of yellow fever and dysentery. Spanish military and civilian losses were never fully counted.

pedagogy.hook: At Havana the Spanish killed about 560 British soldiers. The mosquitoes killed roughly 4,800.

misconception.belief: European armies conquered the tropics because they had better weapons.
misconception.correction: Until the twentieth century, disease decided tropical campaigns. Nine out of ten British deaths at Havana were from yellow fever and dysentery, and the same pattern held in the Caribbean for two centuries. It is the main reason Europeans held islands with fleets and garrisons rather than settling them in numbers.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Havana shows the imperial map as a portfolio to be traded. Britain returned the greatest port in Spanish America, and Manila with it, and kept Canada and Florida instead.

evidence.author: Elena A. Schneider
evidence.work: The Occupation of Havana: War, Trade, and Slavery in the Atlantic World
evidence.supports: The siege, the occupation, the slave trade it opened and the role of Havana's free black militias.

evidence.author: David Syrett
evidence.work: The Siege and Capture of Havana, 1762
evidence.supports: The expedition's own documents, including casualty returns and prize accounts.

events.title: The Nootka crisis
events.summary: Spain seized British fur-trading ships and a post at Friendly Cove on Vancouver Island. Britain mobilised the fleet and Parliament voted a million pounds; France, in revolution, would not support Spain, and Spain gave way in the Nootka Conventions.
events.significance: It destroyed the Spanish doctrine that discovery and papal grant gave title to the Pacific, and replaced it with the rule that only effective occupation counts. Britain then used that rule against Russia in 1825 and against the United States in the Oregon settlement of 1846.

places.name: Yuquot, Friendly Cove
places.note: The Mowachaht village where both empires built and both abandoned; occupied for over 4,000 years.

people.name: Maquinna
people.role: Mowachaht chief on whose land the dispute took place and who was not a party to any of the three conventions

people.name: Esteban Jose Martinez
people.role: Spanish commander who seized the British vessels

people.name: John Meares
people.role: trader whose memorial to Parliament, uncorroborated and self-interested, was the basis of Britain's war threat

people.name: Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra
people.role: Spanish commissioner who negotiated with Vancouver in 1792; the two men could not agree what was to be restored and named the island for them both

pedagogy.hook: Britain and Spain nearly fought a world war in 1790 over a house on a beach in a village that had belonged to the Mowachaht for four thousand years.

misconception.belief: European powers claimed land by discovering it.
misconception.correction: That was the Spanish position and Britain destroyed it at Nootka. The conventions of 1790-94 established that only actual occupation creates title, which is why Britain went on to plant settlements rather than plant flags, and why the doctrine of terra nullius mattered so much in Australia thirty years later.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: A crisis over one cove set the legal rule Britain used to claim the Pacific coast, and neither empire asked the people who owned the cove.

evidence.author: Warren L. Cook
evidence.work: Flood Tide of Empire: Spain and the Pacific Northwest, 1543-1819
evidence.supports: The seizure, the crisis and the three Nootka Conventions.

evidence.author: Daniel Clayton
evidence.work: Islands of Truth: The Imperial Fashioning of Vancouver Island
evidence.supports: The Nuu-chah-nulth context and what Maquinna's people made of the European quarrel.

contested.note: Whether Meares had bought any land from Maquinna is unresolved and probably unresolvable: his own account was written to support a compensation claim, Spanish officers denied it, and Maquinna is recorded as saying he had granted use, not ownership.

events.title: The Paulet affair: Britain rules Hawaii for five months
events.summary: Lord George Paulet brought a frigate into Honolulu, threatened to bombard the town over a consul's land claims, and took the cession of the Hawaiian Kingdom. Kamehameha III signed under protest and appealed to London; an admiral arrived in July, disowned Paulet and gave the kingdom back.
events.significance: The episode pushed Britain and France into declaring Hawaiian independence in November 1843, the first such recognition given to a non-European state. That declaration is still cited in the legal arguments of the Hawaiian sovereignty movement against the American annexation of 1898.

places.name: Honolulu
places.note: Where the Carysfort's guns were trained on the town.

places.name: Thomas Square, Honolulu
places.note: Named for the admiral who restored the kingdom on 31 July 1843; the restoration is still marked there every year.

people.name: Kamehameha III, Kauikeaouli
people.role: King who ceded under written protest and got the kingdom back in five months

people.name: George Paulet
people.role: captain who took the kingdom with no authority from his government

people.name: Richard Thomas
people.role: admiral who reversed his own captain and restored Hawaiian sovereignty

people.name: Timoteo Haalilio
people.role: Hawaiian envoy who secured recognition of the kingdom's independence in Washington, London and Paris, and died on the voyage home

pedagogy.hook: Hawaii was a British colony for five months and six days in 1843, and Britain gave it back.

misconception.belief: The Union Jack on Hawaii's flag means Hawaii was a British colony.
misconception.correction: The Union Jack has been in the corner of the Hawaiian flag since about 1816, when Kamehameha I adopted it as a mark of friendship with Britain. Britain did hold the kingdom, but for five months in 1843, on one captain's initiative, and the British government reversed the seizure and then recognised Hawaiian independence.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire's improvisation and its brakes in the same episode: a captain could take a country and an admiral could give it back, and the whole thing turned on how quickly letters crossed the Pacific.

evidence.author: Ralph S. Kuykendall
evidence.work: The Hawaiian Kingdom, Volume 1: 1778-1854, Foundation and Transformation
evidence.supports: The cession, the commission's five months of rule, the restoration and the 1843 recognition.

evidence.author: Jonathan Kay Kamakawiwoole Osorio
evidence.work: Dismembering Lahui: A History of the Hawaiian Nation to 1887
evidence.supports: The Hawaiian view of the crisis and its place in the kingdom's constitutional history.

events.title: The Treaty of Breda: Suriname for New York
events.summary: The treaty ending the second Anglo-Dutch war left each side holding what it held. The Dutch kept Suriname, which they had taken from England in March 1667; England kept New Netherland, which it had taken in 1664 and renamed New York.
events.significance: It is remembered as the swap that gave England New York, but nobody traded one for the other: Breda simply confirmed possession. At the time the sugar colony looked like the better asset, and most English commentators thought their side had lost the exchange.

places.name: Breda
places.note: Where the treaty was signed.

places.name: Fort Willoughby, later Fort Zeelandia
places.note: The English fort at the mouth of the Suriname river, captured by a Zeeland squadron in early 1667.

people.name: Abraham Crijnssen
people.role: Zeeland commander who took the colony in a single afternoon, flying English colours to get within range

people.name: Johan de Witt
people.role: Grand Pensionary of Holland, who directed Dutch policy and valued Suriname's sugar over a fur-trading town on the Hudson

pedagogy.hook: England did not swap Suriname for New York. It kept what it was holding, the Dutch kept what they were holding, and at the time the Dutch looked like the winners.

misconception.belief: England cleverly traded a worthless swamp in South America for Manhattan.
misconception.correction: Breda worked on the principle of keeping what each side held. Suriname was a going sugar colony with forty or fifty plantations and about three thousand people; New Amsterdam was a fur post of around 1,500. In 1667 sugar was the most valuable commodity in the Atlantic world, and contemporaries thought England had come off worse.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is a warning against reading history backwards. The value of a colony in 1667 is not its value in 1900, and imperial decisions look brilliant or stupid only in hindsight.

evidence.author: Wim Klooster
evidence.work: The Dutch Moment: War, Trade, and Settlement in the Seventeenth-Century Atlantic World
evidence.supports: The Zeeland expedition, the terms of Breda and the relative value of the two colonies.

evidence.author: Matthew Parker
evidence.work: Willoughbyland: England's Lost Colony
evidence.supports: The English colony on the Suriname river and how it was lost.

events.title: The sack of Balambangan

date.note: Accounts give either 26 February or 5 March 1775, probably because Company clerks were still using the Old Style calendar.

events.summary: A Sulu force under Datu Teteng stormed the East India Company's stockade on Balambangan at night, killed several Europeans, looted the warehouses and burned the settlement. The survivors escaped by sea to Labuan and Brunei, and the Company abandoned the island.
events.significance: The Company's attempt at an eastern entrepot for the China trade failed after fifteen months. The role went to Penang in 1786 and Singapore in 1819. What survived was the paperwork: Sulu grants that the British North Borneo Company invoked in 1878 and that the Philippines still cites in its claim to Sabah.

places.name: Balambangan Island
places.note: A low island off the northern tip of Borneo, chosen for its position between the Sulu Sea and the South China Sea.

people.name: Datu Teteng
people.role: Sulu leader who led the assault

people.name: John Herbert
people.role: the Company chief whose private trading and mismanagement left the settlement indefensible; he escaped

people.name: Alexander Dalrymple
people.role: the Company servant who had negotiated the Sulu grants and whose scheme this was

toll.note: Accounts give a handful of Europeans killed and an unrecorded number of Asian employees and Sulu attackers dead. The Company documented the goods it lost, valued at around 375,000 pounds in its own claim, far more carefully than the people.

pedagogy.hook: The East India Company's plan for a great free port in the Sulu Sea lasted fifteen months and ended in one night.

misconception.belief: The East India Company's expansion was a steady advance.
misconception.correction: It failed constantly. Balambangan was burned down in 1775 and abandoned again in 1805; Bencoolen never paid; the Company was driven out of Java, out of the Moluccas and repeatedly out of Sumatra. The successes we remember, Penang, Singapore, Hong Kong, were selected by survival, not by design.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows that empire's archive outlasts its settlements. Nothing British remained on Balambangan after 1805 except three signed grants, and those grants are still argued over in an international dispute between Malaysia and the Philippines.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Sulu and Sabah: A Study of British Policy towards the Philippines and North Borneo from the late Eighteenth Century
evidence.supports: The settlement, the attack and the long afterlife of the Sulu grants.

contested.note: The date of the attack and the value of the goods lost are both uncertain, and the legal meaning of the Sulu grants of 1762-64 is disputed to this day in the Malaysia-Philippines argument over Sabah.

events.title: The South Georgia sealing rush
events.summary: Eleven years after Cook reported seals on South Georgia, British and American sealers began working its beaches. In four decades they took an estimated 1.2 million fur seal skins for the Canton market and left the species commercially extinct.
events.significance: It is the first industrial extraction event in the Southern Ocean and the reason Britain later thought the sector worth claiming. It also set the pattern the whalers repeated a century later: find a resource, exhaust it in forty years, move on.

places.name: South Georgia
places.note: The beaches worked by sealing gangs left ashore for a season at a time.

people.name: James Cook
people.role: whose published journal of 1777 told the sealing trade where to go

people.name: James Weddell
people.role: British sealing master who recorded the collapse of the fur seal population and pushed further south, reaching 74 degrees in 1823

pedagogy.hook: About 1.2 million fur seals were killed on one sub-Antarctic island in forty years, and the survivors were down to a few dozen animals.

misconception.belief: Environmental destruction on this scale is a modern problem.
misconception.correction: The South Georgia fur seal was hunted to commercial extinction between 1786 and 1825, using sailing ships and clubs, to supply hats and coats to China and Europe. The whales followed between 1904 and 1965. The seals have since recovered to millions; the great whales have not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Empire is usually taught as a story about people ruling people. Some of it was a story about extracting animals, and the South Atlantic is where that is clearest.

evidence.author: Robert K. Headland
evidence.work: The Island of South Georgia
evidence.supports: The sealing period, the cargo estimates and the collapse of the population.

contested.note: The figure of about 1.2 million skins is reconstructed from surviving cargo manifests and captains' logs, which cover only part of the trade; American sealers in particular kept their grounds secret. The true total is likely higher.

events.title: The Anglo-French intervention in the River Plate
events.summary: Britain and France intervened in Uruguay's civil war, keeping Montevideo supplied and defended through a siege that lasted eight years, and blockading Buenos Aires to force open the rivers to their shipping. Giuseppe Garibaldi commanded the Italian Legion inside the city.
events.significance: It is informal empire using warships without taking territory: Britain fought in the River Plate for eight years and claimed not one acre. It also failed. Rosas outlasted the blockade, and Britain signed a treaty in 1849 that apologised and saluted the Argentine flag.

places.name: Montevideo
places.note: Besieged from 1843 to 1851 and supplied by the Anglo-French squadrons.

places.name: Vuelta de Obligado
places.note: Where the Argentine batteries fought the Anglo-French convoy up the Parana on 20 November 1845.

people.name: Juan Manuel de Rosas
people.role: governor of Buenos Aires who resisted the blockade for six years and outlasted it

people.name: Giuseppe Garibaldi
people.role: commanded the Italian Legion in the defence of Montevideo, where the red shirts were first worn

people.name: Lucio Norberto Mansilla
people.role: Argentine general who commanded the chains and batteries at the Vuelta de Obligado

pedagogy.hook: Britain blockaded Buenos Aires for six years to force open a river, lost the argument, and signed a treaty in 1849 that saluted the Argentine flag by way of apology.

misconception.belief: Informal empire meant Britain always got its way in Latin America without fighting.
misconception.correction: Britain fought in the River Plate for eight years, blockaded a capital, forced a convoy up the Parana under fire in November 1845, and eventually gave up. Argentina still marks 20 November as its Day of National Sovereignty. Informal empire had limits, and this is where Britain found them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the counterweight to the argument that Argentina was a British dependency. A dependency does not force a great power to apologise.

evidence.author: John Lynch
evidence.work: Argentine Dictator: Juan Manuel de Rosas 1829-1852
evidence.supports: The Anglo-French blockade, the Vuelta de Obligado and the settlement of 1849-50.

events.title: Shots at Hope Bay and huts at Deception Island
events.summary: Argentine troops fired machine-gun bursts over a British party landing at Hope Bay in February 1952. A year later British marines removed Argentine and Chilean huts from Deception Island and deported two Argentines. In 1955 Britain took both states to the International Court, and both refused to appear.
events.significance: This is what an unresolved territorial dispute looks like when three states each build huts to prove occupation. It is also why the Antarctic Treaty was possible: everyone could see where the argument was heading, and nobody wanted a war over ice.

places.name: Hope Bay
places.note: Where Argentine soldiers fired over the heads of a British landing party on 1 February 1952.

places.name: Deception Island
places.note: A flooded volcanic caldera used as a harbour by whalers, and by three states as a place to plant huts.

people.name: Juan Peron
people.role: President of Argentina, whose government pushed the Antarctic claim hard in the late 1940s and early 1950s

people.name: Anthony Eden
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who authorised taking Argentina and Chile to the International Court of Justice in 1955

pedagogy.hook: The only shots fired in anger in Antarctica were fired by Argentine soldiers over the heads of British scientists in 1952.

misconception.belief: The International Court of Justice can settle territorial disputes.
misconception.correction: Only if the states involved agree to appear. Britain filed cases against Argentina and Chile in 1955; both declined the court's jurisdiction and the cases were struck out in 1956. International courts have no power to compel a state that has not accepted them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains why the Antarctic Treaty took the form it did. Law could not settle the claims and force was unthinkable, so the parties agreed instead to suspend the question indefinitely.

evidence.author: Peter J. Beck
evidence.work: The International Politics of Antarctica
evidence.supports: The incidents of 1952-53, the ICJ applications of 1955 and their dismissal in 1956.

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The Anglo-Argentine and Anglo-Chilean rivalry in the Antarctic Peninsula.

events.title: Britain names Queen Elizabeth Land
events.summary: The Foreign Secretary announced that the southern part of the British Antarctic Territory, some 437,000 square kilometres, would be named Queen Elizabeth Land for the Diamond Jubilee. Argentina summoned the British ambassador in Buenos Aires the next day.
events.significance: It shows that Antarctic claims are alive, not historical. Sixty-three years after the Antarctic Treaty froze the argument, Britain was still asserting its sector by naming it, and Argentina was still protesting; naming is one of the few sovereign acts the treaty does not clearly forbid.

places.name: Queen Elizabeth Land
places.note: The area between the South Pole and the British claim's northern sectors, named in 2012.

people.name: William Hague
people.role: Foreign Secretary who announced the naming

people.name: Hector Timerman
people.role: Argentine foreign minister who protested and called it a throwback to colonialism

evidence.author: Klaus Dodds
evidence.work: Pink Ice: Britain and the South Atlantic Empire
evidence.supports: The pattern of British symbolic assertions in the South Atlantic and Antarctic and the Argentine responses to them.

events.title: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance
events.summary: Britain signed a defensive alliance with Japan, its first with a non-European power and its first formal alliance of any kind in decades. Each promised neutrality if the other went to war with one power, and help if it faced two.
events.significance: Three years after abolishing its consular courts in Japan, Britain made Japan a partner. The alliance covered the Japanese fleet Britain had largely built, was used by Japan against Russia in 1904-05 and to seize German possessions in 1914, and was dropped in 1923 under American pressure.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the alliance was signed at the Foreign Office.

places.name: Barrow-in-Furness
places.note: Where the Japanese flagship Mikasa was built, launched in 1900.

people.name: Hayashi Tadasu
people.role: Japanese minister in London who negotiated and signed the alliance

people.name: Henry Petty-Fitzmaurice, Marquess of Lansdowne
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who signed it, ending Britain's policy of standing alone

pedagogy.hook: In 1863 the Royal Navy burned a Japanese city. In 1902 Britain signed a defensive alliance with Japan, and in 1905 the fleet Britain had built destroyed the Russian navy.

misconception.belief: European powers treated Asian states as inferiors throughout the imperial era.
misconception.correction: The 1902 alliance was between formal equals, and it was Britain that needed it: overstretched, worried about Russia in China and unable to hold the Far East alone. Japan had made itself into the kind of state Britain would ally with, and then used the alliance to take Korea and Germany's Pacific colonies.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It marks the moment the treaty-port system stopped being a one-way arrangement, and it is the clearest evidence that informal empire could be escaped by a state that reorganised itself thoroughly enough.

evidence.author: Marius B. Jansen
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Japan
evidence.supports: The alliance, its uses and its abandonment in 1923.

events.title: St Helena builds an airport
events.summary: Britain spent about 285 million pounds building an airport on St Helena to end the island's dependence on a single mail ship. The runway opened to wind shear so severe that the first scheduled flights were cancelled; a smaller aircraft began flying in October 2017.
events.significance: It is the modern shape of the imperial residue: fourteen British Overseas Territories, most of them tiny, subsidised because Britain has not decided what else to do with them. St Helena's airport cost roughly 64,000 pounds for every resident on the island.

places.name: St Helena Airport, Prosperous Bay Plain
places.note: Built on the plain above the cliffs where Munden's men had landed in 1673.

people.name: Andrew Mitchell
people.role: the International Development Secretary whose department approved the airport contract in 2011

pedagogy.hook: Britain spent about 285 million pounds on an airport for 4,500 people, and the wind was too strong for the aircraft it was designed for.

misconception.belief: The British Empire ended in the 1960s.
misconception.correction: Fourteen British Overseas Territories remain, with about 270,000 people between them, most of them in Bermuda and the Cayman Islands.
